Revision 0: February 5, 2012.
Country of publication: India. Hariḥ Om.
By that [merit], may these indeed be for the disciple; Om Ī Phaṭ, and [may there be] the opening of the eyes.
And those which are *viniś*, *bhānt*, *haścanyetā*, and *catuḥ*.
One should place the syllables *jña*, *rva*, *śca*, *ma*, and *śca* in sequence upon the feet; then *pi*, *gri*, *sthi*, *śca*, *mamū*, *ya*, *śca*, *yo*, *ni*, *vā*, *tañ*, and *ca phi*.
Pu, va, sañ, ca, mu, va, śa, rpi, śa, sā, ga, va, sa,
and na— these are known as the deities to be placed in the second enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Vyāna, āsana, na, da, mukta, and aśvaru;
the half-and-a-quarter [unit] is the upward lotus, while the height of the neck is six parts.
Kampantī is one and a half parts, and the neck-joint belongs to Śaṅkara.
The height of the dome (kumucchraya) should be half of five parts; thus is the spire (syūpi) described. In this very manner, one should then have the temple (prāsāda) constructed.
An ardhamanṭapa is prescribed with a measurement equal to half that of the prāsāda.
This work is incomplete. Hariḥ Om.
The Yoga-jāgama.

Therefore, for the sake of success, one should indeed utter these four syllables: *om*, *mī*, *phaṭ*, and *na*; and likewise *nayana*, *prara-i*, *ninīśiś*, and *bhānta*—these are the four groups. || 1 ||
One should place the syllables *jña*, *rva*, *śca*, *ma*, and *śca* in sequence upon the feet; then *pi*, *gri*, *sthi*, *śca*, *mamū*, *ya*, *śca*, *yo*, *ni*, *vā*, *tañ*, and *ca phi*. (2)
Pu, va, sa, ca, mu, śa, va, sa, rpi, sa, ga, va, sa, and na—these are known as the [syllables] to be placed in the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa). || 3 ||
Vyāna, āsana, na, da, mukta, aśvarū, veścarū,
ti-de-sva, and śivaye-bhasmadaśvanā. (4)
One should write KṢA, PA, and VA in the third row;
likewise, GURU, YA, OṂ, BHŪTA, PRETĪ, CA, and NĀ. || 5 ||
The letters beginning with *a*, *oṃ*, *pa*, *śca*, *te*, *ta*, *ṛ*, *pu*, *śca*, and *añcasā*;
and *ga* and *śīra*—their placement is in the fourth enclosure.
Sayavīra, Rajāgo, Jyotāpit, Kiñca, Aścava, Aśvahāpaśva, Śi, Ya, and Sagu. || 7 ||
In the fifth [chapter], the destruction of passion is described:
"Just as for one who is to be known through passion, by whomsoever it is offered, it is not consumed by the earth."
Mayirvasu, Vasthi, Gasuvā, and Pānāyāha are in the sixth position; then there are Aścadyoṃ, Hyotā, Aśca, and Aścaja. (9)
The sounds, the winds, or the number are not recited in sequence; the ends of the days, those to be understood through existence, the cows, the waters, and the rivers [are likewise]. 10.
Maśca te prasaścaiva, the twenty-sixth is the peaceful state, Śa;
Nenaśā, Yo, Vṛṣaścaiva, Guṃguṃ, and the terrible Dyāśca te.
The *ayūnī*, the *mahāmad*, the *bahavaḥ*, the *mataḥ*, and the *vaśca*—these are the names for the eleven *padas*; the fruit of all these belongs to the self. 12.
Pi, tsa, ya, va, and ru, as well as the fifth, pa;
vya, pa, pa, tsa, and mitha, as well as the one whose nature is Mīna (the Fish), and na. 13.
Si, bha, bra, and staruṣan are in the twelfth step.
(p. 4) Śudhyāyavadyaṃ supudena sumedhyaḥ prataddhura. (14)
Pravorava, Astunāśca, Oṃ, in the thirteenth step; Pāyūniya, Tattmaśca, Yaramin, Ma, and Anāni. 15.
Paścañca, Bhakata, Rujña—these are the fourteen;
Vyośiya, Vāya, Nānādya, and Ya also. || 16 ||
With *nāśca*, *aścaryamuśca*, *pathyaiśca*, *cunastvaśca*, and *sa*, the meter in the fifteenth [chapter] is thus known as *vyomavyāpin*. || 17 ||
Make the mantras "vyomavyāpi" and so forth consist of the nature of space;
make the great mantra "vyomavyāpi" its seer (ṛṣi), its meter (chandas), and its deity.
Agastya is the seer (ṛṣi), the Triṣṭubh is the meter (chanda), and Īśvara is the deity there.
Now, I shall state the extraction of the Sadyojāta mantras. (19)
The wheel, situated as the limb of Śiva and devoid of the seven enclosures, should be worshipped with the root mantra; one should then place the *praṇava* as the illuminator.
Having established the syllable *mi* there, it is indeed with the *visarga*;
likewise, *ve*, *va*, with the *visarga*, *mokṣa*, and *vaśaka*. || 21 ||
The letters *m*, *n*, and *y*; the nasals (*manābhyas*); the *visarga*;
*r* and *t* with the *visarga*; and likewise *st*, *d*, *h*, *n*, and *s*. (22)
It is remembered as *ī*, *ca*, *mī*, *ca*, likewise *bru*, *ca*, the letter *śa*, *vo*, and *ca*;
then *dyānabhak*, *bha*, *ca*, *na*, *drā*, *ca*, together with the letter *ma* and the *visarga*. (23)

The letter *na* with the vowel *e*, the letter *ca* with the vowel *ra*, the letter *na* with the vowel *a*, the letter *da* with the vowel *e* joined with *sarva*, the letter *ma* with the visarga, and likewise *tat* and *mantra*. (24)
Oṃkāra, Tākāra, Namā, Śīkara, Paśca, Vaiśca, Ya, Yaśca, Ru, and Naya as well. || 25 ||
Ṇa-tha-taṃ and ma-na-ya-u-ś-ca, va-s-y-o-ś-ca, and sa-ś-ca-na-e-va-ca;
oṃ svaṃ ha phaś-ca, yā-nyā-ta, and likewise bra-hma-tā-ś-ca. || 26 ||
Pra, ya, and likewise nābha, vāma, and also yāra;
ma, bhūma, and from these [comes] sa, along with visarga and āma. || 27 ||
The letters *ma*, *da*, and *vibhūti* are recited in sequence;
likewise, *ta*, *tā*, and *amāndena*, as well as the letter *lā*. (28)
Parvata, and likewise Moḥ, Oṃ Ghoreḥpa, and indeed Peḥ; Viśca, and likewise Adhī, Corvaṣṭa, and Vastu as well. (29)
Jājābha, Sva, likewise Rakaṃpa, Phalasa, Namasya, and Sañcarū. (30)
With "yaya," one should place *prasasa* and *thīpu* as the sixth step;
thus, for the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, there shall be one hundred [syllables] ending in the *bindu*. || 31 ||
The first two syllables are *dyo* and *dyo*, followed by *yaja*, *pāṣāmavilana*, *ṣādavāḥ*, *nīcaiva*, *varaṇeñcaiva*, *saptame*, *saha*, and *bha*;
this mantra of thirty-one syllables consists of six groups of sixty-six [units]. || 33 ||
The Aghora mantra, joined with thirty-six [syllables], the Puruṣa with twenty-four,
and the Īśvara with thirty-three, all combined with the Praṇava. (34)
Now the seers, meters, and deities shall be fully declared:
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Atri. (35)
Parāśara—these five are called the Ṛṣis beginning with Sadyojāta; the meters are Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Āryā, and Vṛtta. (36)
Gāyatrī and these five are known as the meters (chandas) beginning with Sadyojāta;
[their presiding deities are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. || 37 ||
The five states of Sadyojāta and the others have thus been proclaimed;
and the essence of the four Vedas—Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan—is contained therein. (38)
The extraction of the *sadya* and other mantras is declared to be "breaking" (*bhañjya*).
That which is called *gandhabrahma* is remembered as "to be broken" (*bhajya*) in its constituent parts (*aṅga*). (39)
The subtle form of Śiva, preceded by the subtle syllable Oṃ, is said to reside within the gross form that is Brahmā; the gross form is Sadāśiva. (40)
Having placed the wheel in the east without the four enclosures:
Oṃ, Kāra, Śca, Ya-vo-śi, Ca, Te, Śu-ya, and again Phaṭ. (41)
The letter *śa*, likewise again, and further still another; at the end of *sā* there is *sa-ka-sā* again, followed by *va-ja-ja-sa* with the visarga. (42)
Then *ha*, *ta*, *ca*, *ca*, *ga*, *ya*, and likewise *anta* (the letter *m*);
and similarly here, *vāra* (the letter *ra*), followed by *sau* (the letter *sa*) with a long vowel as the second [element]. (43)
The syllable *pu*, the syllable *ra*, and the extensive expansion of the syllable *ha*;
the syllable *ṛ*, the phoneme at the end of the mountain (*parvaya*), and then the syllable *i* followed by the *praṇava*. (44)
Furthermore, at the end of the *carmayā*, one should lead [the breath] again; likewise, there are the *randhyanajña* and the two *hiks*.
Then there are the *daśapra*, the *tathāga*, the *heścamriya*, and finally the *anta*. (45)
By the emission of the *puka-pramā* [vibration], the semen becomes tawny; when released, it causes one to enter the state of the sixth path, which is the abode of the compassionate Śiva. 46.
Furthermore, the letter *ka* and the letter *ha*, moving in sequence, [form] *yakrama*;
then the letter *la*, the letter *tu*, and the letter *cha*, in the path of the *parunā* [are placed]. (47)
Randhrimā, Makara, Ha, and then Ca; Sa, Sā, Hvūya, Taṃ, Hyā, Kilikeśa, and likewise Ya. || 48 ||
Meghanāda, Cakraprāñc,
Uśvan, Svaśau, Śiyavāvākṣu, Vipārucā, and Ma— these are my [sons]. (49)
Kaṭya, Yajvattasūrya, and Ramās; then indeed Prahapralihaśiṣyā and Sataghāta—these are the fourteen.
May the sin of our two-fold transgression not cause us to cease from devotion;
may we, through the command of our own self-knowledge, again attain the state of the Knower.
The syllable *ya*, followed by *kā-ra* and *va-no-hā-śca-ve-dha-ṣṭhā-ca-nu-sta-taḥ*; then *khā-cā-nta-punargā-ca-ha-śca-mo-ca*, and thereafter the syllable *akṣara*. (52)
Then the syllables *marutaḥ*, *tarutaḥ*, *praśca*, and *yayostu*; then *śikamāstataḥ*; likewise there, *vakāraḥ*, *haḥ*, *yaḥ*, and *yavaḥ* followed. (53)
Then again, from that [syllable], there are *yod*, *gate*, and *eva*, as well as *prajñā* and *ca*;
furthermore, *huṃ*, *dau*, *punaḥ*, *tataḥ*, *gamo*, *svātmā*, *ca*, *vandaḥ*, *ca*, *śastaṅgaḥ*, *ca*, and *phaṭ*. (54)
"Saṃ" and "saṃ" likewise, "hāpa" and "ka," "ma" and "śa," "ca" and "ni," "bha" and "u," "ta" and "tha," as well as "utkāra," the two joints, and the *praṇava* itself. (55)
The syllables *magau*, *balatathā*, and those beginning with *gamajuṅkāra*,
as well as *anante*, *vāsuge*, *labdhajuhū*, and the varieties of the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
The All-Self, the heart of the Omniscient One, has seventy eyes;
one should again extract [the letters] in sequence from the syllable Oṃ to the letter Ha.
Therefore, one should extract the auspicious eight-syllable mantra from that;
then, after the letter *jva*, one should extract the eleven-syllable *Śivā* from the *Tārā*. (58)
From that, the syllable *ṣaṃ* is the yellow (*piṅgala*) among the vowels;
then follows the Aghora-weapon mantra, characterized by thirty-two syllables. (59)
Likewise, one should extract the twenty-four *gāyatrīs* in their proper sequence;
from that, one should know the three-syllabled "Eye" (*netra*), which is the supreme abode of names.
This has been described according to the divisions of the heart and other parts, bestowing both spiritual accomplishment and liberation.
Thus the limb of Śiva has been described; now the characteristics of Brahman are stated.
One should install the five names of the five [faces] located at the stages of the word-Brahman (padabrahma). 62.

In the fourth [case], there are three [words]; the middle one ends with *hā* and *āhā*, while the first and last end with the expression of the object of desire; however, the names themselves end in case-endings.
The Śaiva [mantra] consists of sixty-eight syllables; thereafter, following the letter *ta*, there is the "Heart" (*hārda*) as the fifth, which is then diffused throughout the thirty directions. (64)
Then again, the second [syllable] is the syllable *ī*, which is the merged form of Śiva;
thereafter, one should communicate that five-syllabled [mantra] ending in the dative case. 65.

The nineteenth [syllable] is the left one; likewise, the syllable ending in *e* and the syllable *man*. The fourth [syllable] consists of a single pair of words, [to be recited] with the whole being (*sarvātmanā*). 66.
One should place two *va* syllables separated by the moving *ai* (*aikāra*).
From the eighth [syllable], together with the second *i* and the *sa* and *pa*, there is one Śaiva syllable. (67)
Desiring the Brahman beyond the nameless, one should first utter three steps at the beginning and end;
then, by repeating the preceding [syllable] twice, there is another step consisting of a single syllable.
From the beginning of the word *yogādhipati* to the end of the word, there is then another [word]; the eighth word from that word is "anna," followed by two *chindu*s, then "kṣīṇa. (69)
The seventh syllable, pertaining to Śiva, has been indicated; then follows the imperishable syllable (oṃ).
Thereafter, for the sake of concluding the mantra, one should utter the words "muñca muñca" step by step.
The wise one should place the fifth [vowel] and should place the sixteenth seed-syllable in the heart;
[he should place] the two, the gross and the subtle, at the root of the left foot and upon the upper foot.
Then, by means of the letter *e*, the supreme syllable is divided within Rudrāṇī;
from that comes the infinite *piṅgala*, and at its conclusion is the ninth syllable.

Whatever has been performed regarding the Gaṅgās, and furthermore, one should place the subtle state; [one should worship] the name of Rudra ending in the dative case, and the Trimūrti with the three [mantras] themselves.
And from those two [comes] the long *paiṅgala* vowel; from the sound *ḷ*, there are two syllables.
As before, one should apply these two so that the *paiṅgala* may be properly established. (74)

The sixth syllable is the syllable of the sacrificial rite; the first syllable is Paiṅgala. The second is the other [syllable] following that; it is the syllable of the head, which is a limb of the Vidyā. 75.
One should place the Śiva-mantra, which abides in the state of assistance through non-attachment, in a double arrangement;
thereafter, one should follow the Vāmadeva-pada from that [mantra].
Having established [the foundation], one should place the syllable *jhaṃ*, which is of the nature of Piṅgalā;
then, having again established the first of the *la*-vowels there, one places the second.
The knower of the Self should not perform the piercing of the two *ikāra*s;
rather, one should place the *paiṅgala* path of Śiva within the syllables *ba*, *la*, *kā*, and *rā*. (78)
Then, from those two [syllables], the limbs of the Vidyā at the beginning and end consist of two groups of three syllables each;
from the five-syllabled Śiva-mantra, this sixth syllable is likewise declared. (79)
One should place that supreme state, which is the self of all and non-dual,
upon the middle of the back of the third [syllable], which is the taste of Brahman.
One should also assign [the mantra] syllable by syllable to the other object; thereafter, the third is the Śaiva [mantra], which consists of twenty-seven syllables.
The end of the second word is a word that follows a subtle interval;
this very word is proclaimed as the subtle *bindu*. 82.
The wise one should place the syllable *yā* on the limbs and the second syllable [on the face];
thereafter, two syllables of restraint (*niyama*) ending with *trimūrti*. (83)
One should place the mantra for the sake of its completion, as has been further described;
the third part consists of the limbs of the Vidyā, with a syllable following the letter *e*. (84)
Having placed that pada, one should then place [the mantra] beginning with "Ghorārāt";
from the syllables consisting of the Aghora-weapon, starting from the seventh and eighth [syllables] of the Aghora [mantra].
From *re* comes the syllable *bhā*, and then again the two syllables *ka* and *ra*;
having placed the syllable *gha* from Paiṅgala below, those four are situated above it. (86)
One should place the two syllables of every form ending with Ekarudra;
then the eleventh, Aghorāstra, which is the letter *ta* with the *visarga*.
The organ of action is superior to that; Manu, the mouth, and those who are joined [to them], as well as the syllable Om and the Sun—these are to be known as belonging to Śiva alone. 88.
Then again, the form of Rudra, the syllable *tat*, and the two syllables *veśya*;
then, for the fourth [mantra], the Gāyatrī, the three initial syllables of the sixth [verse]. (89)
Having again placed the word "Mahādeva" ending in the dative case, one should then place four syllables of the Gāyatrī following those three words. (90)
And another [letter] between those two is "Na"; the Rudras end with "Śiva" (the letter "Sa");
in the north of Vāmadeva is the heart, which is the sixth syllable of the Gāyatrī. 91.
But for the seventh [syllable], one should then place these [vowels] starting from the middle;
and the eighth syllable is indeed devoid of mind (amanaska), yet endowed with its own [nature].
The wise practitioner should again install the [mantras] beginning with Īśāna in the subsequent positions,
following the sequence from the top of the square to the right of the square containing the *sparśa* consonants of the Mātṛkā.
Furthermore, in the *hārda* [cakra], there are two syllables in the form of the elements (*bhūta*) with the *visarga*;
joined with the *bindu* from the *śa* group, this is considered to be Brahmā and the Supreme. (94)

The letter *e* conjoined with the syllable *ya-so-doṃ-kā-ra*, extending as far as the deity, [is placed] in the word *dhiyaḥ*; at the end of *pha-epo-ta*, the eighth and ninth letters [are to be applied]. (95)
One should place Brahmā at the beginning, as before, with a single interval; then Ananteśa ending in the dative case, followed by Vīra, and Śava as the eighth. 96.
One should place the syllable *stuṃ*, followed by *tarataḥ* and *śaivam*, and then place *ananteśam*;
one should place [the sequence] ending with *ekarudra*, along with the *mūrchita* and *anakṣara*.
Then, the fifth and sixth [mantras], at the very end, consist of the nature of Śiva;
these three mantras are proclaimed as being joined with the Anuṣṭubh meter. || 98 ||
"By means of the *yajñajuṣ* [mantra] and the *vāmadeva* [mantra] in the *gāyatrī* meter, one performs the fourfold [rite].
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the maintenance of mantras in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*, which is born of Yoga.
Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of the rules for purification and ritual sipping (ācamana):
one should recite the mantra upon rising in the morning, once situated in a clean place.
On an anthill, at a site sacred to Śiva, near a body of water, in the presence of a guru, in a thicket of trees, in a cow-pen, on a riverbank, on ashes, or on cow dung. (2)
A wise person should perform his necessary duties near a temple, especially at a riverbank, or upon rocks and mountain peaks.
With his head covered by a cloth and his sacred thread around his neck,
the twice-born who has become Śiva should remain silent and perform his necessary duties.
At night, having placed the sun to his right, or even keeping it to his right,
the wise practitioner of that mantra, having done so, should proceed toward the water.
One should carefully take up the vessel for worship with the left hand;
the wise man should then take a lump of earth in his right hand and water.
One should wash a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit in the left hand ten times, repeatedly using the lump of clay.
One should gradually clean the seven parts on the right side until no residue remains; having performed the purification that removes odor, stains, and impurities, one should proceed slowly.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
23) One should practice purification to the extent that the purity of the mind is achieved.
Thus ends the chapter on the rules of purification in the *Yogaja*.
Now I shall explain specifically, according to the rules, the procedure for sipping water (ācamana) once again:
having turned to face either the north or the east, one should bind the topknot according to the prescribed rite.
Nor while standing in water, nor while laughing, nor likewise while speaking. || 2 ||
Indeed, there are five sacred bathing places (*pañcatīrtha*) on the right hand of Brahmā;
on land, the right foot is placed, while the left foot remains in the water.
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Maghavān"—this is the Śaiva [view]. (4)
For these five sacred sites (tīrthas) indeed exist upon the fingers:
the Ṛṣitīrtha is at the tips of the fingers, and the Daivika is in the middle of the fingers.
The space between the index finger and the thumb is called the pitṛ-tīrtha;
the line on the base of the thumb is declared to be the brāhma-tīrtha.
Like a cow's ear, one should take water up to the wrist with the palm of the hand;
one should sip it according to the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and then wipe the mouth three times.
The Atharvaveda and the Itihāsas—let him proceed with only one [of these] as his staff;
he should perform sprinkling with water at his feet, and this shall be pleasing to Bhūmadevī. || 8 ||
Having sprinkled water on the head at the *brahmatīrtha*, one should proceed to touch the body at the *kṣatra* [tīrtha];
then, with the thumb and ring finger, one should touch the two eyes. (9)
One should touch the two eyes with the thumb and forefinger;
one should touch the heart with all the fingers, and the head with all the fingers.
Having done this, one who knows the mantras should also touch the limbs;
likewise, by sprinkling the head and feet, one satisfies the seven sages.

By the mere touch of the eyes upon the head, as well as by [the touch of] wood upon Śarva and Āditya, there is indeed no pleasure derived from that touch; for the presiding deity resides in the flame.
The two external [points], the navel, the heart, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the head—by touching these very spots on the head, one becomes beloved of all the gods. || 13 ||
In the event of a wound or an itch having arisen, perform immediate ācamana;
after touching the [wound] with the thumb, the ācamana should then take place. (14)
Thus the ritual of sipping water (ācamana) has been declared; now hear the procedure for the mantra-bath.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of sipping water in the *Yogaja*.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme bath that removes all sins.
A lump of clay, cow dung, a flower, sesame seeds, myrobalan, and kuśa grass. || 1 ||
Whether at a pond, a well, or even in deep water in a lake,
one should first rinse one's mouth according to the rules and then wash both feet and hands.
Having first performed the ritual bath in water and thereafter the mental bath,
one should divide a lump of clay into three parts with the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should likewise designate the east, the south, and the north:
with Tatpuruṣa in the east, and with Aghora in the south. (4)
One should also consecrate the northern [side] with the Vāmadeva mantra;
then, one should cast [the offerings] into the ten directions in due order with the Astra mantra.
With his right hand, he should likewise anoint the clay and the limbs with the mantra,
[applying it] respectively to the head, the face, the heart, the private parts, and the feet.
One should smear all the limbs with the "Ghora" mantra at the heart;
then, with the "Uttara" mantra, one should prepare the clay for the Śivatīrtha.
For the purpose of bathing, one should perform the consecration with ritual service using fragrant myrobalan and other substances, as well as the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva.
Furthermore, having smeared [the area] with cow dung, one should bathe [the deity] again;
then, having formed the *kalaśa-mudrā*, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the *prāsāda* mantra. || 9 ||
Having reached that sacred ford, apply ointment at night;
thereafter, having performed your bath and sipped water according to the prescribed rule.
One should consume water with the Sadyojāta mantra, but perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with the Īśāna mantra;
furthermore, one should recite the Tatpuruṣa mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having carefully consumed water with the mantra "sūryaśca," one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and sprinkle oneself with water while reciting "adhikrāviṇṇe."
One should first deposit [the water] in the east with the mantra "bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ";
then, having touched [water], one should mutter the five Brahma-mantras along with their ancillaries.
Having offered libations to all the *kalās* and mantras, as well as to Vyomavyāpin, and likewise to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors in their proper order, (p. 29).
One should worship the gods with the Vāmadeva mantra, the sages with the Aghora mantra, and likewise the ancestors with the Sadyojāta mantra, in this very sequence.

Having offered libations according to the rule and having sipped water (ācamana) again in the prescribed manner, by which sacred part (tīrtha) of the body should one satisfy the goddesses with water mixed with flowers? (16)
One should satisfy all the sages with the *ārṣa* (sage’s) *tīrtha*, and one should satisfy all the ancestors with the *paitṛka* (paternal) *tīrtha*. || 17 ||
Proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction and with three sacred threads over the left shoulder,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, and likewise [recite] the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
Then one should recite the Śrī Rudra, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Viṣṇusūkta; and with the mantra "Huṃ," one should likewise remember the sacred ford (tīrtha). || 19 ||
One should satisfy the sages and gods with flowers, and the ancestors with sesame seeds;
one should perform all ritual acts using kusha grass and flowers for all purposes.
There, one should perform the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra according to one's capacity;
then one should recite the "ud ity añci" mantra and the Haṃsa-śuddhi mantra.
Then, having performed circumambulation as well as the counting of the qualities,
the wise man, holding flowers in his hands, should enter the temple.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for bathing in the *Yogatantro*.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme ritual for bathing with ashes.
By the will of Śiva, five cows arrived on earth from the city of Śiva. || 1 ||
All the mothers of the world are born from the five cows:
Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanā. || 2 ||
Kapila, white-black, and likewise smoky-red;
beginning with Nanta and ending with Sumanas—this is proclaimed to be the [sequence of] colors. (3)
For the sake of benefiting the entire world and for the gratification of the gods,
the Mother Cows reside upon the earth for the purpose of bathing and for the sake of auspiciousness.
Cow dung, yellow pigment (rocanā), urine, milk, curd, and ghee—
these six products of the cow are indeed pure and grant all spiritual accomplishments.
Through cows, sacrifices proceed; in cows, the gods are proclaimed to reside.
Through cows, the Vedas are fully sharpened, along with their limbs (aṅga), sub-limbs (upāṅga), word-for-word analysis (pada), and phonetic arrangement (krama).
At the base of the peak, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally established;
at the tip of the peak reside all the excellent, immobile sacred fords (tīrthas).
O child, perform the washing with the *vatsa* mantras in the center of my head;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rules, one should carry out the twilight rites (*sandhyā-karman*).
The ritual procedure should cause all those who have not yet performed their duties to do so as before.
The Māhendra bath has been described; now hear about the Māruta bath.
Having caused the cow-dung to be mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) during the period of *godhūlī*,
one should then mutter the root mantra while it is permeated with the scent of the cow.

Afterwards, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); one should not act as previously stated. This is declared to be the "wind-bath" (māruta-snāna); now hear about the "mantra-bath" (mantra-snāna). (11)
Having performed the washing of the feet and sipped water according to the rules,
take water in a copper vessel while reciting the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā."
The wise and intelligent man, having sprinkled the gold and the *pavamāna* with *kuśa* grass, should perform all other rites as previously described. (13)
The Vāraṇa, the Māhendra-bhasma, the Māruta, and that which is designated as Mantra—this fivefold bath is most suitable for all ritual activities. (14)

Thus [are described] purification, sipping water, bathing, the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), entering the sanctuary, the opening of the door by the cock, sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and self-purification. (p. 34)

The purification of substances, the purification of the twice-born, the purification of mantras, the preparation of the seat, the invocation and installation of the deity, the rites of presence, near-presence, anger,

the arrangement of limbs and sub-limbs, and the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, bali-oblations, and oblations— this is the procedure for worship, including the perpetual festival and dance in the sacred field.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for self-purification in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme procedure for worship;
worship is said to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others. || 1 ||
Among the stationary lingas, that which is mobile is proclaimed as such;
because it is bound together with the pedestal and other components, the mobile linga is so called.
The stationary *liṅga* is said to be joined with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
it is likewise self-arisen (*svayambhu*), grown (*rohaṇa*), and belongs to the gods, humans, and *rākṣasas*. (3)
The installation of liṅgas such as the Bāṇaliṅga and others is proclaimed to be for the sake of others.
In these, the Lord is eternally present; however, the human [liṅga] is both manifest and unmanifest.
At the time of twilight, he is clearly manifest, while at other times he is unmanifest;
he is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
From the mantra of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, [the faces] beginning with the northern one up to the form [at the top] are named Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna.
The faces beginning with the northern one are recited in sequence;
they arise from the emergence of all dualities, and from the left side, they arise from the waters.
From Aghora, the Taijasa [fire] was produced; from Puruṣa, the wind (vāyu) arose;
from Īśa, space (ākāśa) was born—thus are these the origins of the elements.
Having invoked the seat and the form on that third path,
the seat extends up to Śuddhavidyā, while the scope of the form extends up to Śakti.
Having invoked Sadāśiva together with Śiva, he is declared to be the embodiment of the mantra;
Sadāśiva, who arises from the mantra and is endowed with the thirty-eight kalās.
From the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) up to Śiva is known as Sadāśiva;
this is celebrated as "Mantra" and is remembered as the "Worship of Śiva. || 11 ||
The line arising from space is the second half-moon;
the third is curved in shape, and the fourth arises from fire.
The fifth, however, has the form of a banner; it is proclaimed as the Śiva-mantra, which resides in the heart of all wombs. (13)
The half-syllable, the placement of the words, and the six-word mantra established in Śakti—this installation should be performed daily for the transformative [consecration] of the Liṅga. (14)
The Vidyāṅga weapon, the Śivāṅga weapon, the Aghora weapon, the Pāśupata weapon, and the Kṣīrakṣa weapon—these five are empowered by the mantras of Śiva. || 15 ||
From Śiva, Śakti is produced; likewise, from Śakti, Sadāśiva is produced;
from Sadāśiva arises Īśvara, and in Sadāśiva resides Sthiti.
The Lord was born from Rudra; Viṣṇu arose from Rudra;
Brahmā was produced from Viṣṇu; and from Brahmā came the origin of the universe.
Beyond the reach of speech and mind, he is the one who bestows both the expressed and the expresser;
he is proclaimed as Śiva, the Pure, the formless, the immutable Lord. (18)
The mantra of Sadāśiva is expressible, while the mantra of Śiva is inexpressible;
this secret, more secret than the secret, is realized through one's own direct experience.
For the sake of protecting the world, [one should worship] that which has arisen from Sadāśiva;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship Sadāśiva.
Thus, a wise person should worship that which brings peace to the world for the sake of others;
such worship of the Primordial Śiva (Ādiśaiva) serves both one's own purpose and the purpose of others.
Without a mortal [body], Liṅgekṣaṇa always devours tortoises;
therefore, with every effort, perform the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
First there should be purification of the body, second the purification of the place,
third the purification of the materials, and fourth the purification of the ritual emblem (liṅga). || 23 ||
The fifth is the accomplishment of mantra; these are the five purifications.
One should perform the purification of the body according to the method of the previously stated rule. (24)
One should perform the purification of the body according to the sequence of the deposition of the deities (devanyāsa).
Having made the ground level, one should sit comfortably facing north. (25)
One should perform exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka) for ten measures each;
then, one should begin the clearing of the directions with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) in the ten directions.
In the midst of that water from the conch, the wise one should display the *surabhi-mudrā* and,
joined with perfumes, flowers, and *kuśa* grass, install the *śiva-mantra*.

Then, having sprinkled his own body with water in the auspicious [liṅga] by means of its name, the wise knower of mantras, having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) according to the path of emanation (sṛṣṭimārga), [should proceed]. (28)
This is known as the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* (creation ritual), beginning from the thumb and ending with the little finger;
that which begins from the little finger and ends with the thumb is called the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (dissolution ritual).
On the right, it should begin with the middle finger, and on the left, it should end with the ring finger;
this is declared to be the *sthitinyāsa*, which is the rule for all ritual actions.
The emanation [of the mantras] beginning with the head is proclaimed; one should place those beginning with the feet into the dissolution.
One should perform the placement of the eight starting from Īśāna, and place Sadyojāta into the dissolution.
One should thus perform the placement of the mantras (mantravinyāsa), beginning with Aghora and following the procedure for the placement of stability (sthitinyāsa).
Having placed the Heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the Head-mantra on the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] on the crest, and the *kavaca* between the breasts;
having placed the *astra* with the hand, one should place the *netra* with the eye. (33)
One should especially join the seed-syllables of earth and the other elements to the knees, the navel, the throat, the forehead, and the head of the preceptor.
The seeds of earth and the other elements are la, va, la, ya, ha, and ka;
their colors are yellow, white, red, black, and smoke-colored respectively. (35)
The four-cornered, the half-moon, the triangle, the six-cornered, and the perfect circle— these are the mandalas for earth and the other elements, respectively, in due order.
Then [he should worship] the deity Śiva as seven hundredfold, established in the Praṇava;
the triangular fire-god, and the circle of Indra and Sūrya.
The fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) of both the Moon and the Sun is said to have the very form of a mandala.
[It consists of] the heart, the head, the crest, and the armor. (38)
The six limbs, beginning with the eye, have been proclaimed in their proper order;
one should especially worship the five elements, earth and the others.
Earth and the other elements are the paths; Brahmā and the others are the five forms.
There are five *udghātas*, then four, three, two, and one respectively.
Hlāṃ hrīṃ hvīṃ hrūṃ heṇa—these, along with the letter *ra*, should be raised up in due order:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti. (41)
The wise one, joined with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, [should assign] the elements beginning with earth to the knees,
the navel, the throat, the forehead, and the region of the head.
The practitioner of the primordial Śaiva tradition should bind the heart and other [limbs] with the mantra;
that binding consists of five knots—such is the certainty of the scripture. (43)
One should cut the five knots with the Pāśupata scripture; one should join the elements beginning with earth by means of the mantras beginning with *hlādaya*. (44)
One should join the crest at the tip, twelve finger-breadths long, with the *haṃsa* [mantra] into the Self;
and by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should unite it with the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). || 45 ||
The wise one should place the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ) in the center of the circle of fire;
thereafter, he should burn the body and contemplate it as a burnt rope.
Then, having meditated upon oneself as being filled with the vital energy (tejas) of the deceased,
one should contemplate the Praṇava, a white lotus, and the yoga-pīṭha facing downwards.
Having meditated on the moon in the center of the ground as streaming with nectar,
make the body stable by means of that accumulated mass. (48)
The wise one should bring himself [into the state of the deity] and perform the mantra-ritual as before;
he should install the sequence of phonemes and mantras beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'. (49)
Having placed the syllable *a* on the crown of the head, the syllable *ā* on the forehead;
*i* and *ī* on the two eyes, and likewise *u* and *ū* on the two lips. (50)
One should place *ṛ* and *ṝ* upon the two eyes, and *ḷ* and *ḹ* upon the two channels;
the wise know that *e* and *ai* are on the two ears, and *o* and *au* are on the tongue and the throat.
The wise one should place the syllables *aṃ* and *aḥ* on both armpits; the *ka*-group [of consonants] on the right side... [and so forth].
The *ṭa*-group [of consonants] is on the right foot, the *ta*-group on the left foot;
the *pa*-group is on the right hand, and the *ya*-group on the left hand. (53)
The *lakṣaliṅga* is prescribed for the *apāna*, and the station of the *varṇas* is ordained; one should apply the placement (*nyāsa*) of *kāla*, *śakti*, and *kalā* in their proper sequence.
One should place the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva in their respective locations;
one should place the ten syllables from the head down to the feet. (55)
Thereafter, one should install the palace [of the deity] and contemplate, "I am Śiva.
Then, having performed the worship of the hands, one should subsequently perform the worship of the body.
As before, one should apply the placement of the body (dehanyāsa) in due order;
having done this, one should especially perform the purification of the self (ātmaśuddhi). 57.
One should perform worship for one's own sake three times a day or once a day.
Below the root of the *nāḍī*, there is a lotus measuring four finger-breadths. (58)
This is declared to be the Mūlādhāra; they know it to have the resonance of the sound "śa-ṭṛ-nā-bhi. Joined with Bindu and Nāda, it is designated as Śakti.
In the midst of fire is the station of the sun; in the midst of the sun is the moon;
and in its midst is the Primordial Knower (pūrvajña), which is known as both manifest and unmanifest.
The Self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman) are spoken of;
all these, in their ascending order, are endowed with the qualities of sattva and the others.
One should join the deity situated between the eyebrows with the one established in the center of the navel;
one should perform the yoga in the heart and arrange the oblation at the navel.
One should worship [the deity] constantly in the heart-lotus, either three times a day, twice a day, or otherwise perform the sacrifice once a day with the mind alone. (63)
The sprout is at the root of the navel, while Supratiṣṭhita is established in the heart; having joined Samana with Manyā, [one should perform the ritual]. || 64 ||
The lotus of the six supports consists of four, eight, twice eight (sixteen), and thirty-two petals, doubled [to sixty-four], arranged in order from top to bottom. || 65 ||
With three streams in its lower part and likewise in its upper part, this is declared to be the support of the *haṃsa*, and Sadāśiva is the support of everything. (66)
The yoga of the tongue-bone bell is called its arising;
one should contemplate it in this very manner with the mind. 67.
The purification of the self has been declared; now hear this regarding the secret of the site:
it should be cleansed and smeared, and adorned with canopies and banners. (68)
One should join it with the *śodhanī-mudrā* and the syllable *phaṭ*. Then,
in the form of a square measuring one cubit,
one should invoke the Earth, adorned with all ornaments.

Having two eyes and two arms, dark-complexioned, with a parrot in her hand and tawny hair, she is worshipped with throat-flowers and other offerings by the best of teachers, who utters his own mantra. (71)
This has been declared as the purification of the ground; now hear about the purification of the ritual substances (*dravyaśuddhi*), including the fragrant oil and so forth.
Kaṣāya, scented water, and likewise the prescribed cloth;
water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, as well as perfume, flowers, and incense. (73)
A lamp, as well as an offering, drinking water, and likewise betel-leaf for mouth-freshening, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and the libation (tarpaṇa). || 74 ||
A fly-whisk, a palm-leaf fan, an umbrella, and sandals made of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal; || 75 ||
One should increase the vessels made of conch-shells and the like, as well as the water-vat. || 76 ||
One should purify all the three-footed [pedestals] with the root mantra,
in sequence, in the east, west, south, and north.
Having arranged them in sequence, they have come down through the tradition of the five faces. || 78 ||
Tamā, Ātara, Akṣarā, Niṣṭhā, Dhṛti, Kṣānti, Smṛti, and Kṣamā—
these are indeed the eight powers (śaktis) of the Aghora families, respectively.
One should place the digits (kalās) of Aghora in the heart, the region of the throat, the two shoulders, the belly, the navel, the seat (pīṭha), and the chest.
Ratippālī, Kāmā, Saṃyamanīyakā, Kṛṣṇā, Mohā, Kṣudhā, Cintā, Grāmaṇī, and likewise Bhrāmiṇī—these are the queens. || 81 ||
The thirteen Śakti-missiles of the Vāmadeva-kalās are located in the secret place, the anus, the two hips, the two knees, and also the two shanks.
In the *Pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], one should place the portions of Vāmadeva on the sides of the hips:
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, the second Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Praṇā. (83)
If, however, one intends to fashion eight mantra-less digits upon the divine body,
one should place them on the two feet, the two thighs, and likewise on both hands.
The external part of this nose is indeed the portion of Brahmā situated at the base;
the middle portion shall be the portion of Viṣṇu, and above that is the portion of Śiva. || 85 ||
The fourth part is the portion of Śiva; one part is said to be the *pada*;
the second is the portion of Jaṃbha, and the third is indeed Maru. (86)

The fourth is the region of the hips, the fifth is above the waist; the sixth is known as the portion of the lord (the back), the seventh is the region of the navel, and they know the eighth to be the belly.
The eighth is said to be the heart; the ninth is from the middle of the breasts; the tenth would be the region of the throat; and the eleventh is recorded as the chin. (88)
The lower lip and the upper lip are known as the thirteenth;
the forehead should be the fourteenth, and with the fifteenth, one places [the breath] upon the head. 89.
One should place the thirty-eight digits (kalās) from the crown of the head down to the feet:
Śaśinī on the uppermost head, and Aṅgadā on the eastern head.
One should worship Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the right face, Marīci on the northern faces,
Jvālinī on the five faces, and the upward-facing one with the syllable *praṇava*.
It is known as the Unmanifest Power (avyaktakalā) and is remembered as having its face turned upward;
it consists of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti, with Śāntyatītā remaining at the end.
One should sprinkle with water that has been transformed by the *śipī* [mantra], using the root-vidyā. || 93 ||
Thus the purification of the substance is accomplished; now hear how the *liṅga* is purified:
the wise practitioner should take flowers with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger. (94)
One should release with the thumb the flower worshipped during the morning twilight;
at the time of that dismissal, one should place the flower upon the head.
Having performed the sequential deposition of the body (dehanyāsa), one should clearly contemplate this manifest form of Sadāśiva as the mantra-body among the unmanifest lingas. || 96 ||
In that *liṅga* dwells the Lord Sadāśiva, both manifest and unmanifest;
he is manifest at the time of twilight, but unmanifest at other times.

(54) Whether in the acts of invocation (*āvāhana*) or dismissal (*visarga*), one may be at ease even if impaired; one should rub wood against wood according to the method arising from the *Prakriyā* doctrine. 98.
This Lord of All has arisen; pervading all, he is made manifest by Śiva.
By his very nature he is called auspicious (śiva), like fire within wood. || 99 ||
Having reached the limit of the secondary wood (upakāṣṭha), he becomes Sadāśiva;
as long as he is the initiator of Śiva’s divine play, he is called Sadāśiva.
The teacher of knowledge, yoga, and ritual action should bind Sadāśiva;
at the time of worship, one should extract that Śiva by means of ritual action, like fire.
The word *svāhā* is said to be unmanifest (*avyakta*) [at the time of the ritual], yet it becomes manifest (*vyakta*) at the moment of action;
its form is like a water-pot (*kuṇḍa*), its head is shaped like a vessel, and its body has the appearance of an *āmalaka* fruit.
The form of the *kūśmāṇḍa* fruit, the appearance of the *panasa* fruit, and the shape of the palmyra fruit— this is called the *ārṣa* liṅga. (103)
The nimba, the coconut, the bilva, and the kapittha; the mango, the citron, the kadamba fruit, and the mallikā. || 104 ||

Thus, the human *liṅga* is said to be endowed with the [five] auspicious marks (*dakṣiṇa*), whereas those of the *svayambhū*, the *ṛṣis*, and the gods are without the three lines and the bud-like protuberance. 105.

That which is endowed with a form according to one's desire, with its own limbs being tawny (piṅgala), and joined with three threads and without the *akula* [seal], is called the human *liṅga*. || 106 ||
One should place one part of the length of the *liṅga* as the digits (*kalā*) of Govijātaka;
now I shall describe the digits of Gaurī, which arise from the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Gaurī. (107)
Tārā is to be known as a portion of Īśa; one should place the portion of Vidyā’s face with the Heart-mantra on the exterior here, and [the portion of] Svaśana in the region of the navel. (108)
O Goddess, one should indeed place these digits of Vāmadeva upon the two thighs, the two knees, and also upon the two rows of teeth within the body.
One should specifically perform the placement (nyāsa) of the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' upon the head, forehead, eyes, ears, and both cheeks. (110)
One should place the sixteen vowels upon the face, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the tongue, and the cavities of the palate. (111)
The *ka*-group [of consonants] is on the right hand, the *va*-group on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group is on the right side, and the *ta*-group on the left foot.
The letters *pa* and *pha* shine on the right side, while *ba* and *bha* indeed shine on the left side;
the letter *ma*, however, is recited in sequence at the region of the throat. (113)
One should place the weapon of taste (rasāstra), beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *sa*, as well as flesh, body, bone, marrow, and semen, in their proper sequence.
Having placed the letter *ha* in the heart, one should place the letter *la* on the testicles;
one should especially perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the letter *kṣa* in the region of the penis.
The fullness of the six paths is known as the divine body;
namely, earth, water, fire, air, and space. (116)
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
and speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth. (117)

The mind, the intellect, the ego, primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the person (puruṣa); passion, illusion (māyā), and knowledge (vidyā), as well as limited agency (kalā) and necessity (niyati). || 118 ||
Vigraheśvara together with Sakala, as well as Śuddhavidyā;
that which consists of the purity of Śuddhavidyā is known as the pure Śiva. (119)

The thirty-sixth principle has been described; the sense of smell is said to be the principle. The path of the parts (kalādhvan) is called the limb, as well as the vital breath (prāṇa) and the principle itself.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is endowed with the banner; the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) is accompanied by blood;
the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is the hair-pores; and the path of locations (padādhvan) is indeed the entrails. 121.
Then, having performed all the rites for the seventeenth deity, Śiva, who resides within the Praṇava, as before, one should thereafter invoke Śiva.
Kapālīśa is unborn, O knower of bondage, the crusher of the body; he is the pervasive lord, the imperishable teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the sovereign of the thirty gods. (123)
Thus, these ten deities are proclaimed to be in the eastern quarter:
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Ghātaka, and Hara. (124)
The blazing ones, the burners, the tawny ones, the end of ash, and the end of destruction—these ten deities are proclaimed to be in the direction of Agni (the southeast). || 125 ||
Yāmya, Agnīna, Hara, Ghātā, Vidhātā, as well as Īśvara;
the doer, the enjoyer, the ordainer, the sustainer, and likewise the Lord of Dharma. || 126 ||
Thus, in the sequence of their respective directions, these ten deities are proclaimed:
Nṛti, Maraṇa, Hantā, Krūradṛṣṭi, and Bhayānaka.
(60) "With hair standing erect, with distorted eyes, and possessing smoke-colored and red fangs"—
thus are the ten deities proclaimed in the direction of the Nairṛta (southwest). || 128 ||
Bāla with noose in hand, Mahīha, Calī, Śveta, Jayabhadra with divine hand, Jīlādhipa, and Meghanādaka. || 129 ||
And the deity known as Sugāda resides in the western direction;
he is swift, light, possessing the speed of wind, subtle, and the ender of the destruction of moments. 130.
Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana—thus the ten deities are proclaimed in the region of the northwest. (131)
The Lord of Treasures is handsome and blessed, established in a gentle body;
he is the bearer of Fortune, the bearer of jewels, the bearer of prosperity, and the bestower of grace. (132)
Thus, in the region to the north of these, ten deities are proclaimed:
Vidyādhipa, Īśa, Tridaśa, and all [the others]. (133)
Jñānabhuk, Vedapāra, Sureśa, and Sarva; Jyeṣṭha, Bhūtapāla, and Balapriya as well. || 134 ||
In the northeastern quarter of the region, ten deities are proclaimed:
Brahmā, Vṛṣadhara, and Anantakrodha; || 135 ||
Marutāśanagrāsana, Uduṃbarīśa,
Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭrin— these are the deities in the downward direction.
Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Trinetra, Tridiveśvara, Saṃvāhana, Vivāna, Nabhas, Vismṛti, and Locana. (137)
Thus, the ten deities are proclaimed in the upward directions;
above them, one should place Vīrabhadra and the two Bhadrakālīs. (138)
One should install Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara in sequence;
thus, the wise practitioner should invoke the seven hundred deities.
The earth-tattva, which is the digit of cessation (nivṛttikalā), is said to be the phoneme *kṣa* in the mantra;
the heart-mantra [is formed] with all [the syllables], and the portion consists of Kālāgni and Krūramāka. 140.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are proclaimed as the presiding deities;
within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the worlds are proclaimed to be Rudra.
And by the *nivṛtti-kalā*, the principle of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*) is expressed;
in the letter *kṣa* is the phoneme, and for these [letters], there are one hundred and eight worlds.

Salutations again and again to Śiva! Oṃ, O all-seeing one, O all-auspicious one! Subtle one, subtle one! Sound! Knowledge of sound, knowledge! O tawny one, tawny one! O bird, bird! Fierce one, fierce one! Witness, witness! Abiding from of old, abiding from of old! Worshipped, worshipped! Supreme to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra!
"O maker of all presence! O bestower of happiness upon all beings! O source of existence! Bhava Bhava! Śarva Śarva! Prathama Prathama! Release, release!
To the Lord of Yoga, the one of great splendor, the Lord of true being, Mahādeva! Thus ends the great mantra, Savyomavyāpin, which consists of twenty-eight words.
It is known as that which pervades the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) for the sake of the time of cessation (nivṛtti). || 143 ||
I shall describe the installation (pratiṣṭhā) by means of its constituent parts (kalā): water, fire, wind, and ether;
64) as well as the five subtle elements (tanmātra), beginning with sound, which constitute the nature of the moving breath. || 144 ||
The organs of action are considered to be speech, hands, anus, and genitals;
the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are considered the organs of cognition. (145)
The mind, the intellect, and the ego—these are remembered as the three internal organs (antahkaraṇa).
The qualities (guṇas) are called primordial nature (prakṛti); thus, there are exactly twenty-four principles.
The twenty-three phonemes beginning with *ga* and ending with *ha* are placed on the head; thus, two mantras for the left [side] are here declared. (147)
It is traditionally taught that there are fifty-six worlds in their proper sequence:
Amareśa, Prabhāsena, Naumīśa, and Puṣkara are recorded [as the first]. (148)
Therefore, Siddhi, Muṇḍī, Hāra, Bhrī, Tilaka, and Kulīśvara—
thus the state of the eight principles has been recollected as the reality. (149)
Madhyama, Eka, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and Bhairaveśvara—these are proclaimed as the eight [deities] within the fire-principle (agnitatva). || 150 ||
Gaya, Kurukṣetra, Nāgalocana, Khas, Vimaleśa, Aṣṭabhāsa, Mahendra, and indeed Maheśvara; || 151 ||
Thus, these eight worlds are proclaimed as belonging to the principle of space (ākāśatattva):
Cakraddhaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, and Maṇḍaleśvara; || 152 ||
Kālāñjana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Samūleśvara are remembered [as the lords];
thus, this eightfold world-realm is situated within the syllable Aṃ. || 153 ||
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra,
Sauma, Śaila, and Brahma— these eight are established in the intellect (buddhi). (154)
The Akṛta, the Kṛta, the Bhairava, the Brāhma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Aumaka, and the Śrīkaṇṭha—thus it is described. (155)
Thus, the eightfold practice of yoga is said to be the nature of the qualities (guṇaprakṛti).
In this way, there are nine groups of seven;
the twenty-first position is in the center, consisting of the heroic exploits of Maheśvara.
Śaṣarva! Become the one whose end is Śiva. O Endless One! O Without-End! Oṃ Bhuvaḥ! Dhū dhū dhū! Nā nā nā nā! O Beginningless One! O Ashless One! O Smokeless One!

O You Whose Form is Fire! O Formless One! O You Who Are Not the Light of Fire! O Light! O Radiance! O Radiance of Radiance! O Primordial One! O Primordial One! O Formless Maheśvara! From the very foot, you are the one who possesses form. (p. 67)
One should contemplate the fivefold path beginning with Ananta as pervaded by the *kalā* of *Pratiṣṭhā*. Thus, there is the sixfold path of pervasion (*vyāpti-vidyā*) within the *kalā*.

Furthermore, the seven principles (*tattvas*) are Puruṣa, Rāga, Vidyā, Kālāgni, Niyati, Māyā, and Niṣkala. The phonemes (*varṇas*) end with the letter *gha*; the mantras are those of Aghora and Śiva. There are twenty-seven worlds (*bhuvanas*). [The lords of these worlds are] Vāma, Bhīma, Tūgra, Bhuva, Īśa, Era, and Vīra; [and further] Puruṣa, Pracaṇḍa, Umāpati, and Aja.

Ananta and Ekavīraka constitute the pentad of worlds (*bhuvanapañcaka*). Rāga and Krodha belong to the *Vidyā* [tattva] of Caṇḍeśa; Jyotis, Saṃvartaka, and Kāla belong to the *Sūka*; and Antaka belongs to the other [tattva]. Ekavīra, Śikhākāla, Mahātejas, or Mahādeva belong to the Earth (*Bhū*); Udbhava, Ekapiṅgala, Eke-kṣaṇa, and Īśāna [belong to the Water (*Ap*)].

"Measuring a thumb's breadth" refers to the eight lords of the mandala and Māyā; thus, there are twenty worlds, deities, baths, and steps. [Salutation] to the Pervasive and Non-pervasive, the Sky-like and Non-sky-like, the Insentient and Sentient, the Supreme Lord, whose form is the supreme light, who is authorized in all yogas, the deathless protector, more secret than the secret.

Oṃ namaḥ! Salutation to the one whose form is Sadyojāta, whose secret is the deity of space (Vyomadeva), whose heart is Aghora, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, whose head is Īśāna, the source of all and the sovereign lord; oṃ namaḥ! [Salutation] to the one whose food is meditation (dhyānāhāra). Thus, beginning with Vyāpin and ending with Dhyānāhāra, there are fivefold paths pervaded by the *vidyā* and *kalā* categories. Furthermore, within the *śāntikalā*, there are the three principles (*tattva*) known as Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva-Śiva.

The three phonemes *kha*, *ga*, and *ka* are the mantra. From it arise the eighteen worlds: Puruṣa, Kavaca, Prabhū, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Karālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī. These nine worlds belong to Śuddhavidyā.
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetraka, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkhaṇḍa, and Śikhaṇḍin; || 157 ||

The eight worlds (*bhuvana*) are within the principle of Īśvara. The worlds called Sadākhya and Sadāśiva consist of eleven steps (*pada*). These steps are: *nityayogine*, *yogapīṭhasaṃsthāya*, *dhruvāya*, *śivāya*, *sarvavyāpine*, *vyomāya*, *rūpāya*, *vyomavyāpine*, *nityayogine*, and *ādivyomavyāpine*.

Thus it is fivefold. Having transcended the sixfold [categories], one should contemplate the pervasion of the *śāntikalā* (the power of peace); this is the pervasion of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvavyāpti*). Furthermore, within the *śāntyatītakalā* (the power beyond peace) lies the *śivatattva* (the principle of Śiva). The sixteen phonemes are the vowels beginning with *visarga* and ending with *a*. [In this state] there is the *śiva-īśa-astra-mantra* and fifteen worlds. Likewise, there are *nivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, and *śānti*; in the *śāntyatīta* is the *bindukalā* (the digit of the point).

The worlds (*bhuvana*) are as follows: *īlikā*, *dīpā*, *rocikā*, *mocikā*, and *ūrdhvagāmī*. The worlds of the *kalā* of the *nāda* of *nīti* are *vipinī*, *vyomarūpā*, *ananta*, *anāthā*, and *anāśritā*; these are the worlds of the *kalā* of *śakti*. Then there is *vyomavyāpin*, *mantrādyota*, and *kṛtapada*. Thus is the fivefold path (*adhvapañcaka*). (p. 71)

"One should contemplate the pervasion of the *kalā* of peace"—thus is the sixfold pervasion of the paths (*ṣaḍvidhādhvavyāpti*). In this very way, the pervasion of the six paths of the Mothers (*mātṛṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) has been explained.

Therein, the *kalās*, the five *tattvas*, and the thirty-six [categories] are included; the letters (*vārṇas*) are fifty; the mantras are eleven; the worlds (*bhuvanās*) are two hundred and twenty-four; and the words (*padāni*) are eighty-one. Thus, one who possesses knowledge of the six paths is liberated; he releases [others] from the bondage of the fetters (*pāśabandhana*).
The six paths consist of the feet, the path, the channels, the flesh, the semen, the marrow, the bones, and the skin; he whose nature is these six paths of Sadāśiva is known as Prāṇaśiva. || 158 ||
Complete with the heart and other limbs, he assumes his full form during meditation;
he has the luster of a jasmine flower, the moon, or crystal, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair. 159.
He has five heads and five faces, endowed with fifteen eyes;
he is adorned with all ornaments and possessed of ten arms. (160)
In the right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and a vajra, as well as the gesture of granting fearlessness;
in the left hands, he holds a noose, a serpent-goad, a bell, and fire. 161.
The left [face] should be like milk, the right one should resemble blood;
the Aghora [face] should be like collyrium, and the Puruṣa [face] should have the luster of saffron.
The eastern face is said to have the luster of pure crystal;
the northern face is remembered as having the color of gold. (163)
The god was wearing celestial garments, adorned with celestial flowers, his limbs anointed with celestial perfumes, possessing a tranquil form and a smiling countenance. || 164 ||
One should determine [the state] according to the form of the *liṅga*: whether standing, seated, or reclining.
A standing *liṅga* represents the present; a seated one, however, represents Śiva as preeminent. (165)
The "three-part bed" (trairāśika-śayana) is to be known as a great [structure] consisting of three equal sections.
Having multiplied by twenty-four, one should assign the Brahma-portion to the front, the Īśa-portion to the middle, the Viṣṇu-portion to the year, the nine-fold Śiva-portion,
and half of that to the [remaining] portion.
One part each for Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and likewise a portion exceeding that for Śiva.
It is declared that [the portion] exceeding Śiva should be equal to the equal segments;
by means of thirty-one divisions, the portions for Brahmā and Viṣṇu are ten each.
It is declared as "Rudra-Arudra" and is remembered as consisting of three portions;
it should stand with the same form as the liṅgas beginning with Svāyambhuva.
(74) It shall be taught that sitting is performed with the thick root [of the kuśa grass] facing the tip;
lying down is appropriate when the thick tip faces the root of the kuśa grass. || 169 ||
The forms of those possessing the three types of karma and those with medium or large lingas are recorded;
having invoked Śakti upon the pedestal, her form is recited there.
The *upāna* is said to be one foot, and the *jagatī* is called the shank;
they say the *kumuda* is the belly, and the *kampaka* is indeed the two arms. (171)
The "karṇa" (ear) is said to be [the part] at each ear, while the "adhare'dhara" (lower lip) is the lower fillet;
the "mahāpaṭṭimukha" (great fillet-face) is to be known, as well as the "kṛtavārīśiras" (constructed water-head).
In the extraction of the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should visualize her as having two eyes and endowed with two arms,
red in color, her body in the triple-bent posture (tribhaṅga), and encircled by a variegated hue.
(75) Adorned with all ornaments, with full thighs, hips, and breasts,
she has anklets on her feet and is equipped with a waist-band. || 174 ||
And one should visualize the goddess Sumukhāṅgā, adorned with flowers and a golden casket, holding a lotus and a blue water-lily, with her hands granting boons and fearlessness. (175)
Having meditated thus, one should contemplate the body of Gaurī upon an excellent seat;
indeed, these twenty-six kalās should be deposited within the body of Gaurī. (176)
One should arrange the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' in sequence as before;
the yogi situated on the circular seat [should visualize] Gaurī on the auspicious throne-seat (bhadrapīṭha).

The bed should be on a *bhadrapīṭha*, while for others it may be superior or inferior; having thus meditated according to the specific nature of each seat, the knower of mantras [should proceed]. (178)
One should worship the deity while standing either in the southeast (Agni) or the southwest (Nirṛti);
one should worship the deity while standing at a distance of more than one cubit. || 179 ||
One should worship the lingas, which are dependent on the hands and dependent on happiness, as being the support, the self-abode, and the primary object worthy of honor. 180.
When it is said that the pure state is the station of knowledge (ājñā), the supporting powers (ādhāra-śakti) are meant;
the support (ādhāra) is said to be the anus, while the svādhiṣṭhāna is the generative organ (liṅga). 181.
It is situated in the middle of the navel like water filling the ocean; likewise, it is to be known as existing in the heart like fragrance in flowers or like oil in sesame seeds. 182.
The Viśuddha [cakra] is in the region of the ears; the Ājñā is proclaimed as being without a second.
77) The support (ādhāra) is declared to be the seat (āsana), and the supported (ādheya) is the supreme Śiva. || 183 ||
It is proclaimed as the Nāda-liṅga and remembered as the Bindu-pīṭha;
there is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is Śiva without her. 184.
And because power resides in the body like the vital breath (prāṇa), one should therefore worship it appropriately;
for through the union of Śiva and Śakti, there arises another form. 185.
Just as the power of support (ādhāraśakti) is the form, so too is Manonmanī that very form;
she is to be known as the fragrance in flowers and likewise as the oil in sesame seeds. (186)
From the union of Manonmanā and Śiva, Sadāśiva and Gaurī arise; from the union of Sadāśiva and Gaurī, Maheśa and Mahānī arise. (187)
They call him by the name Maheśa; he is remembered as the embodiment of dance. Maheśa arises from the union of Bhavānī, originating from Umā and Rudra. (188)
From the union of Viṣṇu, Śrī, and Bhūmi, Brahmā and his consort Śivagāyatrī arise;
from the union of Brahmā and Sarasvatī, Diti and Aditi are born. (189)
From the union of Brahmā and Sāvitrī, the birth of Diti and Vedhas occurred; from the union of Aditi and Aja, the birth of Āditya and the others occurred. || 190 ||
Through their conjunction with the twelve Ādityas, they are endowed with eleven qualities;
these thirty-three deities indeed dwell in the heavenly world.
Thus the Creator, through the conjunction of hearing, brought forth the origin of giving and protection;
and at the appointed time, the goddess Uṣas arose, joined with the Sun.
From the conjunction with Āditya and Uṣas, Manu was born as Brahmā;
from the conjunction with Dānava and Rakṣas, the Rākṣasa was born from Yakṣi. (193)
Through union with Manu, Brahmā, and others, the creator is produced;
however, the fetter (pāśa) is remembered as being born from the bird through union with the creator. 194.
A Rākṣasa arises from the union with a Yakṣa; serpents are remembered as being born from Amṛta;
and from the union of a serpent with Amṛti, there arises the origin of reptiles and trees.
Just as the union of a reptile with a tree is well-remembered for trees, so too is it remembered for humans, deer, beasts, birds, and reptiles. (196)
Among all trees indeed, they are remembered in their proper order:
from the Great Unmanifest (mahad-avyakta) is remembered the Manifest (vyakta), and from the Manifest is remembered space (ākāśa). 197.
From space arises that which is known as wind; from wind, fire is remembered [to arise].
From fire, water is produced; water is remembered as earth. (198)
Inclined toward the conjunction of earth, water, fire, air, and space,
that which is established as the vital breath (prāṇa) is declared to be like the space within a jar.
If, however, at the time of its [dissolution], it remains dissolved like space, then every living being is born from it and likewise dissolves into it. (200)
They say that the sign (liṅga) is like space; it is called a sign because of the wind.
From the sign comes the act of reaching, and from the word "ga" (from *gam*), movement is traditionally understood. || 201 ||
Movement belongs to all living beings, and the dissolution of all living beings occurs [therein]; this is declared to be the nature of the *liṅgas*. One should always worship that *liṅga*. (202)
One should worship Sadāśiva in a house provided with inner chambers;
the first of all principles (tattvas) is known as the Śiva-tattva. (203)
The second is the Śakti-tattva, while the third is known as Sadāśiva; the fourth is the Īśa-tattva, and the fifth begins with Śuddhavidyā. (204)
This pure reality (śuddhatattva) is said to consist of the five principles beginning with Śivatattva;
it is traditionally remembered as the play (līlā) of Śiva, consisting of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.

When there is neither decrease nor increase in the power called action (kriyā), that is known as Sadāśiva; however, [the state] of Īśvara is produced from the powers of will (icchā) and knowledge (jñāna). || 206 ||
The principle of Īśvara is traditionally defined as the preeminence of cosmic cycles, knowledge, and action;
the principle of Vidya is traditionally defined as limited knowledge devoid of action. || 207 ||
That which is known as Vidyārudra consists of the pure tattva in five ways;
the characteristic of the tattvas is said to extend from the letter *e* up to the earth (*ava-ni*). (208)
Within Māyā, [the principle] born of Time is fixedly remembered as Māyā;
that which is born of Time from Māyā is remembered as Śuddhavidyā. || 209 ||
One should know that from the unmanifest arises passion at that time;
from passion comes the birth of the unmanifest, and from the manifest, the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas) is remembered.
That great quality is said to be threefold, beginning with the Sāttvika;
it is traditionally remembered as being Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa in sequence.

From the quality [sattva], it is designated as intellect (buddhi); from intellect, indeed, the ego (ahaṅkāra) is remembered. That which is produced from the ego and deposited in the mind (cetas) is thus called [the internal organ]. || 212 ||
From that egoity (ahaṅkāra), which is characterized by enmity and desire, the faculty of cognition (buddhīndriya) is produced.
From the egoity known as *bhūtādi*, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise. (213)
The mind is produced within the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) as the limit of the sense-faculties;
just as all this has arisen, so too is its dissolution proclaimed. || 214 ||
The specific characteristics of each principle, beginning from Māyā down to the earth, have been declared;
for all these principles, birth is from Śiva and dissolution is into Him. (215)
Here, one takes refuge in Sadāśiva through the flames of the digits of *nāda* and *bindu*;
that very group of conscious beings is united with Sadāśiva. (216)
That very group is called the "Varga" (class) and is known as insentient; it has emerged from the principles (tattvas) of Īśa and the others, beginning with Ananteśa, up to the Vidyeśas.
All this, including the mantra and its meaning, arises within the reality of Vidyā;
in this very manner, the emergence of the principles (tattvas) is traditionally taught. (218)
In this very manner, once it has been accepted, perform the worship of the Śiva-liṅga;
for it is traditionally taught that if an ignorant person touches it, the liṅga incurs all defects.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the worship of knowledge;
touched by that which has arisen, it brings about all prosperity and happiness. 220.

As it has been proclaimed regarding the contact with the setting and rising [planets] according to their respective gains, so too is the contact with the setting and the disappearance [of a planet] remembered as involving all defects. || 221 ||
One should worship with the Śiva-mantra at both sunrise and sunset;
one should worship the paths established within the Adhyātma-Śiva.
The *liṅga* is situated in the middle of the *bhaga*, and the *bhaga* is situated in the middle of the *liṅga*. (p.
85) The *liṅga* is the seat of Sadāśiva; the *liṅga* is the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) of the seat. || 223 ||
The seat of meditation for the teacher is situated on the ground at the pedestal;
thus, the twilight rite is performed mentally, and the Supreme Power is generated.
Ambī and Guṇāmbī, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, Umāmbikā, and Īśānasyāmbikā are to be known [as such]; likewise, Gaṇāmbikā belongs to Tatpuruṣa. || 225 ||
The Gaṅgā is the Śakti of the left face; Gaurī-Śakti is [known] by means of the Śaktis. In the Aghora [face], the Ūrmikā is to be known as the Śakti; thus it is designated. || 226 ||
Worship performed at the disappearance of the moon or sun brings all prosperity and happiness;
however, worship should never be performed during the Saṃkrānti or the Viṣuva.
It is proclaimed that worship performed during the times of the sun, the moon, or eclipses is fruitless.
Then, one should discard the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering) and wash the *liṅga* and its pedestal with water. (228)
Having cleansed and washed them, one should again place flowers [upon the linga].
This is declared to be the purification of the linga; now hear the purification of the mantra. || 229 ||
The five Brahma-mantras, the limbs of Śiva, the Kṣurikā and Pāśupata weapons, the Vyomavyāpin mantra known as Śiva, and the Śakti-mantra for the hands. || 230 ||
And likewise for all of them, [he should recite] the Gāyatrī, the Śrīsūkta, as well as the Vidyeśvara, Gaṇeśa, the Guardians of the Quarters, and their ten weapons. || 231 ||
The ten-syllable mantra, the secret syllable, the attendants, and the gatekeepers;
the Śrīsūkta, the Pavamāna, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Tryambaka [mantra]. || 232 ||
The Brahmasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Gaurīgāyatrī mantra, the Ariṇanvariṇa Rudra, and likewise the Jyeṣṭhasoma; (p. 87) || 233 ||
One should worship Vikarṇa and Jātavedas with the mantra "devasya tvā," as well as the Durgāsūkta,
the Umāsūkta, and the retinue of door-keepers.
One should extract the mantra of Gaṇapati, the mantra of Skanda, the mantra of Sūrya, and that of Sarasvatī; likewise, one should extract the mantras for the worship of all other deities. || 235 ||

The *liṅga* is contained within the *ālaya*, and Śiva is contained within the *liṅga*. Having established [the *ālaya*] in the middle of the *kuṃbha*, what need is there to install Śiva into the *liṅga*? (236)
Just as fire exists within the hearth, so does the flame reside within the practitioner;
one should then place the mobile *liṅga*, which is the connection between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Wherever one recites the mantra of the Tantra after having performed worship,
one should contemplate the divine play (*līlā*) of the gods such as Umā and Skanda. (238)
Having meditated upon the Preceptor in one's mind—whether he be standing, in a dancing posture, or reclining—one should prepare a seat for him. 239.
Having honored him with his form, one should there recite the mantra;
one should extract the mantras beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ.
Having understood the sequence of the five purifications, one should subsequently recite [the mantra];
one should worship the gatekeepers at the doors of the mandala’s entrance. (241)
Standing on that spot with palms joined in reverence, Nandikeśvara is situated;
Mahākāla is proclaimed to be in the south and at the eastern gate.
Nandisūcimukha has his hands joined in *añjali*;
Daṇḍadhārī and Nāgadhārī are proclaimed to hold [their respective implements] in their right and left hands respectively. (243)
In the right [hand] there is the *halapadma-añjali* and the *kālahastaka*;
in the left hand there is the *daṇḍadhara-mudrā* and the *kālaka*.
The left foot is bent like a staff and positioned on the right;
slightly in the *tribhaṅga* posture upon the Gaṅgā, the left foot is indeed bent. (245)
Adorned with a crown and a basket, formidable with fangs in his mouth,
possessing three eyes and four arms, he is endowed with the nature of Rudra.
Wearing a waist-thread and a belly-band, clad in a sacred thread, and adorned with serpent ornaments, he stands upon a lotus seat endowed with the characteristics of a [divine] earring.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings by his own name, the preceptor [should know that] Nandīśa is red in color, while Kala is indeed the color of Viṣṇu. (248) p. 90)
One should meditate upon him as possessing a fierce form and adorned with all ornaments;
or else, another method regarding the form of his hands will now be described. (249)
Nandīśa is dark-complexioned, has two arms joined with another [deity], holds an axe in his left hand, and a bamboo staff in his right. (250)
Nandīśa, however, has the luster of saffron and holds an axe and a bamboo staff;
he has two eyes and three arms, and is likewise the slayer of Nandi and Kāla. (251)
Where the two great-souled ones, Nandin and Kāla, stand at the eastern gate, Ananta and Paśupati are the guardians of the southern gate. (252)
Ananta is red in color and is equipped with the vajra weapon; Paśupati is blue in color, holding a spear in his hand, and has fierce eyes. (253)
The two gatekeepers of the western door are Siṃdhu and Muṇḍin; likewise, at the front of the Sindhu [gate] is Pāhaṃ, who has fierce fangs and holds a bird in his hand.
O Bhṛṅgīśa, Vijaya and [Vijayā], who possess the color of a jasmine flower and the moon, as well as the color of a blue lotus, are the guardians of the northern gate. 255.
Vijaya, terrifying with a trident in hand, has a portion of Indra and Gaurī;
Bhṛṅgīśa, who is the color of a bhr̥ṅga bee, is equipped with a knife as a weapon in his hand.
The Tribhaṅgī posture, the Kuñcika, and the foot endowed with fierce fangs are proclaimed for the door of the temple pavilion and for every door.
At the locations of the gateways of the gopuras, one should have the forms of spirits fashioned; namely, Saṃvṛtta, Śriyāvṛtta, Kuṇḍodara, and Bṛhadudara. (p. 92) 258.
The lion-faced and the elephant-faced [deities], as well as the one-legged and the downward-facing, are all white and dark in appearance, and are each endowed with a sword in hand. (259)
Some beings at every gate held tridents as weapons;
indeed, [these] were stationed at the four gates of the enclosure and the gate-towers.
Having the color of a conch shell, with black eyes, stationed at the door of the pavilion, he has two eyes, is dark-complexioned, holds a trident in his hand, and bestows fearlessness. (261)
The spirits with monkey faces, horse faces,
and human faces were fashioned as the dance pavilions at the four gates, appearing like the very walls and gate-towers of the city.
We shall thus describe the external gate-towers (*gopura*) as follows:
[they are] Virūpākṣa with feet upwards, Kalaṅka, and Vakrapādaka. (263) p. 93)
Vāmana, Galaka, and the very powerful Daṇḍapāla are known as the bearers of bamboo staffs at the gate of the great gopura.
The gatekeeper should assign [these] for all [the deities] starting from the southeast:
one dark-blue, one resembling yellow, both holding tridents as weapons and joined with their respective consorts.
At each and every door, one should place the two-eyed ones, the various [deities], and the Bhūtakas;
at the western door of the inner sanctum, one should install Sulabha and Sumukha.
One should visualize the white and yellow [deities] as holding bamboo staffs; for all of them, one should assign the masculine gender as the door-keepers. (267)
In the female gate, there shall be only femininity; one should arrange them in due order.
Having first worshipped those stationed at the gates, the gatekeepers are the second. (p. 94) 268.
The third [enclosure] begins with Vṛṣabha and so forth, while Indra and the others constitute the fourth;
the fifth is the Bhadrapīṭha—thus is the outer enclosure arranged.
Wherever there is an entrance for the door, the preceptor should specifically offer oblations to the seven deities at each of those places.
On the upper and lower sections of the cloth, the wise one should worship Vighneśa,
as well as Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Śrīdevī, and Sarasvatī.
