The wise one should worship [the deities] on the right and further to the right in due order;
here, the pair of yogas is said to be Bhuvaṅga and Pataṅga. || 272 ||
One should worship Vimala and Subāhu at the two door-panels;
having worshipped Vimala on the right, one should sacrifice to Subāhu on the left. (273)
One should especially worship [the deity] with the mantra consisting of one's own name alone;
then one should worship the retinue, beginning with Vṛṣa and ending with the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha). || 274 ||
First, having worshipped Vṛṣabha in the east with the mantra "tīkṣṇaśṛṅgāya," and having fully worshipped Durga in the southeast with the mantra "kātyāyanī. || 275 ||
On the right, one measuring seven units, holding a severed head upon his vehicle;
one should worship him specifically with the very first letter of his own name.
One should place Vīrabhadra in the east and Vighneśa in the west;
one should worship both Vīrabhadra and Vighneśa for seven measures of time.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa in the southwest with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," [one should worship] Sukumāra in the west with the mantra "subrahmaṇyāya. (278)
Having worshipped Jyeṣṭha in the northwest with the mantra "To the one whose banner is a crow" (kākadhvajāya),
and having honored Viṣṇu in the north with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu" (This is Viṣṇu).
Having worshipped Caṇḍa in the northeast with the mantra for Caṇḍeśvara, one should worship Indra and the other world-protectors, bearing their respective colors, vehicles, and emblems.
One should worship the weapons there, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise with the first letter of each deity's own name, as well as the deities of childhood and youth.
One facing either east or north should likewise worship Āmoda and Pramoda, the two creators of obstacles who ensure the absence of obstacles, upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
In front of the Bhūtapīṭha, one should arrange the Candrapīṭha;
one should worship [the deities] in their respective places, starting from the southeast (Āgneya) up to the northeast (Īśa). || 283 ||
Therefore, one should especially worship the world-protectors, such as Indra and the others, either outside the mandala or even within its walls. || 284 ||
On the northern side of the door, the wise man should worship Brahmā; between the two Pitāmahas, he should likewise worship Asvara and Gaṇa.
One should worship the seven Rohiṇīs between Varuṇa and Vāyu;
the wise man should worship the sages between Yama and Nairṛta.
One should worship the eight Vasus between Vāyu and Soma;
one should worship the eleven Rudras between the North and the Northeast. || 287 ||
Whether it be of two kinds, or again of three kinds,
or even of one kind, one should worship in that location which has been described as the proper place. (288)
Having worshipped the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) at the aforementioned place, it is further described as follows:
then, having prepared the sacrificial pedestal, one should especially [worship] in the four directions. (289)
One should install the pedestal at the eastern gate, both externally and internally;
within is the Mṛta-pīṭha, and the external pedestal is the Piśācaka.
The seat of the Yakṣas is in the south, that of the Rākṣasas in the west, and that of the Gandharvas in the north; the central one is in the east and west. || 291 ||

The wise one should likewise [employ] fierce mantras for external [enemies] and gentle ones for internal [affairs], using a mantra beginning with his own name, preceded by the syllable Oṃ and ending with "namo 'stu te. (292)
One should strike the great bell with the mantra *huṃ*;
then, having recited the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should also bring the cloth [painting] there. (293)
Then, having reached the inner sanctum (garbhageha), one should worship at the entrance of the womb (garbhadvāra):
Jñānaśakti should be on the right, and Kriyāśakti on the left.
One should worship the two-armed, dark-complexioned [deity] by its own name;
then, having reached the inner sanctum, one should remain either seated or standing. (295)
In the midst of the water in the conch, one should subsequently place the Śiva-mantra, accompanied by the Amṛtasurabhimudrā and joined with perfumes, flowers, and kuśa grass.
Power alone is said to be the seat (āsana) through its connection with the support and the scripture;
it is a great lion-throne in the form of a quadrangle, fashioned from the feet. || 297 ||
The lion-throne for the ritual bath is said to be square and elongated;
the yoga-seat, however, has ten points, is multicolored, and is most beautiful. (298)

Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) with the ten-syllable mantra, proceeding clockwise from the east and so forth, one should [place] the Great Vṛtta of four feet, which sustains the four Vedas. || 299 ||
Having covered [the area] with the three qualities (guṇas), one should place small boundary-markers (kṣulikā) in the four directions;
thus is the yogic posture (yogāsana) described, and one should invoke Sadāśiva.
One should cause [the deity] to be conveyed by means of the *sadyojāta* mantra, endowed with the characteristics previously described;
[one should perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*), the seat (*āsana*), the union (*yoga*), and the pure bath (*snāna*) upon the seat.
The practitioner of mantra should offer water for the feet with the heart-mantra and cause the water for sipping to be given;
he should cause the deity to meditate upon the lion-throne and perform the consecration.
One should take water from a wooden trough and sprinkle it upon the *gaṇḍikā*;
the wise one should then bathe [the image] with fragrant substances filling an *āḍhaka* in due order. (303)
One should consecrate [the body] with the powders of *āmalī* fruit and the weapons of Śiva;
then, having smeared the body with the powder of *puṣṭa*, one should rub it again.
One should bathe [the image] slowly and worship it according to the proper sequence.
Afterward, one should apply a paste of turmeric and worship with scented water.
Three bhāras is declared to be the best; two bhāras is remembered as the middling.
One who knows the Dharma should worship this water in sequence using eight *droṇas*;
likewise, one should include *uśīra*, sandalwood, and what is known as *jayotipa*.
One should offer the mantra-flower with the head and cause the oblation to be given with the mantra.
At the conclusion of the bath, having put on a garment, one should discard the wet cloth. (308)
The study of the Vedas accompanied by instrumental music and song in the four directions, along with the five Brahmans, the Śivāṅgas, the Tryambaka mantra, and the Viṣṇusūkta; 309.
The Brahmasūkta, the Gaurīsūkta, the Śrīrudra, the Pavamāna, the Varuṇasūkta—these six hymns—and thereafter the Tvaritarudra. (310)
Having performed worship at the proper time, one should recite the Svastisūkta for all;
one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with the ten-syllable mantra and indeed with the heart-mantra.
Afterwards, one should prepare the Anantāsana and worship it especially;
then, one should place the sprout and stalk of the seed-syllable of Śakti, followed by Dharma and the other [virtues].
Then there is knowledge of the Dharma, dispassion, and thereafter sovereignty.
Dispassion arises from the yellow element, and sovereignty from the white water. (313)
One should place knowledge of the Dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty in the cardinal directions;
these are the four spheres (gulakā), the four ages (caturyugā), and they are males, not neuter.
Their colors are white, red, yellow, and black;
the pair of heads is in the northeast, while the pair of feet is in the southwest.
In the southeast he should place a four-footed [seat], and in the northwest a four-footed [seat];
upon these he should sequentially install the eight Vidyeśvaras.
One should place [the deities] from Anantarya to Ekanetrānta in the eastern directions;
one should place Īśāna in the cardinal directions and Ekarudra and the others in the intermediate corners.
The five japā flowers, the bandhūka, the aśoka, and saffron (kuṅkuma),
along with padmanābha and janābha, are the pigments for the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas). (318)
Three-eyed, four-armed, and serene, adorned with a crown of matted locks, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, dark-complexioned, and bearing an axe. || 319 ||
Having thus performed the ritual placement according to the rule, the seat of Ananta is here described;
one should worship the seat of Ananta in this manner with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
That lotus, worshipped and shining, has its stalk turned upwards;
it is fashioned with eight petals above and is endowed with filaments. || 321 ||
Having reflected in meditation, one should place the powers upon the eight petals:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī in the west, north, and south respectively.
Having placed Kāliñca in the eastern direction (Aindra), Kalavikaraṇī in the southeast (Pāvaka),
Balavikaraṇī in the southwest (Nairṛtya), and Balapramathinī in the northwest (Vāyu). || 323 ||
The Sarvabhūtadamanī, however, is in the direction of Īśāna; she is Manonmanī, resembling the Atasi flower, two-eyed, and likewise Dhāraṇī. (324)
Vāmī, Jyeṣṭhī, Dhūmravarṇī, Pāśamahābalā, Balavikaraṇī, Kṛṣṇā, Paraśuhastā, and Triṇetriṇī. || 325 ||
The goddess Balapramathinī is red in color and holds a pair of weapons;
the goddess Sarvabhūtadamani has a mace in her hand and wears beautiful garments. (326)

Having meditated thus according to the prescribed rule upon Manonmanī, who has the luster of the color of pure crystal and holds a rosary of beads, one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 327 ||
Vāmadeva is the stalk joined with the fresh sprout;
Aghora is the cluster of petals; and Puruṣa shall be the pericarp. (328)
One should offer the Īśāna vessel and the vessel marked with the lotus;
thus is the lotus-seat described. Afterwards, one should give water for sipping (ācamana) with the left hand.
One should offer the sacred thread with the *hṛdayatantra* and the *kavaca*,
and give perfume with the *vāma* mantra, while offering flowers with the *īśāna* mantra.
The crown, the earrings, the waist-thread, and the belly-band should be given with the *śikhā* mantra; the necklace should be given with the *hṛdaya* mantra. (331)
With ornaments and golden flowers, one should give with a devoted heart;
[there should be] a golden archway, a golden leaf, and fruit adorned with the art of leaf-cutting.
It should be given with armor; one should wrap it in a multicolored cloth.
(p. 107) With various fine fabrics and divine garments, [one prepares] a five-colored woolen blanket. 333.
Adorned with all ornaments and beautified by flower garlands,
one should offer incense according to the proper rule and specifically in the correct sequence.
Aloe-wood, sandalwood, resin, and likewise *gulphala*, along with camphor and musk, combined with honey, clarified butter, and sugar. || 335 ||
One should offer incense endowed with all fragrances in the proper sequence;
specifically, one should smear the pedestal of the Liṅga with sandalwood paste while reciting the Heart-mantra.
One should likewise grind together musk and camphor for an ointment;
thereafter, one should offer clothing and ornaments, and finally present incense.
Having drawn aside the concealed cloth, one should strike the great bell;
incense should be offered to the east, accompanied by the sounding of the bell. (338)
Holding a bell in his hand, [he should approach] the pinnacle which is one cubit in length;
taking incense in his right hand, he should hold a wood-apple fruit measuring one cubit.
In this manner, incense should be offered; one should cause the āyāmananta to be presented.
Grasping a flower with the hand, it should be joined with the *padmāvakra* [mudrā]. (340)
Having first offered the fivefold oblation (pañcamukha) to the upper direction and others, one should thereafter cause water to be offered;
at the conclusion of that, one should offer a lamp accompanied by the ringing of a bell.
Having offered water with a conch vessel while holding it with both hands,
one should then make a handful of flowers and display the *surabhi-mudrā*.
Then, having received the *liṅgamudrā*, one should cause the *nīrājana* rite to be performed.
109) One should offer mouth-freshener (*mukhavāsa*) together with ashes and the five roots (*pañcamūla*). || 343 ||
The forehead, the heart, the navel, and the feet in due order, as well as the two arms and the two ears, are joined with the horns of the bull. 344.
Alternatively, in another manner, having specifically applied ashes endowed with thirty-eight kalās, or likewise sixteen at the joints; || 345 ||
Having washed one's hands at that time, one should likewise worship Gaurī;
thereafter, one should perform the entire [rite] according to the sequence not yet mentioned.
But at the conclusion of the worship of the *liṅgas*, one should perform the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*).
The first enclosure shall consist of the limbs of Brahmā, as well as the Vidyēśvaras and Gaṇēśvaras;
then the guardians of the directions and the ten weapons—this is the fivefold enclosure of the Lord in due order. (347)
That which is called "obstruction" (varaṇa) should be deposited in those respective locations. || 348 ||
White, red, yellow, blackish, and resembling milk—these are the colors of Brahmā, beginning with Sadyojāta; she has three eyes and four arms. (349)
Equipped with an axe and a trident, and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons—this is called the peaceful Īśāna; others are remembered as the fierce (raudra) forms. || 350 ||
Having worshipped with the six limbs— consisting of the heart, head, crest, armor, weapon, and eyes— one should then worship the limb of Brahmā.
Japanese indigo, the *cakra-bandhūka*, the *aśoka*, and saffron; the *padmanābha* and the *janābha* are the pigments for the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*). (352)
Three-eyed, four-armed, and gentle, adorned with a crown of matted locks, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and bearing a dark axe. || 353 ||
One should worship the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśāna), endowed with these characteristics, possessing the luster of pure gold, lapis lazuli, and rubies. 354.
The emerald, the lotus leaf, that which resembles the autumnal moon, silver, and red-colored [pigments] are the colors for the Gaṇeśas. (355)
One should worship the lords of the Gaṇas, endowed with the characteristics previously described:
white, red, yellow, black, white, and smoke-colored. (356)
Silver is like white, and it may also resemble the color of a very young child;
it possesses the color of its respective weapon and is endowed with its respective form. (357)
The moving [forms] are the buffalo, the lion, the elephant, the tortoise, the deer, as well as the bull; for these, the respective vehicle is indeed their mount. (358)
Having performed the worship of the five enclosures together with perfumes and flowers, the wise one should thereafter offer incense.
One should offer incense, a lamp, flowers, a palm-leaf fan, a chowrie, a bell, and a mirror with the heart mantra. || 360 ||
Subsequently, at the time of the ritual worship of the Sakala [deity], one should perform the retention of the entire [mantra] accompanied by the chanting of the mantra,
excluding the fifth enclosure (pañcamāvaraṇa).
Afterwards, one should arrange the *vimalāsana* and indeed the *bhojāsana*.
The *vimalāsana* is said to be circular and resembles pure crystal. (362)
One should place Guṇāmbikā to the north, and likewise Mahātapa in the eastern quarter;
then one should cause Gaurī to be placed in the east, and [the remaining deity] in the western quarter.
Their colors are yellow, red, white, and black; they have two eyes, beautiful faces, and full, elevated breasts. (364)
Having established [the offerings] in the four directions, one should worship them with perfumes and other articles;
then, above the pure seat, one should meditate upon Sadāśiva.
One should cause the oblation to be offered to the deity according to the procedure for the naivedya;
thus is the mental [offering] described, which one should perform at the appropriate time.

The invocation-seat (āvāhanāsana) is for the yoga-bath; the lion-seat (siṃhāsana) occurs during worship; the infinite-lotus seat (anantapadma) is for the offering; and the stainless seat (vimala) is for the meal. (367)
The "fivefold seat" (pañcāsana) has been proclaimed; these consist of the five elements.
They should be visualized at their respective times as the seat in due order.
The lion-throne is said to be fourfold, the foremost among yogic postures;
likewise, there are the self-seat, the lotus, the infinite, and the tortoise-vajra.
White, red, yellow, black, and variegated. || 370 ||
Then Keśava, the first foot [of the mantra], covered with the three qualities (guṇas),
shall cover the silk cloth of all the seats.
One should place the fire in sequence with fire, sun, and moon;
then one should place rajas, tamas, and sattva upon it. (372)
One should place the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self,
having worshipped them equally with perfumes and other offerings, accompanied by their own seed-syllables using the Heart-mantra.
Having meditated upon the form of Sadāśiva, endowed with the characteristics previously described,
and having thus meditated upon Sadāśiva with the mind, one should worship him in due order.
One should worship with the mantra "brahmajajñānam" in the forenoon, with "tryambakam" at midday,
and with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu" in the evening.
Then, the earth, water, fire, air, and space—these five elements constitute the pedestal (pīṭha) that extends from the exterior to the interior, and indeed to the limit of space. || 376 ||
In this manner, one should perform the mental visualization and worship according to the sequence;
then, above the pure seat (vimalāsana), one should cause the sacrificial oblation (havir) to be offered. (377)
Whether it be one *āsaka*, half of that, or even a *droṇa* or half a *droṇa*, the rice is said to be made of gold, white in color, and consisting of *śāli* grain. (378)
One should cook an equal amount of sugar and ghee, or even half that amount, having combined it with jaggery and curd along with milk. (379)
One should cause a coconut accompanied by *upadaṃśa* (side dishes) to be offered;
one should present it with the [mantra] addressed to Puruṣa and perform the *bali* offering in that very direction.
One should then announce the retinue of all [deities], beginning with Kāla;
thereafter, one should maintain the perpetual fire and perform the supreme fire-ritual (agnikārya).
Then, having performed a perpetual festival accompanied by dance and song,
singing should take place at the time of the oblation, and after that, one should have dancing performed. (382)
After the *culikodanta* [rite], one should perform the worship of the scriptures (*āgama-arcana*).
In this manner, one should perform it in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. (383)
There is a certain distinction here: one should perform worship in the evening;
then, having reached the beginning of the night, one should clean the dance pavilion.
Having first sprinkled [the deity] with the Puruṣa-sūkta and removed the previous flowers, one should adorn the Dancing Form and meditate upon the Pure Dance. || 385 ||
But for the courtesan, having specially adorned all [the deities],
it should be accompanied by instrumental music and song, and provided with the sixty-four arts.

One should always cause the musical instruments and the recitation to be performed; at its conclusion, having offered incense and a lamp, the preceptor should provide protection according to the path of the scriptures. (387)
One should provide protection from the evening and set down the vessel for the spirits;
the characteristic mark is a hand of cotton, and there should be a lamp-vessel and a flower.
Having placed the five vessels upon a three-legged stand, starting with the vessel for the deity,
one should offer incense and flowers separately for each of the vessels.
The practitioner should offer the *surabhi-mudrā* and also perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
One should arrange three, five, seven, or nine lamps.
One should cause the deity and the goddess to perform circumambulation three times;
then, having thrice circled a lamp and cotton ash, one should cast them away.
Having placed everything with the lamp, one should cause the Rudrakanyās to be offered;
having set them down before the pedestal, one should thus install the *yaṃ* [syllables] in sequence. (391)
The evening protection (sāyarakṣā) should be bestowed, and afterwards one should perform the worship;
for where there is no time [for it] at dawn, the protection should indeed be given in the evening. || 392 ||
One should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony at all times and likewise scatter ashes;
or else, one may do so in another manner, especially during the night. (393)
A crown and a golden flower, a crescent moon and a sphere;
a sacred thread and a bracelet, all adorned with gold and jewels. (394)
A garland for the head, a garland of Rudrākṣas, and upper garments for the officiating priests;
one should perform the ritual cutting of leaves, and the Bilva trees should be variegated according to the season.
The archway (toraṇa) of this [deity] should be adorned with golden ornaments and the figure of a deer;
having prepared it thus, one should worship it in due order in the evening as before. (396)
One should arrange a flower mandala, either made of gold or silver, adorned with all kinds of jewels, or whatever else may be beautiful.
Whether during a transit [of a planet], at the time of the birth of a kinsman, or even on one's own birthday, someone may experience either victory or even death on that day. (398)
On other auspicious lunar mansions and on Sundays, it is prescribed that one should fashion a five-faced *liṅga* made of seven parts of gold, which is infinite [in merit]. (399)
One should fashion a linga-shape out of gold, silver, or even copper;
this indeed should be globular in form and endowed with five faces.
One should place that *liṅga* into the [receiving] *liṅga* and worship it according to the previous sequence.
Worship (*arcana*), adoration (*pūjana*), and the rite for pacification (*śāntika*) are thus threefold. (401)
Worship ending with the lamp is declared to be the "childhood" (bālya) rite;
worship ending with the festival is declared to be the "pacifying" (śāntika) rite; thus one should perform the ritual action in three ways. || 402 ||
Alternatively, in another manner, the wise one should worship Sadyojāta and the others in the chamber of the western door; now the retinue is described.
One should place the bull in the position of the prince and the prince in the position of the bull;
on Sunday, at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the daily festival.
In the eight directions, the courtesans should perform a dance,
each holding a staff in her hand while executing various individual movements.
Having done this, one should especially worship Sadāśiva;
then, having removed the *nirmālya*, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa. (406)
One should cause betel-leaf, mouth-perfume, and water to be offered.
Now hear about the pacification of everything, beginning with the powers of the five enclosures. || 407 ||
Ambī, Gaṇāmbī, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Umā—these are known as the powers (śaktis) of the five Brahmans, together with the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga). || 408 ||
Brahmī, Svadhā, Kānti, Gṛhapuṣṭi, Śruti, as well as Kīrti—these are the eight powers (śaktis) of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas). || 409 ||
Padayā, Devanāyī, Kuntī, Mantriṇī, Kālī, Mālinī, Umā, Vajriṇī, and Gaṇaśānā. || 410 ||
Śaśī, Devī, Pralomī, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā;
Kālakālī, Jātārī, Nīlī, and Sukeśinī. (411)
Lāyinī, Mahinī, Liṅginī, and likewise Mahiṣī; Vṛtti, Nivṛtti, Vasudhā, and Svarūpiṇī. || 412 ||
Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī—these are the twelve powers (viśakti) of the world-protectors;
likewise, Vilāsinī, Virūpī, Dhāriṇī, and Vimukhī. || 413 ||
Nikhī, Damukhī, Matiśrī, and Haṃsamālinī—
these ten weapons are the Śaktis of the five enclosures.
First, one should prepare a seat; second, one should invoke Śiva;
third, the water for washing the feet (pādya); and fourth, the water for sipping (ācamanīya). || 415 ||
The fifth [offering] is the arghya to be given; one should offer incense as the sixth.
124) The seventh is the consecration, and the eighth is the perfume and flowers. || 416 ||
The ninth is clothing and ornaments, the tenth is incense and lamps;
the eleventh is the mudrās, and the twelfth is the food offering. || 417 ||
One should offer the thirteenth *bali*; the fourteenth is for the perpetual fires; the fifteenth is the perpetual festival (*nityotsava*); and the sixteenth is indeed the dance (*nṛtta*). (418)
Thus has been declared the sequence of worship performed according to the fivefold purification.
Now I shall explain the sequence of the manifestations (vyūha), beginning with the manifestation of the Vidyā.
Here, the great Vidyāvyūha, beginning with Vāmadeva and others, is to be known;
it is situated in the Vanaparvan and serves as a path of memory for those who take hold of it. 420.
These powers, beginning with Vāmā, are known as the *vidyā-vyūha* (the array of knowledge).
That which is proclaimed as the eight [powers] beginning with Aghora is the *vigraheśvara-vyūhaka* (the array of the lords of the body). (421)
The non-terrible, the exceedingly terrible, the non-terrible, the subtle, Śiva, and likewise Sarva from all [aspects] and for all [beings]—he is remembered as being in the form of Umā. (422)
The arrays of Vigraheśvara are proclaimed to be eightfold:
Ambikā, Brahmavetālī, Triguṇī, and also Sthāṇimanī. (423)
Rūpiṇī, Mahājvālā, and likewise the other, Mālinī; Suvetālī shall be Gaurī, and Śaktyaghorā is Nandinī. || 424 ||
In the elevenfold array, there are the Dhūta, Vyūha, and Mahābala for kings; the two Rudra arrays are fierce, and it is surrounded by those possessing great strength.
Joined with the upward-facing *kogi* (the letter *u*), it is a circle (*vṛtta*) established in the principle of Īśvara;
there, Vidyeśvara and the others, as well as Mūrtīśa and Gaṇeśvara, are to be joined. (426)
One should install the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas), beginning with Ananteśa, in their respective arrays according to the sequence of the arrays:
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, and Bhava. (427)
One should worship the array [of deities] according to the sequence of the arrays, beginning with Īśāna, Mahādeva, Bhīma, and the Vasus, and starting from Umā up to Gaṇeśāna.
Then, the reality of Sadāśiva remains thus as the supreme pervader;
therein, through the Brahma-mantras and the limbs [of the mantra], Nada, Bindu, and Sadāśiva are established. (429)
The power Śāntyatītā, Ambikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, as well as Mocikā, the upward-moving (Urdhvagā), Vyāpikā, and Vyomarūpiṇī. || 430 ||
She is infinite, without protector, and likewise without support;
she is the source of mantras, Mahāmāyā, and furthermore, the partless Śakti. (431)

Śiva is beyond the senses; His [nature] is partless, devoid of qualities, imperishable, and declared to be of the nature of consciousness. In the state of purity, there is this pentad of principles (tattva-pañcaka).
Since the ten [objects] beginning with sound are endowed with qualities, and since [the senses] are equal [in number],
the distinction [between them] is established by the relationship of primary and secondary (aṅga-aṅgin), starting from the sense of sight.

The Self as the Imperishable Brahman (akṣara-brahman), the Brahman of the phonemes (varṇa-brahman) immediately following it, and the Brahman of the worlds (bhuvana-brahman)—this is declared to be the name of Brahman. || 434 ||
Sadāśiva, Liṅga-kumbha, Maheśa, Yāgamūrti, Utkrama, and Rudradaivatyam—these are the presiding deities. || 435 ||
One should deposit all the *vidyā-tattvas* in the *ātma-tattva*, which is gentle;
one should deposit the *śiva-tattvas* in the center, [visualizing] Sadāśiva at the time of meditation. (436)
In this very manner, at the three junctions of the day, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva rites,
including the offering of the *nirmālya* and *naivedya*, and then observe the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
The wise man should indeed cast the discarded offering (nirmālya) onto the ground, into fire, or into water;
he should also cause it to be given to cows and to laboring servants.
One should likewise worship the sixteen [deities] and the first [group], as well as Vighneśa and Kṣetrapālaka,
together with their retinues and others, along with the Guru, the Book, and the Fire.
Viṣṇu and Brahmā, along with Durgā, Kālī, the gods of the Sun, and all other deities, [are present] for the Yakṣas, the lords of Nāgas, and the Yogīs. || 440 ||
One who possesses the heart-mantra should smear the *liṅga* and the pedestal with fragrant *agaru*, camphor, sandalwood, and musk, along with white pigment (*gaurikā*). (441)
Jātī, kanaka, kadamba, dvikarṇī, trikarṇikā, nandyāvarta, śriyāvarta, nīlotpala, and mallikā. || 442 ||
One should worship with such fragrant flowers and garlands;
one should especially honor the Lord of Gods with the Śiva-mantra. || 443 ||
One should establish Gaurī with the mantra "gaurīrmimāya" and Gaurī with the left [hand];
one should meditate on the form of Śiva with six faces and contemplate the form of the Goddess. || 444 ||
One should offer incense in sequence with the Aghora mantra, accompanied by the ringing of a bell;
likewise, a lamp made from cotton wick and fueled by camphor.
Having lit a lamp made of cow-dung, three finger-breadths in size is considered the best;
one should especially offer the lamp with the mantra beginning "praśāntāya. (446)
A portion of *droṇa* rice, accompanied by a portion of *guṇa* vegetables, along with *marīcī*, salt, coconut, and green gram. 447.
Cake should be offered as food for the crows, mixed with jaggery;
one should also present plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, and the three myrobalans (triphalā). || 448 ||
There, one should cause water to be given, accompanied by a mouth-cleansing cloth;
there, betel-leaf with camphor and mixed with oil [should be offered]. (449)
One obtains the fulfillment of desired objects; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, what was intended for those seeking specific desires has been declared, and the presiding deities have been proclaimed. (450)
One should offer eight flowers, three fragrances, and seven waters;
likewise, three flowers, three kinds of incense, the bell, and the seat—these eight. (451)

One should indeed cause the mudrās of four [deities] to be given in secret; for two, one should provide them during the invocation, the arghya-vessels, the bathing, the incense, and the anointing. (452)
Having seated [the deity] and then dismissed [any preliminary offerings], one should properly apply the eight flowers.
One should properly apply fragrance in three instances: during the water-offering (arghya), the unguent (pralepana), and the bath (snāna).
In the rites of invocation, the offering of arghya, bathing, sipping water (ācamana),
the presentation of food, and dismissal, one should employ water seven times.

At the invocation, at the end of the worship, and likewise at the conclusion of the dismissal, the knower of mantras should offer the *arghya*; thus one should arrange it for these three occasions. (455)
At the time of offering the seat, at the conclusion of the bath, during the worship, and likewise at the time of offering the food and the dismissal, one should employ water seven times. (456)

At the invocation, at the end of the worship, and likewise at the conclusion of the dismissal, the knower of mantras should offer the *arghya*; thus one should arrange it for these three occasions. (457)
At the time of offering the seat, at the conclusion of the bath, and also during the worship—or alternatively, at the end of the worship—the great incense is highly recommended. (458)
At the commencement of the bath and at its conclusion, especially when offering incense; at the time of the food offering and at its end; at the beginning of the festival and at its conclusion—(459)
At the conclusion of the dance, the wise one should strike the great bell;
likewise, during the removal of the used garlands and during the act of decorating with flowers.
At the time of the offering, at the end of the twilight rite, the "concealed cloth" (pracchannapaṭa) is prescribed;
however, at the invocation and at the conclusion of the worship, the display of mudrās is required. (461)
One should offer fragrance along with a flower, and join the flower with fragrance; one should offer incense along with a lamp, and join the lamp with the lamp. || 462 ||
At the time of worshiping the gods, [the image] should be covered with a concealed cloth;
[one must avoid] those afflicted by sinful diseases, those who have fallen from their vows, atheists, and those who defile religious observances.
One should avoid from afar those who have made it their purpose to revile the gods, as well as Rākṣasas, Asuras, Piśācas, and Brahmarākṣasas. || 464 ||
One should go outside the enclosure accompanied by the sounding of bells;
having performed the recitation of the root mantra, one should contemplate the presence of the deity.
All men should contemplate Śiva within themselves with devotion;
personal worship is supreme, and only thereafter should one begin to eat. (466)
If one is unable to perform worship, one should at least perform the touching;
if one is unable even to touch it, the sight of the liṅga is supreme.
Day and night, at the three junctions of the day, one should enter the temple of Śiva;
however, at the outer enclosure, one should perform circumambulation by the right-hand path.
Moving by way of the left and right paths with the burden within, one should perform a circumambulation;
then, one should perform a circumambulation and cross over the *somasūtra*.
One should cause the crossing over of the Śakti above the Soma-thread;
otherwise, by crossing over the Nirmālya, one falls to the surface of the earth due to that fault.
[One] is born upon the surface of the earth as a worm, an insect, a moth, or the like;
therefore, with every effort, perform [the practice] with both the left and the right hands. (471)
By performing a circumambulation twice over, the fruit of prostration shall be attained;
thus the wise man, having performed the five-limbed and the eight-limbed prostration. || 472 ||
On the two outer ears and on the head—these five locations are known as the "Name of the Lord" and are called the "Five Limbs. || 473 ||
Having offered salutations with effort by means of both hands and from the head,
it is called the "staff-prostration" (daṇḍa-namaskāra), which is joined like a staff to a rope.
With his two feet, both knees, both hands, forehead, and ears, he should touch the earth. (475)
Renowned as the eightfold [path], it bestows all sovereignty and happiness;
having performed this mentally, one goes to the world of Śiva. (476)
Having performed circumambulation and prostration, as well as the offering of oneself, or otherwise, one should act in whatever way is accessible through devotion. || 477 ||
After that, for the purpose of purifying the body, I shall describe the ritual service (upacāra) for the sake of the city, namely the worship of the deity. (478)
At the end of the ten-fold ritual service (daśopacāra), there will be sixteen;
at the end of the offering (bali), twenty-five; and thirty-six at the conclusion of the tāṇḍava dance.

The invocation, the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the bath, the scents, the flowers, the incense, the food offering (naivedya), and the dismissal (visarjana). || 480 ||
One should perform [the rite] up to the point where it is said, "to be known through the ten services" (p.
Having established [the deity] during the invocation, one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering. (481)
Bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, and flowers.
Incense, lamps, and food offerings are used during the salutation and the dismissal. || 482 ||
One should perform the ritual with exactly sixteen services;
having invoked [the deity] and established [him], one should offer a welcome and the honors due to a guest.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya), as well as the bath, a lower garment, and an upper garment;
ornaments, fragrance, and flowers, as well as incense, a lamp, and another arghya offering. || 484 ||
The lustration with the waving of lights (nīrājana), the application of collyrium (añjana), the fly-whisk (cāmara), and the mirror (darpaṇa) here;
likewise, the display of the ten mudrās and the worship of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa-pūjana). || 485 ||
The rite of food offering, the fire oblation, the presentation of bali, as well as recitation,
meditative absorption, hymns of praise, prostration, festival, song, and dance; (486)
The dismissal is traditionally known as the thirty-six-fold service;
likewise, at the conclusion of the dance, even in rites for prosperity, there is worship of the deity for the sake of others.
I shall speak of the ritual procedure for one's own sake; listen to me! [I will explain] the invocation, the installation, the welcome, and the confinement. (488)

The arrangement of the limbs and minor members, as well as water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya), along with perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and likewise the bath; 489.
Garments, the sacred thread, perfumes, flowers, incense, a mirror, the lustration rite (nīrājana), ornaments, song, and likewise drama and dance. || 490 ||
The visualization of the mudrās has been taught, as well as the worship performed with circumambulation;
likewise, the rite of food offerings and fire oblations, meditative absorption, and the recitation of mantras. (491)

Having performed circumambulation and prostration, and having offered water for the head, water for the mouth, and water for sipping according to the forty-fold ritual procedure, there is no worship performed for one's own sake.
I shall describe the definition of *sasandhyā*; listen with a one-pointed mind.
A blink of the eye of a healthy person is known as a *tuṭi*, which consists of four parts. (493)
Two of those [nimeṣas] are declared to be a laya; two of those [layas] would be a nimiṣa.
Fifteen nimiṣas are known as a kāṣṭhā, and fifteen kāṣṭhās are remembered as a kalā.
Thirty *kālamuhūrtas* constitute two *ghaṭikās*;
starting from sunrise, three *nāḍikās* [constitute] three-quarters [of that]. (495)
This is declared to be "the end of the night"; having understood this, one should perform everything accordingly:
namely, the collection of water and likewise the collection of flowers. (496)

The installation of the deity, the pilgrimage site (tīrtha), especially at the end of the night, as well as the remaining worship, constitute the "latter part of the night" consisting of ten nāḍikās. || 497 ||
That which begins at sunrise and ends at sunset is proclaimed as the four watches; likewise, that which begins at sunset and ends at sunrise is praised as the four watches. (498)
That which is known as eight watches is traditionally remembered as a day and night;
one should perform all the preliminary consecrations (adhivāsana) at midnight.

From sunrise until midday and the end of the day, one should perform rites such as *pratiṣṭhā* according to their suitability; the afternoon is not to be used, so perform [the rites] in the order of the animals (*mṛga*).
Uśīra, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and arthaka—these combined are known as the materials for *pādya*; one should pour the *pādya* upon the feet. (501)

One should cause the person to perform the six-limbed sipping of water (ācamana), providing the substances for the sipping, which include cardamom, cloves, and camphor, as well as the fruits of the preliminary worship.
Water with the tips of kuśa grass, barley, white mustard seeds, rice,
and dūrvā grass combined with barley— these are proclaimed as the materials for the arghya offering.
Agallochum, sandalwood, nutmeg, and saffron—half or even a quarter of these, combined with camphor. (504)
This fragrant substance has been described, and its ritual procedure is now stated:
white, red, and likewise black are known as the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. (505)
The yellow and red [colors] have been described;
143) the white should be given by the Sadyojāta [face], and the red by the Vāmadeva [face], according to the mantra. || 506 ||
The yellow [flower] is for the Puruṣamantra, and the black flower for Aghora;
it is taught that the five-faced [mantra] is worshipped with flowers of various colors.
A flower equal to the blue lotus has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
one should offer the *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, and the white *arkā* at sunrise.
One should place the *karavīra*, the *droṇa* flower, and the lotus at midday;
likewise, the *mallikā* and the *durdhūrā* are said to be the *paṭṭacañcaka*.
In the evening, however, [the offering] should be presented; all other things should be caused to be given.
At midnight, jasmine, gold, *daṃba* flowers, and *dvikarṇī* should be offered.
The *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, the *mandāra*, the *śatapatrikā*,
the white *arkamālatī*, the *punnāga*, and likewise the *kurava* [should be planted]. (511)
In these and similar cases, we declare the flowers to be of the *sāttvika* nature;
likewise, the red lotus (*raktotpala*), the lotus (*padma*), the *bṛhatī*, the *dhūpa*, and the *pāṭalī*. (512)
Such things as these, being red, are said to be of the nature of *rajas*.
Likewise, the *karṇikā*, the *dhurdhura*, and the *puṣpikāraśraya* [are also so described]. (513)
These and other such [plants] are known as the "Mixed" (miśraka) group:
Tulasī, Nṛpa, Jaṃbūka, and Nāganandikā. (514)
A single-petaled lotus, likewise viṣṇukrāntī, apāmārga preceded by kuśa grass, five bilva fruits, and likewise śamī. (515)
These are said to be the *tāmasa* varieties among the types of leaves.
145) One should worship [the deity] at all times using any of these leaf varieties. || 516 ||
Then, other than the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), those belonging to the quality of darkness (*tāmasa*) are proclaimed to be the *karañja*, the *vakula*, the *ketaka*, and likewise the *mādhavī*. (517)
One should avoid the lākulī, dhūka, nirgaṇḍī, and kiṃśuka flowers;
one should also avoid those that are over-ripe, unripe, or still in bud. || 518 ||
Those pierced by a silk-worm, those covered by spider-silk, flowers that have fallen of their own accord, and those gathered upon a cloth; 519.
One should especially avoid flowers that have been left overnight;
likewise, [one should avoid] śamī, bilva, apāmārga, kuśa, dūrvā, and mahā.
Nāganandī, Rudravallī, and Dhātakīpatra;
Bhadrī, Mahābhadrī, and likewise Droṇarūpa. (521)
Among all species of leaves, it is equal to the bilva leaf;
among all species of flowers, it is equal to the blue lotus.

The characteristics of flowers have been declared; now the characteristics of incense are being stated: agarwood should constitute one part, while the resinous exudation may be of lesser quality. || 523 ||
Sandalwood is said to be threefold, while sesame is called the middling [oil]. Oil from tree seeds may be used, but one should avoid the lamp of Śiva [for this purpose].
In the absence of incense materials, one should prescribe clarified butter and flowers;
in the absence of that, however, one should worship with pure oil.
If pure oil is unavailable, one should light a lamp with madhūka oil;
if bathing substances are unavailable, one should perform worship with pure water. (526)
If products derived from cows are unavailable, one should indeed consecrate with clarified butter;
if even sacrificial oblations are unavailable, one should worship by offering lamps.
But in the absence of garments, one should worship with wicks;
and in the absence of mantras, one should worship with the five-syllabled mantra. || 528 ||
But if even fragrances are unavailable, one should perform an anointing with ashes;
and if gold and other materials are unavailable, one should worship with leaves.
If the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are not available, one should worship with ghee alone;
if no substances at all are available, one should meditate upon everything mentally.

At the three junctions of the day, an offering (bali) should be given from afar to another seat; one should cause the offering to be presented along with the weapon-mantra (astra) directed toward the specific directions and locations. || 531 ||
One should offer a seat consisting of the great elements, beginning with fragrance and so forth;
or one should cause an offering (bali) to be given, either the size of an āmalī fruit or a handful.

Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers accompanied by instrumental music and rhythmic clapping, the offering of the bali-oblation is prescribed; one should then present water and the other items in their proper sequence.
At the conclusion of this performance of the bali-rite, the wise practitioner should maintain the perpetual fire (nityāgni).
In the southeast, one should perform the rites as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya). || 534 ||
One should offer into the fire, in due order, fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, kadamba, plantain, and mango.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) one hundred times, or fifty, or twenty-five, or twelve and a half.
The substances for the oblation are safflower and fuel-sticks, sixteen in number. (536)
Make either a fire-pit or a sacrificial mound circular and preeminent;
[the former] is for the householders as the Gārhapatya fire, and the southern fire is for the ancestors.
I shall now describe the various forms of the Āhavanīya fire of the gods;
it is proclaimed to be threefold: as the fire of childhood, youth, and old age. || 538 ||
The fire-ritual for children should be performed in the *pratiṣṭhā* fire during rites concerning time;
one should cause festivals and other such rites to be performed in the fires of youth.

One should perform the remaining rites according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya), maintaining the perpetual fire on both the left and right sides, as well as the ancestral fire and the daily oblation. || 540 ||
Having thus worshipped the Fire, one should then perform the daily festival:
a flower-liṅga in the forenoon, and a food-liṅga at midday. (541)
In the evening, one should prepare an arghya-liṅga measuring twelve finger-breadths;
at all times, [one should perform] the ascending [rite], provided there is no obstacle.
Having carefully placed a flower upon the *liṅga* of the Moon-crested Lord,
or having fashioned it as a mere form adorned with all ornaments,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and then perform the mounting of the sandals (*pādukā*).
The temple-maiden, having lifted up Śiva and performed circumambulations in due order,
[offered] gold, emerald, crystal, silver, and copper.
One should fashion sandals and a royal linga made of gold; one may likewise have it made of copper, emerald, or crystal. (p. 151) 546 ||
One should likewise [visualize] the form of the Liṅga, originating from Kautaka, with the hand of Śiva placed above it;
[one may also visualize him] as riding upon a palanquin, or roaring while mounted on a vehicle drawn by fire,
or indeed mounted on a man, adorned with all ornaments.
And having placed the *uṣṇīṣanyūnā* and the *uttara* purifiers joined together in the hands. || 548 ||
One should carry the head slowly and steadily around the night-eaters (demons) in a clockwise direction,
accompanied by pure dance and joined with song and instrumental music.
Accompanied by the recitation of mantras and joined with the chanting of auspicious benedictions;
provided with canopies and banners, and equipped with parasols and chowries.
Accompanied by the dance of the staff and joined with the dance of the rod.
One should perform [the fanning] with fans and palm-leaf whisks in due order. || 551 ||
Adorned with peacock-feather whisks and joined with white chowries, it was illuminated by lamps and accompanied by a shower of flowers. || 552 ||
One should cause a perpetual festival to be held, joined with the dance of the staff, accompanied by the dance of the rod, and joined with the dance of the swing.
One should first perform a circumambulation, especially at the inner gate;
one should perform a second circumambulation, especially at the middle gate. || 554 ||
If the main gate (gopura) is devoid of musical instruments, one should perform the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) without offering oblations (bali);
having gone back to the inner entrance, one should then perform the circumambulation once more.
First, one should perform a circumambulation accompanied by auspicious cymbals and musical instruments;
then, one should perform two circumambulations for the retinue. (556)
For Vṛṣa, the Vṛṣatāla should be offered, as well as the Aṅgiṇī;
for the Mothers, the Caṇḍa-rhythm, and for Vighneśa, the Ṭhaṅkarī.
In the western quarter, at Carcapuṭā, there is Jyeṣṭhā;
at Punnitālakam, Taṭaprahārasaumyā; and at Vighnacaṇḍaka, Viṣama.
At the city gate, accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and the blare of conchs,
one should first stand in a line and then perform a circumambulation.
Then, having entered the interior of the Śāmbara balipīṭha,
one should cause a circumambulation to be performed in a single continuous manner.
The house should consist of three types [of sections] and the *pīṭha* should have a single circumambulation path.
At the location of the Gandhāra door, there should likewise be a Kauśika [section] in the south-east. (561)
Kāmara is in the south, and Tarkarāgaka is in the southwest;
Kollī is in the western region, and Nṛpasaṅkara is in the northwest.
In the domain of Rāmagirīśa, it is said that Sometakekaśi, along with Balipīṭha, Aṇḍakī, and Tāla, accompanied by song, [are present]. (563)
And likewise the *Magharājāvaka*, sung in the presence of the gods;
having thus chanted these songs in the vernacular language, one should then perform the circumambulation.
Having thus performed the circumambulation, the wise one should enter the temple.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of worship in the *Yogaja-tantra*, the *Pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.

The worship of the sandals (pādukā) should be performed in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; then, accompanied by pure dance, one should worship the Deity in its own place. || 1 ||
Then one should visualize a courtesan performing one hundred and eight dances;
especially at the conclusion of the dance, one should focus particularly upon the God of gods.
That which is the act of making [the deity] face [the worshipper] is called āvāhana (invocation);
once the worship is completed, [the deity], having gone to the mouth [of the practitioner], remains outside.
At the time of every ritual worship, however, the seat should be prepared either excluding the fifth enclosure or as it has been described in the section on worship.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings by his own name, the wise preceptor should perform the ritual worship of the Āgama and enter his own home.
p.
156) In that worship characterized by constant celebration,
one should perform the *śrībalin* at the three times of day with regular offerings.
One should offer the bali at midnight, especially for the sake of fulfilling specific desires.
Thus, in due order, according to the rules, as extensively as one’s means allow—
this concludes the chapter on the ritual for the worship of the sandals (*pādukā*) in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Now, I shall specifically describe the supreme characteristics of the mudrās.
One should strike the cymbal with the two hands; thus one purifies it and becomes a purifier. || 1 ||
One should place the thumb upon the root joint of the index finger;
this is known as the conch mudrā (śaṅkhamudrā), which one should display at the time of bathing. || 2 ||
Then one should form the *maṇibandha* (wrist-binding): the two thumbs are placed in the middle of the palms;
the middle fingers are said to be joined at the joint at the base of the index fingers.
The *nāmī* [mudrā] is formed by placing the two little fingers inside; thus, the *surabhi* is remembered. Having joined both hands together, a hollow space is made in between. (4)
At the time of bathing, one should display the mudrā shaped like a closed bud;
having placed the thumb and palm together, the remaining fingers should be gradually joined and directed upwards.
Having performed what is called the "mounting" (vāhana), one should likewise perform the invocation (āvāhana);
having formed a fist with the four fingers, one should join them to the back of the hand.
The two little fingers are extended and long for the purpose of blocking the exit;
one should place the two thumbs in the middle, joined with the extended little fingers. (7)
The seed-mudrā called *Yama* should be displayed when conceiving of the Śakti;
the two palms should be joined together with the tips of the middle fingers meeting.
Joining the index and ring fingers, with the two thumbs [pressing] the little fingers—
this is the five-faced mudrā, which one should display during the rite of clothing.
Having formed a *añjali* with both hands, that [mudrā] which consists of the mouth [is formed];
those [fingers] which are joined together at their tips, while the remaining ones are spread out.
This is the material mudrā; in the absence of material objects, one should display it. Afterwards, one should join the palms upward and form the jewel-binding gesture (maṇibandha). || 11 ||
Extending the two middle fingers brings about the mudrā called Śivā, which effects installation;
the fingers of the left hand are extended, and the thumb is joined at the top of the head. (12)
On the right, the right fist has the thumb positioned upwards;
having formed the fist with the thumb pointing upward, the wise know this as the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
Having placed the two hands palms upward, with the little fingers joined to the thumbs, the index and middle fingers joined together, and the ring fingers positioned above as a seat; || 14 ||

Thus ends the chapter on the characteristics of mudrās in the illustrious *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*. [One should prepare] vessels for the feet and so forth, filled with the previously mentioned substances; there should be the previously mentioned cloth and oblations, and one should fashion the *kūrca*, threads, and creepers.
One should place the lid for all [the vessels] here, starting from the Śiva-kumbha;
one should place the primary kumbha in the center within the Śiva-vyūha.
The two vessels [at the front] are filled with one āḍhaka each, while the remaining ones are filled with half an āḍhaka;
the arrangement of the principal substances will now be described in their proper order.
Having placed the moon (the letter *i*) in the vowel *ī*, one should place the sugarcane in the vowel *ḷ*;
the plantain fruit in the vowel *e*, and the *gulima* in the vowel *ai*.
One should place the *lāja* seeds upon the syllable *oṃ*; one should place nine *oṃ*s. Sesame is prescribed for the syllable *aṃ*, and one should place *satu* upon the syllable *aṃ*. || 5 ||
Having placed a mustard seed on the letter *sa*, a white mustard seed on the letter *kha*,
a coconut on the letter *ga*, and bamboo seeds on the letter *gha*.
Having placed ashes on the letter *da*, and a *mātulunga* on the letter *ka*;
having placed a *panasa* on the letter *cha*, and a mango (*āmra*) on the letter *ja*. (7)
Māṇikya, vajra, padma, padmapravālaka,
puṣpa, sphaṭika, and vaiḍūrya— these are the gems for the maker of the egg (the cosmic egg).
Having placed iron here that is combined with gold, silver, lead, copper, brass, bronze, and steel, one should have it fashioned.
In Saurāṣṭra, having applied realgar and collyrium that are dark like yellow orpiment, one should then place them with the syllable *ṭa* and the stars of refined gold.
Śyāma, priyaṅgukā, and kāśyāmā, along with sesame, ṣaṣṭhika rice, and mustard; yavanī, vāraka, and dravya—these constitute the seed-liquid (bījoda) together with korakas.
Fresh butter, navel [fragrance], light camphor leaves, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, saffron, and jasmine—these are the substances. (p. 162) 12.
At the end of the section joined with the *laghukaca* cloth, there should be fragrant water in the bud of the *ḍaka*;
it should be oceanic water situated on the horn of a bull, produced from fields and mountains. (13)
One should prepare an elephant-tusk, kuśa grass, root, karkaṭā, and clay; this is called "water with clay" (mṛdāmbhas), and one should deposit it with the syllable Ḍha.
Viṣṇukrāntī, Sahadevī, Śaila, Dīśvara, Mokṣara, Kṛtāñjali, and Śirīṣa [are used] for the Daṇḍakāraka [application], as is Mārjāra. 15.
A lotus, dūrvā grass, a goad, white mustard seeds, and bhadra—
these are said to constitute the "cleansing" (parimārjana) when water is used for the purpose of concluding the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Tulasī, bilva, apāmārga, śamī, bhṛṅga, and bakāraka—
this is declared to be "water with leaves" (patrodaka), which one should place in the vessel for cutting. (17)
In Padmaka he held a trident and a sword; in Kandhakāraka, an axe;
and in Añjana, weapons fashioned from half-a-niṣka of gold.
The wise one should indeed place this supreme water for the weapon upon the syllable *na*;
[using] coconuts, mangoes, jackfruits, plantains, and citrons. (19)
One should place two oranges along with water as "fruit-water" (phalodaka) there;
one should set it down upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at the letter Pa.
The group of Palāśa, Plakṣa, Jambū, Kāpārgala, Udumbara, and Nyagrodha—water that has been consecrated with these [is used for purification]. || 21 ||
It is said that water for drawing [the deity] should be placed in the syllable *pa* in due order; it consists of three parts of mica, pearls, and water, along with one *āḍhaka* of rice. (164) 22.
The wise one should place the syllable *ma* in "jalaṃ," which is said to mean "beautiful water";
and [he should place it] in "śrīkṛṣṇe," which is joined with the head and the lotus (*puṣkara*). (23)
In the Mūloda Sthānaprakāraka, it is as if with two fat female elephants;
[the substances are] cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass. (24)
One should place a bee with a peacock’s crest upon the beautiful altar of the hollowed palms; water from the *jalakātī* plant is prescribed for placement in the healer.
Water mixed with the two types of *lodhra*, *lavaṅga*, and *bhūrja* is called "flower-water" (*puṣpodaka*); the wise one should place it upon the syllable *ra*.
At the letter *la* and at *godhūmni*, there should be *vāra*;
at the letter *u*, there should be *śakāra*; at the letter *ṣa*, one should place *gandhataila* and *cama*. (27)
And at the syllable *va*, one should apply a powder of *janī* mixed with a little camphor; and at the syllable *ka*, half of that, combined mentally with the leaf of the dead. (28)
Thus, it should be provided with a lid; this is proclaimed as the Vyūheśāna.
Facing the Vyūha, there are two coverings for the pitcher (kalaśa).
Lakṣmīdātā, Kuśa, Mūrvā, Apāmārga, Bilvaka, Śamī,
and Aṣṭā belong to the first enclosure of all the arrays.
The Campaka, the lotus, the Tulasī, the Nandyāvarta, the Mallikā, the Jāti, the Droṇa, the Mandāra, the Advikarṇī, and the Karavīraka. || 31 ||
Viṣṇukrāntī, white Arka, and the red lotus;
likewise Vakula, Kurava, and the red water-lily. (32)
And for all the arrays (vyūhas) as well as for the second enclosure,
one should place the Dharma-kūrca and the wheel and other implements within the ritual jars (kalaśas) and cover them.
In the ritual formation (vyūha), there should be facing [the deity] and so forth, as well as circumambulation to the right for all;
furthermore, there is the installation, worship, and dismissal of the triad of the highest [deities].
One should carry the water-pot of all the deities upon one's head;
if a fruit that is quickly ripe cannot be obtained, one should employ an unripe fruit instead.
Upon obtaining a *vṛtra* flower and the like, there should be a flower; upon obtaining a flower, a root; and upon obtaining wealth, water should be filled—such is the certainty of the scripture. (36)
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for bathing in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Now, I shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual for the *śītakuṃbha* (the cool-water jar).
It destroys fever and epilepsy, and it causes the burning away of hemorrhoids. || 1 ||
For the destruction of all diseases,
one should prepare a rain-offering consisting of thirty-two full *prastha* measures of the substance produced from the image.
Having wrapped it with three threads with an interval equal to the width of a barley grain,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva, provided with eight petals.
Having adorned the sacrificial mound with parched grain, darbha grass, and sesame seeds,
one should fill the excellent pitcher with water filtered through a cloth.
It is endowed with all fragrances and provided with the five jewels;
it is accompanied by a cloth, a lid, a tuft of hair, and gold.
One should place the jar upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and arrange all the mantras there;
equipped with the instruments of ritual action, one should offer perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth. (6)
On the preceding day, or otherwise, he should perform a vigil at night;
the preceptor, having touched the disciple’s water-pot with his left hand, should perform the recitation of mantras.
One should touch [the patient] while reciting the Vyomavyāpin Mahāmantra for the pacification of disease;
thus, the fire sacrifice (homa) should especially be performed before him.
At dawn, one should place the Lord of the Gods upon the crown of the head;
having established the four legs with auspicious sacrificial wood and fibers.
Above the *liṅga*, one should fashion a pedestal (*utsedha*) extending in all four directions,
either circular or square, with a width of sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
A hollow in the center is said to be one tāla in measure;
the jar is wrapped in cloth and adorned with flowers and garlands. (11)
At its base, the wise man should cause a cavity to be made in the vessel; the tube should be made of gold and measure the length of the tip of a "needle of greed" (lobhasūcī).
The length of the milk should be double [that of the water], and likewise the honey triple;
having carefully placed the pitcher with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should proceed.
The wise man, having established the Śiva-pitcher upon the sacrificial mound as before, [should perform this] specifically for seven days, five days, or three days. (14)
It is taught that by placing [the substance] on the head for a day and night, it brings about all peace;
especially through regular worship at specific times. (15)
One should worship there with double [the usual] devotion, or indeed worship according to one's capacity; having placed water or even milk into a small jar (upakuṃbha), [one should proceed]. (16)
One should perform the rite for peace from the time of the descent from the pitcher until its completion;
there, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
Having set aside half of the pitcher, the wise knower of mantras should perform the ceremonial bath according to his ability and as prescribed, using the Astra-mantra.
Having offered abundant oblations according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should cause food, drink, and other necessities to be given to all the devotees.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the Cool Jar (*śītakumbha*) in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*. (p.
171) Now, I shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual for the festival of Śiva (*śivotsava*).
For the sake of the cessation of all faults, it brings happiness to the entire world. || 1 ||
It shall be for the purpose of pleasing all the gods and bringing happiness to all living beings;
it is a means for achieving the increase of the king’s victory and for the sake of total protection.
The festival is said to be ninefold, consisting of Puṣkala and Vijaya;
"Sava" is called creation, which is to be honored as expressed by the word.
Because it brings about creation, the festival (utsava) is said to be "celebration" (utsava) in due order;
[he taught] the procedure for the installation festival and the sequence of the monthly festival procedures.
Beginning from the new moon day, there is the month-long observance,
as well as the ritual for the spring festival and likewise the Puṣya festival during the month of Puṣya.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Caitra, for both the month and the fortnight,
and in Vaiśākha until the Viśākhā constellation, there is indeed the Vasantotsava festival. (6)
On the day of the sacrificer and likewise on the day of the king,
the sequence of rites for the great festival must be performed throughout all the months.
One should begin at the time of dawn, undertaking [the practice] at all times;
having determined the month and the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), the Murasa [rite] is likewise prescribed.
The sixteenth [day] is for the sake of all protection; likewise, the twelfth is ancestral (paitṛka).
Ninefold happiness is proclaimed; the seventh day brings prosperity.
The wise man should cause the festival to be performed for five days as the Pārthiva, for three days as the Sāttvika, and likewise for one day as the Śiva.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Gods of gods, one should inform him: "Perform the festival, preceded by the hoisting of the flag on the twenty-seventh lunar mansion."
Beginning first with the sounding of the drum, it shall last for twenty-eight days;
indeed, after the preliminary rite of offering the sprouts, one should subsequently worship the banner.
On the night preceding that day, one should perform the sacrifice of the bull (vṛṣayāga) and construct the pavilion according to the sequence beginning with the installation (pratiṣṭhā).
The banner-cloth and its characteristic mark should indeed be made of white cotton;
it should be twelve cubits long, or perhaps ten, or even nine cubits.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be one-fifth of the length of the banner-cloth and exactly one cubit;
the tail (puccha) is said to be half a cubit, and the triple-tailed [portion] is likewise specified.
Having divided that cloth into five parts, one should paint a bull in the central section;
above that, Bhastradevala; and above him, a parasol and chowries.
On the side, however, one should fashion a lamp and a low pedestal;
it is called "the color of the sacrificial post" (yūpavarṇa) and is adorned with full water-pots. || 17 ||
White and red flowers, as well as every kind of ornament,
and a bull with white-colored limbs— one should employ these for the sake of all types of accomplishment.
The wise one should depict a black snake with a color red as if stained by desire for wealth, either standing or lying down, and likewise a bull.
The two horns have the luster of red color and are adorned with a yellowish-green [mark]; the eye is black in color, while the dark [portion] is red-blue.
One should construct a pavilion before Śiva, adorned with all ornaments and decorated with all kinds of flowers, and likewise smeared with cow dung. (21)
Having encircled it with a garland of *darbha* grass and suspended it with a string of pearls and red silk,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in its center and place the "sleeping jar" (*nidrākumbha*) there.
On all sides, one should place eight footprints according to the previous sequence;
in their center, one should invoke the Bull (Vṛṣa), accompanied by golden flowers.
Having placed eight cloths all around, one should install them with their respective seed-syllables:
Ukṣan, Gopati, and likewise Śaṅkukarṇa. (24)
Likewise, one should worship Tīkṣṇaśṛṅga, Nandin, Vṛṣāṇin, Paśu, Mahodara, and Akṣama by their respective names. || 25 ||
One should sequentially place [the substances] into the bull-pitcher with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
In front of that, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using white sand.
The preceptor should make it a square of equal dimensions measuring one cubit;
there should be a cord for the east and likewise a cord for the north.
With the mantra "brahmajajñānam," the wise one should draw the central line;
with the mantra "nāke suparṇam," he should draw on the south.
With the mantra "āpyāyasva," one should draw [the lines] on the north;
likewise, with the mantra "yo rudraḥ," one should draw the thread toward the north.
One should draw the eastern line accompanied by the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," and one should draw the middle line with the mantra "indraṃ vo."
Having sprinkled Śivā with water, one should worship Bhava first;
one should then worship Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśī. || 31 ||
Having established the fire in its center and performed the oblation, the wise one should perform the consecration of the fire as before; O Vṛṣabha, you should worship [the deity].
Having honored the Brāhmaṇa in the south and Viṣṇu in the north,
one should strew the darbha grass for the encircling border starting from the east.
Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel above, one should then place the *praṇītā* vessel;
thereafter, one should prepare the *ājyasthālī* and set down the *carusthālī*.
Having placed the praṇītā and prokṣaṇī vessels, as well as the ghee-pot, face down,
one should place the sruk and sruva ladles to the north and likewise turn them face down.
With a fuel-stick (*samidh*) measuring a span (*prādeśa*), and likewise with the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); preceded by the two fuel-sticks for Vāyu, it is provided with the *viṣṭara*. (36)
There one should prepare the fuel and kindle the fire in due order;
one should offer three oblations and perform the *vyāhṛti* homa in sequence. (37)
The wise one should indeed offer oblations in sequence with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
he should offer mustard seeds with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra and with the armor (kavaca) mantra.
Likewise, one should offer oblations of a *āḍhaka* measure of mung beans and black gram to the sufferer of colic;
with the *Śiva-mantra*, one should offer ten oblations for each [type of grain]. (39)

One should perform the Jaya and other oblations, and then shake the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings in their proper order; finally, one should offer the Pūrṇāhuti while holding it with the head and recollecting the seed-syllable of Agni.

At the conclusion of the *homa*, there should be a bull-pitcher (*vṛṣakuṃbha*); indeed, for each of the [five] forms (*mūrti*), there should be a bull-pitcher. At the end of that, one should place the respective divisions upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). (41)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are proclaimed as the presiding deities;
[one should offer] fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering.
One should worship the deity Bherī and strike the Ācārya in due order;
one should strike it first in sequence with the mantra *brahmajajñānam*.
One should strike the third [eye] in sequence with the Tryambaka mantra.
Then, having summoned the musicians as well as the pure Pāraśava,
he should likewise [invite] one who is endowed with the complete limbs and accompanied by Śakti.
A wise person should avoid performing [the rite] without one who possesses power;
having invoked Nandikeśvara, he should place the musicians within his heart as a sealed vessel. (46)
The sacrifice consists of incense and lamps; one should place a flower in the hand.
Having offered that flower and having paid obeisance, one should then present the water for washing the feet (pādya) to the drum.
The teacher has declared the seven-fold division for both the disciple and the deity of the weapon; having worshipped the deity of the weapon, one should place Rudraka upon the central petal.
One should place Brahmā on the right petal and Janārdana on the left petal;
likewise, one should place Gaurī at the base of the middle [petal] and Sarasvatī on the right.
The wise one should worship Lakṣmī on the left petal, and at its base,
Gaṇeśa within the middle of the vessel, as well as Skanda at the tip of the stalk.

One should place [the deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin upon the protective enclosure; likewise, one should place Kṣetrapāla in the northeast, and Daṇḍa in the middle, according to the ritual manual.
One should worship Caṇḍeśa with a staff at the root on the southern side during the lunar mansion Antaka; one should include him among all the deities. 52.
Having invoked all the deities, one should perform the rite with the Astra-mantra alone;
incense and lamps should be offered, as well as the food-oblation (naivedya) for all the gods.
The weapon-deities, other liṅgas, as well as the vessel for offerings,
the image, the bearer of the moon, and likewise the bull-bannered god [Śiva].
One should perform the circumambulation of the village and worship the junctions;
having invoked the deity of the day, one should place him either before the pedestal or at the tip of the banner.
The first is the Night of Vighna; the second is that of the Piśācas. The third is the Night of Brahmā, and the fourth is that of the Gandharvas. (56)
The fifth is the Bhūtarātra; the sixth is the Guharātra;
the seventh would be the Ṛṣirātra; and the eighth is the Nāgarātra. || 57 ||
The ninth should be the Aindrarātra, the tenth the Viṣṇurātraka;
the eleventh should be the Rudrarātra, and the twelfth the Śivarātraka.
The thirteenth is the Gaṇarātra, and likewise the fourteenth is the Rākṣasa;
the fifteenth should be the Pañcadaśarātra, while the sixteenth is the Śaktirātra.
The ancestral festival begins with Vighna and ends with Śiva;
likewise, the festival of happiness begins with Vighna and ends with Indra.
From Vighna and the others up to the end of the Ṛṣirātra, the third [section] occurs;
likewise, from Vighna and the others up to Bhūta, there is the festival of Pārthiva. (61)
The earthly festival extends from Vighna (Gaṇeśa) up to Brahmā,
and the sattvic festival extends from Vighna up to Bhūta.
First, for the *gaṇarātra*, one should offer cakes and sesame flour;
for the *śuddhānna* [rite], it should be offered as an oblation, and during the *vighnarātra*, one should cast the *bali* offering.
On the second day, one should offer pure food and rice with three curries, accompanied by curd and meat, while reciting the Paiśāca mantra.
Pure food, Brahman rice with mustard seeds, curd,
and milk should be given on the third day, while recollecting the Brahma-mantra.
On the fourth day, one should offer rice cooked in broth, sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), clarified butter, plantains, and sugar-cane juice, while reciting the Gandharva mantra. (66)
On the fifth day, one should offer rice mixed with pearls, along with molasses, honey, milk, and ghee, while recollecting the mantra of Bhūta.
On the sixth day, milk-rice, ghee, plantain, and jaggery should be offered while reciting the mantra dedicated to Skanda.
On the seventh day, one should offer pure food mixed with ghee and the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant, while recollecting the mantras of the ṛṣis.
On the eighth day, pure food mixed with mung beans and molasses combined with ghee should be offered while recollecting the name-mantra.
On the ninth day, one should offer pure food, ghee, milk, and likewise the fruits of the jackfruit and mango, while recollecting the mantra of Indra. (71)
Pure rice mixed with curd, combined with jaggery and sugar-candy, along with plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, and coconut fruits. (72)
On the tenth day, while recollecting the mantra of Viṣṇu,
one should give food made with black gram mixed with ghee, as well as milk, jaggery, and sugar-candy.
On the eleventh day, one should perform [the rite] while recollecting the Rudra-mantra,
combined with the rules for the extraction of the mantra and joined with the root of the Bṛhatī plant.
On the twelfth day, the Śiva-mantra should be offered and the bali-oblation should be cast;
likewise, one should offer kṛsarā-rice, molasses, clarified butter, honey, milk, and fruit.
On the thirteenth day, one should give [the offerings] while reciting the mantra of the Gaṇas;
it is said that for a month, one should provide black gram food (māṣānna), along with molasses, milk, and ghee.
On the fourteenth day, reciting the Rākṣasa mantra,
one should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee and combined with jaggery and sugar-candy.
On the fifteenth day, recollecting the scriptures and mantras,
one should always offer the daily oblation (bali) in sequence after invoking the deity of the day.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna;
it should consist of pure food mixed with ghee, along with curd and milk. (79)
But at the palace on the western gate, one should offer the bali-oblation for the Vāstu-spirits in due order.
(187) One should perform this sequence of offerings, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Nirṛti, and proceeding clockwise from Varuṇa; one should thus cast the offering constantly. || 81 ||
Having offered a bali-oblation at that gate, one should offer a bali with the respective names of each deity, beginning with Jyeṣṭhā and ending with Vighna, to the bull situated there in the west.
Having invoked the deity of the day, one should offer the bali-oblation either before the pedestal;
on its specific day, however, one should invoke Mahālakṣmī, and in the cow-pen, Sarasvatī.
And in the Bhūpa [quarter], one should recite the Mahāmodimantra and offer the bali;
in the Īśāna [quarter] and in the Devikoṣṭha, one should likewise offer the bali to Sundarī. || 84 ||
The *liṅga* itself is the great seat (*mahāpīṭha*); one should not discard the *liṅga*. One may cast it into water, but one should discard an *anna-liṅga* (a food-made *liṅga*).
One should perform the *āvāha-bali* and cast the *udvāhana-bali*; one should perform the *bali* on the thirty-second day and likewise on the sixteenth day. (86)
One should perform the twenty-fourth offering on the twelfth day itself;
one should perform the eighteenth offering, which is prescribed for the attainment of happiness.
Manu and Kauśika likewise performed the sequence of offerings for a single day;
thus has the number of offerings been declared—now hear the procedure for the festival.
The wise one should cause a festival to be held during an auspicious lunar mansion;
however, if the installation and the festival are deficient, he may perform them at his discretion in any month.
On the day of his birth-star, which brings happiness and joy,
the king [established] the great seat (mahāpīṭha) and the temple, reaching even to its pinnacle.

One should perform the festival as well as the installation and so forth up to the pinnacle [of the temple] when it possesses the all-pervading *liṅga*; however, in the case of a deficient [temple], the wise one should avoid the festival. || 91 ||
The primary limbs, secondary limbs, and minor limbs, together with their retinues, as well as the palaces, gates, and pedestals—this is what is here called the "limb" (aṅga). 92.
