But in the case of an inferior festival, the wise man should avoid it;
however, if a festival has already commenced, he may proceed as desired for that month.
Having first performed [the rite] when [the deity] has suddenly arrived, one should subsequently celebrate the festival;
and if the previous festival was omitted, one may spend the month as desired.
One should perform the rite of expiation and carry out the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma). || 95 ||
The supreme festival concludes with the lunar mansion Mṛgaśirā, the month, the asterism, and the sacred ford;
likewise, the installation asterism concludes with the village asterism, the lunar mansion, and the sacred ford. (96)
On the lunar mansion of his birth, the wise king, by the power of his sacrifice,
established what is called the Candranakṣatra, a holy ford that removes all planetary afflictions.
One should perform the festival every month in its proper sequence;
the festival is of three kinds: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). || 98 ||
One should perform the perpetual festival constantly, and especially the occasional one; as it is said, "according to one's desire," the festival is thus of three kinds.
Thereafter, one should perform the perpetual festival (nityotsava) and then the occasional festival (naimittikotsava);
furthermore, a wise person should cause the optional festival (kāmyotsava) to be performed in the month most desired for that purpose.
(191) Where there is no constant festival, one should perform a great festival;
having caused the banner to be carried forth, the wise man should then conclude it. 101.
One may act according to the sacrificer's wish or proceed as desired;
however, a banner with a banner should not be made—one must make a banner with a bull.
O twice-born ones, one should perform a festival that rises with great joy; even when there is an obstacle, a Śiva-festival should be held.
It is said that this is indeed the auspiciousness of Viṣṇu, and one should carry out the rites pertaining to the limbs of Śiva.

There, one should perform the rite for Śiva’s body and carry out the sacrifice to Viṣṇu; even during the auspicious festival of the gods, one should not cause the king’s welfare-rite to be performed. (104)
In the village, in the city, in the town, and in the capital, everyone should perform the festival of the gods together in a single location. 105.
The *hari-pṛṣṭha* should be very peaceful, while the *hara-pṛṣṭha* should be adorned;
one should perform the festival of all the gods according to the sequence of the strength of the single site (*ekavāstu*). (106)
The wise one should cause the Puṣyaka festival to be celebrated in the month of Puṣya;
that which ends with Mākhya in the month of Māgha, and that which ends with Uttarā in the month of Phālguna.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, especially under the asterism Rohiṇī, when the month and the asterism are complete, a bath in the ocean is most excellent. (108)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, [the asterism] Pūrvāṣāḍhā;
in the month of Kārttika, until the end of Kṛttikā; or in Mārgaśīrṣa, until the end of Ārdrā. (109)
In all months, the supreme festival should be performed ending with the Ārdrā asterism;
however, in the intercalary month (Amāsa), the Ārdrā asterism is fruitless, and the solar month (Sauramāsa) is recommended.
(193) Or else, with every kind of festival, let there be a calculation according to the solar number;
their undertaking shall be threefold, beginning with the hoisting of the banner.
Preceded by the striking of the bell and preceded by the offering of sprouts, the bull sacrifice is established with the consecration of the bull. || 112 ||

The second [auspicious sign] is the sprout of the festival, which is the moon in conjunction with the asterism Māyā (Mṛgaśiras); the third is the sprout of the sacred ford, which is bathing in the ocean under that same asterism. 113.
The sprout, which is the most excellent of all, is of three kinds: leading, liberating, and likewise, that which consists of water and latent impressions. || 114 ||
The preceptor, with his hand bearing the ritual implements, should perform the opening of the eyes;
and a bull should indeed be placed within that [space] filled with rice grains.
In those eight directional jars, one should place the bull-jar (ukṣāṃ kalaśe).
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and perform a fire sacrifice (homa), especially.
At an auspicious moment, the wise one should fashion a golden ladle;
likewise, he should prepare honey, clarified butter, and a small stone for the eyes.
Likewise, one should offer incense and lamps arising from the sight of grain;
one should present a mirror, an ablution, and an offering of mung-bean rice.
Then, having finished the craftsmanship and likewise smeared it with cow-dung,
one should make the middle level and prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center.
One should place a lotus there in the center, along with a bull and a water-pot;
on all sides, one should place eight jars, beginning with the bull, in their proper order.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should touch the opening of the eyes, which possess the gaze of a serpent. || 121 ||
The wise one should display the consecration (abhiṣeka) joined with ritual substances as well as the libation (tarpaṇa);
he should also cause the installation (pratiṣṭhā) to be performed, including the residence upon the surface of a mirror.
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva and likewise smear it with cow dung;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) within the pavilion using eight dronas of rice.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center of that, one should install the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva).
The wise practitioner should bind the marriage-thread (kautuka), made of gold or a thread of royal silk.
Alternatively, there may be a cotton thread; one should tie it to the two horns of the bull.
One should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day and then bind the *kautuka* (wedding bracelet) in due order.
With the *triyaṃbaka* mantra, one should tie a thread around the right [arm];
one should prepare a bed and a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of that, along with a bull and a water-pot.
One should place the eight items beginning with *ikṣu* (sugarcane) in order around the perimeter;
having established the fire in front of that, one should perform the *homa* offering as previously described.
In front of that, there should be the deity Bherī; one should cause a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared there.
To the west, one should gradually prepare a sacrificial mound with rice grains for the deity Astra.
Having adorned it with parched grain and flowers and provided it with a garland of darbha grass,
the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation according to the path prescribed for the fire-rite.

One should place the vessel for sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), the praṇītā vessel, and the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī). Having prepared a seat in the north, one should arrange it facing downwards. || 130 ||

Having taken the *prokṣaṇī* vessel containing water mixed with *kuśa* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), along with a blade of *kuśa* one span long and three finger-measures of the palm, [he should perform the sprinkling]. (131)
One should sprinkle the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the praṇītā vessel, the upward-facing vessel,
the kuśāgra, and likewise the prokṣaṇī water.
Having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water, joined with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
and having invoked Janārdana, it should indeed be placed in the north.
On the right, however, one should worship Brahmā with a *kūrca* (a bundle of grass) accompanied by flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*);
likewise, there should be water for the three-fold touching (*trisparśana*) along with a *prādeśa*-length *kūrca*.
In this manner, one should perform the consecration of the fire and likewise the consecration of the clarified butter;
having filled the ghee-pot with clarified butter to the height of a span using a grass-bundle (*kūrca*).
One should perform the touching at a distance of three *prādeśas*, and then dismiss the fire;
one should circumambulate the *darbha*-grass fire and also perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*). || 136 ||

Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, black gram, rice, barley, sesame, mustard, milk and the like, as well as jaggery and sugar-candy, are declared to be the ten [offerings]. (137)
Having performed the spreading [of grass], the enclosing sticks, and the three seats,
and having placed fuel-sticks above that, he should perform the sprinkling [of water] in between.
In this manner, the consecration of the fire and the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) are performed;
the fuel-stick (samidh) is offered with the Sadyojāta mantra, while the clarified butter is offered with the Vāmadeva mantra. || 139 ||
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and the parched grain (lāja) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
[he should offer] sesame seeds with the Īśāna mantra, and mustard seeds with the Kavaca mantra.
Mudga beans, māṣa beans, and barley are empowered by the Śiva-mantra;
likewise, the root of the vṛṣa plant and the Gāyatrī are empowered by reciting them one hundred and eight times. (141)
Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," one should perform the *jayādi* rites,
the *abhyādhāna*, and offer the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations in their proper sequence.
While recollecting the seed-syllable of Agni with his head bowed, he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
thereafter, he should cause betel to be offered to the image within the bull-vessel (vṛṣabhakuṃbhaka).
Then the knower of mantras should perform the placement of mantras (nyāsa) using the root-mantra of Vṛṣabha;
thereafter, he should make the sound of a drum, and then the invocation (āvāhana) is described.
After summoning the musicians, the pure Pāraśava likewise shall strike the preceptor of all those who have been initiated in due order.
He should also provide a new cloth for an upper garment and a sacred thread,
adorned with all ornaments and decorated with all kinds of flowers. (146)
Accompanied by a handful of flowers and joined with the Gaurī-yoga, both the preceptor and the disciple should perform nine rhythmic beats (tālas). || 147 ||
Having fully worshipped the entrails, the invocation of the deities should take place;
perform the rite of invocation for all the deities from Śiva down to Caṇḍa.
The wise one should offer the oblation (havis); he should offer it to all the gods, together with the vessel for the bali-offering, as well as the food, the emblem, and the weapon.
Having likewise taken up the banner, Caṇḍeśvara, and the circumambulation of the village,
as well as the other [implements], one should fasten the banner-cloth in due order.
Having invoked the deity of the junction (sandhidevatā) together with the deity of the day (dinadeva),
one should offer the internal oblation (antarbali) according to the sequence previously established, or otherwise, cast the oblation at the conclusion of the sacrifice. || 151 ||
The wise one should worship everything and afterwards cast the *vāstu-bali* offering;
having performed the circumambulation of the village, he should cast the *bali* upon the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*).
The banner-cloth and the small vessel should be well-secured at the base of the staff;
the characteristics of the staff have thus been described, or one may have it made of wood.
The wood for the seat should be of *khadira*, *bilva*, and *campaka*, combined with *devadāru*, *kramuka*, and *khaṇḍadaṇḍaka*. || 154 ||
Mayūka, Arjuna, and likewise Kṛṣṇavṛkṣa; together with Munivṛkṣa, Kramuka, and Veṇudaṇḍaka. || 155 ||
Crooked, split, hollow, and likewise containing worm-holes;
with internal pith, with a male [seed], and likewise with fire-pith. || 156 ||
It may end in *sūpa*, or end in *gulā*, or be level with the *ukṣasthala*;
it may also be level with its neck (*grīva*) or level with the *gopura*. || 157 ||
It is said that for the Trayastriṃśa [mandala], it should be twenty-five cubits; alternatively, it is prescribed that the length of the staff (daṇḍa) should be exactly one cubit.
The wise one, having taken a milky tree and fashioned a sacrificial post (yaṣṭi) measuring four cubits in length and provided with three tiers, [should proceed]. || 159 ||
The fire-corner is said to be one finger in thickness; that is indeed the *vaṣaṭkāra*.
Both of these are joined with a hollow, or else there is a moon in the middle.
The bamboo staff is prescribed according to the measurement of the *upadaṇḍa*.
One should make the best [image] nine *tālas* in height, and the middling one seven *tālas*. (161)
The staff for the minor [deity] should be six or five tālas in length;
it should be joined with a handle-band and adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass.
One should fasten either an iron ring or a secondary rod, or else a cord made of cotton thread, which is twice the size of the ring. (163)
Having established the base of the staff with a circumference equal to the little finger,
one should perform the sprinkling of the ground and then dig into the earth.
One should dig a pit measuring three cubits by two cubits in sequence;
one should then establish a staff topped with a tortoise made of rice grains.
That which is made of jewels and that which is made of silver, as well as the tortoise-seat made of metal—
one should join these together with the five metals upon the trident. (166)
There, at an auspicious moment, the wise man should cause the proclamation of a "holy day" (puṇyāha).
The characteristics of the altar have already been stated for both stone and brick.
Alternatively, having taken clay provided with three girdles,
one should make the circumference of the hand and the height one cubit in measure.
Its height should be one *ratni* measure, or even just a fist's breadth;
its width and height should be one *hasta*, which is the best.

One should fashion the hand at the base of the staff to measure twenty-four finger-breadths according to the *mātrā-aṅgula* system; this is declared by the wise to be the characteristic of the pedestal (*vedikā*). 170.
The wise one should remove the carving and likewise the coating of cow dung;
he should then bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) very firmly there, in the middle of the staff. (171)
One should worship Vināyaka there and then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
or else, one should take a cord with its loops, doubled over and resting upon the base.
The wise man should fasten a banner-cloth adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass and beautified by a flower-garland, decorated with small bells and flowers. (173)
The image should be that of a bull or a jar, provided with incense and lamps;
and at an auspicious moment, one should perform the hoisting of the banner.
A wise person should bind [the patient] firmly with small doses administered repeatedly;
for a contrary condition caused by another disease, an expiation is prescribed.
Having invoked all the deities, one should join them at the base of the staff. || 176 ||
Having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should sequentially bind the cords of the directions (diktāla),
accompanied by dance and song and endowed with all musical sounds.
One should offer mung-bean rice as a gift, and one should also offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then, one should indeed fashion nine pindas in each of the directions.
One should first cause the [initiate] to give the "womb" (garbha), which is associated with the arising of the womb;
likewise, for an inauspicious girl and for one firmly afflicted by epilepsy. || 179 ||
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
one should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva and smear it with cow dung.
And one should bind the *umā* (wool) of the God of gods as a marriage-thread (*kautuka*) in due order,
whether it be made of *svaśra*, *rata*, or even cotton (*kārpāsa*). (181)
In the rite of binding the protective thread, one should place a small vessel and rice using the Tryambaka mantra, and within that, the protective cord.
In the manner of circumambulation by the hand of an attendant, [the image] is provided with new cloth and endowed with all auspicious qualities. || 183 ||
One should place [the image] at the forefront of everything and recite the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) in due order;
the preceptor should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the *Aghora* mantra.
One should fasten a protective thread with the Tryambaka mantra;
it is taught that [the deity] is indeed accompanied by Umā and is Candraśekhara himself.
p.
208) One should especially bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) in sequence upon the sixteen images, whether they have one form, two forms, or three forms. || 186 ||
Then one should construct a sacrificial hall, or likewise a peaked structure (kūṭa) or a pavilion (maṇṭapa),
in the direction of Indra, or Agni, or Yama, or even in the direction of the Rakshasas.
Likewise, [place] Vāyu and Soma in the northeast, as well as the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa). One should thoroughly decorate the pavilion and construct an altar (vedikā) in its center.
It should be one *ratni* in height, resembling the surface of a mirror,
and two cubits in width, provided with a small altar-like ledge.
Thus, nine fires constitute the highest [type], while five fires would be the middling;
one fire is declared to be the lowest. [The altar] may be either circular or square. (190)
Or else, one may establish a single fire, as well as the eastern and western ones;
one should worship the water-jar at whichever door the Liṅga faces. (191)
In front of that, the wise practitioner should either prepare a fire-pit or perform the fire-oblation (homa);
[the pavilion] should be provided with sixteen pillars or twelve pillars.
It was provided with four pillars, endowed with four gates, joined with yoke-shaped arches, and adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass. || 193 ||
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) situated on an altar, provided with body-coverings, canopies, and banners, using eight droṇas of śāli rice.
Half of that [space] is said to be for rice, and half of that again for sesame seeds;
in the middle of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.

In the center, one should place Sadāśiva and the *kuṃbha* (vessel), and likewise the *vardhanī* (overflow vessel) to the north; these eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) should be installed in order starting from the east. (196)
Then, having lifted the Śiva-pitcher while recollecting the Śiva-mantra,
one should worship the Śiva-śakti in the Vardhanī vessel, together with the Parā-śakti.

These eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras), indeed, having taken up the door-pitchers with their respective mantras according to their names, are said [to be worshipped] starting from the east and ending in the northeast. (198)

The *prāgbhūta* (earth) is in the eastern pitcher; *tadekāgni* (fire) is in the southern pitcher; *avaideha* (water) is in the southwestern pitcher; *naiṛtya* (nairṛta) is in the southeastern pitcher;

the group of six *vāruṇya* (Varuṇa) is likewise [in the western pitchers]; *aiśvinī* (wind) is in the northwestern pitcher; *some* (moon) is in the northern pitcher; *yugasyātri* (Atri of the age) is in the northeastern pitcher; and *kuṃbha* (pitcher) is in the northeast.
One should worship the door-jar with the name-mantra specific to each,
invoke all the deities, and honor them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 200 ||

Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) accompanied by incense and lamps, the wise practitioner should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited there and should bind the protective thread (kautuka) in due order.
The fire-pit (kuṇḍa) for the marriage ceremony and each [other pit] specifically—the purification of the pit itself and its pure flame have been described. (202)
The procedure for the fire-ritual has been declared; one should perform the oblation in each individual pit.
The wise preceptor, joined by his disciples, should perform the oblation.
The palāśa, the udumbara, the apāmārga, the upaplakṣa, the bilva, the khadira, the nyagrodha, and likewise the vahnī. || 204 ||
A sacrificial ladle made of *vaikaṅkata* wood and saffron from Kashmir are thus prescribed; likewise, there should be a layering of *darbha* grass and three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). (205)
Having kindled the fire in the east and upward, and having likewise worshipped the two [deities] in the west,
one should worship Brahmā in the south and Janārdana in the north.
Then one should perform the sprinkling (pariṣecana), as well as the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the vessel itself;
having taken up the praṇītā vessel, one should worship Janārdana in due order.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the clarified butter (ājya) are declared to be accompanied by the syllable Svāhā;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should present the offering (bali) and place it upon the girdle (mekhalā).
One should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors with their respective individual name-mantras;
one should perform the external bali-rite and then perform the internal bali-rite.
At the side of the sacrificial pit, one should offer oblations of fire both inside and outside;
first the eight Nāgas, and secondly the twelve and so forth. (210)
Having offered the strength of the Nāgas and others, one should then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
recollecting the mantra of the fire, one should join it with "svāhā. || 211 ||
Having invoked the form of Agni, one should properly unite it within the center of the pitcher;
there, one should present the sacrificial oblation intended for all the gods.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), there should be the sounding of kettledrums in nine rhythmic patterns;
then, having summoned the attendant, the preceptor, and the disciple [should perform the rites].
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, there should be the sounding of drums; one should offer the *vāstu-bhūta-bali*.
First, one should perform the internal offering (*antarbali*), and second, the offering to the deities of the day (*dinadevatā*).
(214) Listen to the sequence for the offering of oblations up to the end of the sacrificial pedestal and the raising of the banners;
likewise, [the procedure for] circumambulating the village of the god Umāskandeśvara. (215)
One should place the deity in either a chariot or a palanquin,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and endowed with the chanting of the Vedas.
It was accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and auspicious sounds from those who recite benedictions;
there were also a parasol, two chowries, a fan, and a banner. (217)
Everything was provided with lamps, including those in the immediate vicinity;
likewise for all the devotees, the kings, and even Brahmā himself. (218)
The preceptor is on the right side, the king on the left side;
the central position belongs to the daughter of Rudra, while the Gāndharva is at the front of Śiva.
One should perform a circumambulation of the village as well as the assembly pavilion,
[offering] water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering, accompanied by incense and lamps. (220)
The wise man should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony; the learned one should cause the sacred ash (*bhasma*) to be offered, as well as the mirror, the fly-whisk, the fan, and the umbrella. (221)
One should perform the rite of heating with ashes together with devotees of the King, along with coconuts, jackfruit, and plantain fruits. 222.
Then the officiant should offer it and present betel;
starting from that very day, the sacrifice shall last for seven days.
On the seventh day from that date, one should not perform the oil massage ritual;
instead, one should prepare the assembly pavilion with an auspicious smearing of cow dung.
There, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice.
In its center, one should place oil together with previously consecrated unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the wise man should likewise apply oil to the head and place upon it *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having likewise performed the oil massage accompanied by the sounding of celestial drums and other instruments,
one should then cause the ritual bathing to be performed with fifty or twenty-five [measures].
Clad in pure garments, adorned with white garlands, endowed with pearl ornaments, and anointed with white sandalwood paste. || 228 ||
It was provided with abundant offerings of food (naivedya) accompanied by side dishes (upadaṃśa), dressed in pure garments, and adorned with white garlands. || 229 ||
Adorned with pearl ornaments, anointed with white sandalwood paste,
provided with abundant food offerings, and accompanied by side dishes. (230)
She should offer betel-leaf accompanied by incense and lamps;
a woman endowed with such characteristics as these should avoid [intercourse] with a man. (231)
It is joined with *aṅgāli*, endowed with *hastālpi*, joined with *abhiniryā*, and combined with *tālavindāla*. || 232 ||
Accompanied by all ornaments, consisting of pure dance and song—this, endowed with such characteristics, is declared to be *gāndharva*. || 233 ||
For one who has been initiated, dancing is proclaimed to be a fault;
in order to neutralize that fault, there should be twenty-five ablutions.
One should worship the *liṅga* or the *kautuka* with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
first, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) at night with pure dance and other such offerings. (235)
In the northern part of the pavilion, prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice;
there, one should arrange a bed and provide various types of flowers.
In the midst of that, having remembered me, it is said that one should cause the Rudra-women to lie down;
then, having tied the *kautuka* (auspicious thread), one should thread it with a golden wire.
A dancer, a drummer, a singer, a flute-player, as well as a silent one and a musician, one should cause to perform their service during the night. (238)
There one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with four droṇas of śāli rice;
half of that with another mound, and half of that again with sesame seeds.
Having established nine jars endowed with the nine Śaktis, provided with *kūrca*-grass, covered with lids, and accompanied by cloths and sprouts. (240)
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, accompanied by incense and lamps,
one should lift it up at the time of dawn, preceded by purification and sipping water (ācamana).
One should especially perform a bath accompanied by the purification of the teeth;
having established [the image] with nine jars, while recollecting the initiation mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer garments and ornaments;
then, with the heart mantra, one should place a flower upon the head.
Having placed a flower in his hand, he should always recite their names— Rudra and Nārī— in due order, as the flower falls.
Afterwards, one should perform a circumambulation clockwise and cause [the deity] to enter the temple;
having paid homage to Vighneśa, one should offer fruit, flowers, and sacrificial oblations. (245)
One should worship Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and the goddess Śrī;
having offered perfume, flowers, and oblations, one should also present betel leaf.
At midday, the wife of Rudra should partake of a fine meal of milk-rice;
thereafter, she should enter the pavilion together with the women of the retinue.
Beginning with Īśāna, one should worship the Vāstu deities well;
at evening time, one should offer the bali-oblation to the presiding deity of the pavilion.
In the center of that pavilion, prepare either a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or a pit (anila).
Having placed the face [of the deity] in its center, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 249 ||
Having covered [the image] with a new cloth, one should cause sacrificial offerings (haviṣya) to be presented;
then, having worshipped Nandikeśvara in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (250)
First is the purification of the self, second is the purification of the hands,
and third is that known as the lineage-beat, which is declared to be the group of the syllable Oṃ.
The fourth is the purification of the song, the fifth begins with the face [of the deity],
the sixth is joined with instrumental music, and the seventh is the offering of flowers.

One should cultivate the eighth, the wrist-bond (*maṇibandha*), and the ninth, the *navaraṃbhā*; the tenth is the complete dance (*nṛttasaṃpūrṇa*). These are the characteristics of dance (*nṛttalakṣaṇa*). || 253 ||
The preceptor is comfortably seated on the right side of the deity;
the two dancers are comfortably seated on the northern side of the deity.
To the western side of the deity stands the attendant;
the Nardaka and the Mardakas are stationed to the south. (255)
The singer and the flute-player are stationed to the north.
Having prepared a seat in the east, one should perform the oblation of fuel-sticks (samidh).
One should offer the fuel-stick with the Sadyojāta mantra, or the clarified butter (ājya) with these mantras. || 257 ||
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and the parched grain (lāja) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
[he should offer] sesame seeds with the Īśāna mantra, and mustard seeds with the Kavaca mantra. || 258 ||
Mudga beans, māṣa beans, and śāli rice are offered with the Netra-mantra;
milk-rice (pāyasa) and jaggery-sugar balls (gulakhaṇḍa) are offered with the Śiva-mantra. || 259 ||
One should perform [the rite] in that same manner for each [deity], and then again perform the Puṇyāha ceremony;
with the Tryambaka mantra, one should [perform the rite for] the Naṭeśvara marriage-thread. (260)
The wise one should bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) with the left hand;
the *kautuka* belongs to the weapon-deities, or rather, the deer is the *kautuka*. || 261 ||
One should worship with incense, lamps, and the *ārātrika* rite;
specifically at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*), one should bind the protective thread (*kautuka*) with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
There, one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with knowledge of the four Vedas;
and dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the recitation of Purāṇas should be performed in due order. || 263 ||
The wise practitioner should offer a cake accompanied by many offerings;
then the mantra-reciter should present betel-leaf as an offering.
One should worship with incense, lamps, and the *ārātrika* rite;
then one should sequentially display the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the mirror. (265)
O King, the wise one should cause the devotees to receive the remaining ashes,
having adorned them with new garments and performed the protective rite (kautuka) according to the previous sequence.
Adorned with all kinds of ornaments and decorated with pearl jewelry, it should be embellished with white flowers and smeared with white sandalwood paste. || 267 ||
A flower equal to a blue lotus has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
it is endowed with the radiance of a sacrificial altar and possessed of the splendor of a reflected image.
One should perform a circumambulation of the palace, standing before the assembly pavilion, especially offering the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) accompanied by incense and lamps. || 269 ||

Having prepared the ashes, one should cause them to be given; one should display the parasol and the fly-whisk to the king and his devoted subjects, and cause the remaining ashes to be given [to others]. (270)
Beginning at the time of dawn, one should perform the sequence of rites for the festival of perfumes;
likewise, one should carry out the bathing of the Preceptor at every individual bath.
Having adorned it with variegated cloths and decorated it with all ornaments,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before the deity using eight droṇas of śāli rice.
Having drawn a lotus in the center of that [diagram], one should place three-legged stands there;
having filled a vessel with rice mixed with black fragrant substances.
And one should offer musk and camphor mixed with fragrant scents, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums, and by hymns and auspicious recitations. || 274 ||
Having entered the pavilion of the site, one should perform a circumambulation of the village;
once one has reached the presence of the deity, one should especially perform a fire sacrifice (homa).

Having established the fire as before, the wise and discerning practitioner should perform the rites prescribed for the fire-sacrifice; having performed the oblation, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Combined with all fragrances, yet primarily characterized by black fragrance;
at the conclusion of the fire-offering (homa), there should be black fragrance, and one should smear Naṭeśvara with it.
Having approached Śakti, Śiva, and Naṭa at an auspicious moment, the wise man should feed the Brāhmaṇas there according to their respective Sūtras.
Then the Astra-deity should strike the drum and the soft musical instruments;
the primary image (mūlabera) should be fragrant and accompanied by its retinue.
One should cause the Lord of Yogins among the gods to be offered black sandalwood paste;
having performed the recitation of the four Vedas, one should feed the Brahmins in due order. (280)
Pure dance, especially when accompanied by song and instrumental music, becomes a vision of the Goddess upon seeing the maiden. (281)
Having placed the hand upon the preceptor, one should strike the drum;
one should strike it especially with the mantra beginning "gandhadvārā". || 282 ||
Having summoned the musicians, one should afterwards offer incense and flowers;
having paid homage with a handful of flowers, one should strike the musical instruments in sequence. || 283 ||
Having proclaimed the procedure for the seven palm-claps (saptatāla) to either the disciple or the teacher himself,
the preceptor should strike the earthen drum while reciting the Nandi-mantra.
One should strike the teacher, or one should beat the musical instruments in succession:
the jhallarī, the mukha, the paṭaha, and likewise the mardala. (285)
Endowed with the great dance and accompanied by the great sound,
one should likewise perform this sevenfold great dance.
Having paid homage to the God of gods, and having offered water for the feet and water for sipping,
one should especially perform the lustration ceremony accompanied by incense and lamps.
The wise one should cause ashes to be given, perform the rite, and show the mirror in due order;
likewise, the umbrella, the two chowries, and the fan, each in their proper sequence.
And the king, especially endowed with the fragrance of the remaining [incense], [bestows] that very fragrance upon all his devotees. (289)
(229) To all the devotees, one should offer fragrance as well as betel-leaf, along with the great sacrificial oblation. || 290 ||
One should worship the *ārātrika* lamp together with incense, having adorned it with all kinds of flowers and accompanied by all types of women. || 291 ||
Accompanied by the sound of conchs, joined with kettledrums and mridanga drums, endowed with the radiance of flowers, and possessed of variegated splendor. || 292 ||
Then, having entered the assembly pavilion, one should prepare seven houses equipped with a chariot or a palanquin, along with an umbrella and a lamp.
One should then offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya), accompanied by incense and a lamp;
thereafter, one should perform the waving of lights (nīrājana) and, in due order, cause the sacred ash (bhasman) to be given.
Having caused betel-leaf together with coconut, plantain, and breadfruit to be given, one should then show the mirror in due order. (295)
Having performed the ceremonial bathing accompanied by parasols, fly-whisks, and the sounds of song and instrumental music, one should thereafter [offer] twenty-five [items]. (296)
Having performed the ceremonial bath (snapana), one should arrange everything as before;
the wise person should take palm-powder, once-pounded powder, and water. (297)
There, one should perform the consecration and carry out the ceremonial bathing in due order;
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited there, accompanied by the sound of the Vedas.
Clad in pure garments, adorned with white garlands, and anointed with white sandalwood mixed with camphor. || 299 ||

The wise one should offer a white sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), a white lower garment, and a white upper garment; he should present the oblation (*havis*) and provide betel (*tāmbūla*) there. (300)
Then, one should perform a circumambulation around the perimeter at the edge of the palanquin;
one should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva and enter the assembly hall pavilion.
Accompanied by incense and lamps, provided with the *ārātrika* ceremony, joined with the dance of the *piśācas*, and accompanied by a great dramatic performance. || 302 ||
Beginning at the time of dawn, [the image] should be wrapped in a variegated cloth, endowed with all ornaments, and adorned with every kind of garland. (303)
Accompanied by all auspicious musical instruments, conchs, and drums, one should perform a circumambulation of the village and enter the inner chamber. || 304 ||
Having stood in the pavilion of the assembly, provided with incense and lamps,
accompanied by the *ārātrika* rite, and having especially applied sacred ashes [to the disciple]. (305)
One should show the mirror, the umbrella, the chowrie, and the fan in succession;
thereafter, one should apply the remaining ashes, especially in the case of a king.
And having given sacred ash to all the devotees, one should cause them to receive it along with a coconut, a jackfruit, and a plantain fruit. (306)
Having performed his bath according to the prescribed rule, he should offer the great sacrificial oblation;
then, commencing the hunt, he should perform the preliminary consecration during the preceding night.
One should first perform the Tripuraghna rite, as well as the auspicious and beautiful Vājiyajñas; at their conclusion, go to where the elephant is.
p.
233) Some [carry] wooden [images] by chance during the festival of Śiva at the proper time;
some indeed carry swords, and others likewise carry axes. || 309 ||
Likewise, all the enclosures and the various wealth were likewise;
at the commencement of the battle, everything quickly became agitated. || 310 ||
A deer, a bird, a boar, a peacock, and likewise a cock, all adorned with every ornament and accompanied by a forest procession. || 311 ||
Accompanied by his devotees, he should go to that place called Helālīlā;
likewise to Gaurī, Caṇḍeśa, Nandīśa, Mahākāla, and Vṛṣa.
One should perform the circumambulation of the village and enter one's own abode;
likewise, at the time of evening (pradoṣa), one should perform the consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha).
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva using eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
one should make it beautiful in the center and place a tripod there. (314)

Having filled the sacrificial mound with rice, one should place the marriage-thread (kautuka) upon it in the center with the heart-mantra, together with the deities of the mantra: Umā, Skanda, and Īśvara. || 315 ||
Having worshipped the deity Gaurī as well as the image of Caṇḍeśa,
the wise man should likewise bind the marriage-thread (kautuka) for Umāskandeśvara.
Having performed the *puṇyāha* rite as before, one should bind the protective amulet with the heart-mantra;
one should firmly tie the protection-thread with the *tryambaka* mantra.
One should perform the rite of the *astra* and the binding of the auspicious knot (*kautuka*) for the drum;
this should be done with the seal of the river or lake, conjoined with the sacred site (*tīrtha*) of the *astra*.
One should perform the invocation of all the deities accompanied by the seven sacred bathing places (tīrthas);
there, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and place nine jars.
There, he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), accompanied by fragrances and flowers;
the preceptor, together with the disciple, should perform the seven-fold tāla ritual.
Having performed his bath along with all the devotees,
he should perform the circumambulation of the village and then enter the temple.
Having performed the consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha), listen now to the account of the great tīrtha,
beginning from the morning until the supreme concluding bath (avabhṛthasnāna).
At the conclusion of the morning twilight prayers, or at the end of a sacrifice,
one should perform the circumambulation of the village in due order, as well as that of Umā, Skanda, and Īśvara.
Having stood in the assembly pavilion provided with incense and lamps, one should then perform the powder festival, especially at the front of the pavilion. (324)
On a pure ground smeared with cow dung and adorned with white powders,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its center using a mortar and pestle.
The mortar has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the pestle has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity;
one should surround them with Darbha grass and flowers, together with cloth and Dūrvā grass.
Having performed a special bath with a mortar, along with the powder of *rajanī* and *droṇa*,
combined with the water of the *rudrakanyā*.
One should cause [the image] to be given, adorned with white garments, marked with the triple line of sacred ash (tripuṇḍra), accompanied by incense and lamps, and with flowers in hand. || 328 ||
Having paid homage to the mortar and the powder of *rajanī*,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and provided with all kinds of musical instruments, (329)
At night, having filled the vessel and joined it with the presence of the deity,
one should place oil, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and flowers, along with the *kūrca* and the mantra.

Having covered [the area] with auspicious sprouts at a favorable moment, the wise man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited there, as well as the offering of ghee upon the head.
In the rite of oil-anointing for the retinue of Mūladeva,
one should likewise [anoint] Umāskandeśvara, as well as the Astra-bherī drum with oil.

Having especially worshipped [the deity] on the head with sprouts of *durvā* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), accompanied by incense and lamps, and provided with the *ārātrika* ceremony. || 333 ||
Having placed his hand [upon her], he should especially cause her to take betel-leaf there;
having done so, he should show her a mirror, as well as a chowrie and a fan. (334)
There, one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are well-versed in the four Vedas;
and for each month, the head of the image of the weapon-deities should be made from powdered pigments.
At the commencement of the oil-rite, the wise practitioner should suddenly reduce it to powder;
the vessel of powder and the vessel of oil are both accompanied by the deity of the weapon-mantra.

Accompanied by the sound of conchs, one should quickly proceed in a circumambulatory manner around the enclosure wall, performing the ritual sequence of offerings to the deities of the site (vāstudeva) with great diligence.
It was joined by lords of the earth and accompanied by great crowds;
it featured the music of lutes and other instruments, dancing, and was attended by courtesans. || 338 ||
One should perform [the rite] equal to the commencement of the oil-pressing, accompanied by water-sports;
with a covering of vessels, one should worship the nine jars. (339)
Having invoked all the deities together with all the sacred fords (tīrthas),
it is declared that the ritual consists of seven palm-tree heights (saptatāla), whether performed by the preceptor or the disciple.
A bath together with all the devotees is prescribed by means of the Astra-mantra;
one should perform the circumambulation of the village and then enter the temple. || 341 ||
One should perform the ritual bathing of Mūladeva as well as the bathing of the image;
one should worship there during the sacrifice and then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, having lifted the Śiva-pitcher along with the preceptor and his attendants,
one should perform a circumambulation of the village and likewise of the pavilion in front of Śiva.
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
[one should also perform] the circumambulation of Vāgīśvara and even of the gods externally. (344)
There one should perform an ablution; having eaten with a cloth [over one's shoulder], one should likewise cause an ablution to be performed there for Umāskandeśvara. (345)
One hundred and eight is the best; fifty or twenty-five [is also acceptable].
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before the deity with eight droṇas of śāli rice, || 346 ||
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and perform the ritual bathing and sprinkling;
[the deity] should be clothed in pure garments and adorned with white garlands. (347)
There, one should offer betel-leaf accompanied by abundant food offerings;
having presented incense and lamps, one should especially perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
All of them, observing a vow of silence, performed the circumambulation of the village while holding parched grain and flowers, accompanied by Brahmins pronouncing blessings. (349)
Then, having entered the Ālaya, one should worship the Preceptor, taking up the ritual offerings along with garments, gold, and rings. (350)
There, one should feed the Brahmins through the attendants of the devotees;
having worshipped the deity of the banner, one should offer an oblation of mung-bean rice.

One should perform the removal of the [impurity] accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kāhala trumpets, and mṛdaṅga drums, joined with the resonance of kettledrums (bherī), and adorned with all ornaments.
In that manner, having circumambulated [the site], one should perform the Caṇḍayāga,
provided with the location for Caṇḍeśa and equipped with garments and ornaments.

242) One should then begin the fire-ritual (agnikārya) joined with the fire-oblation (homa) before Caṇḍī. At the conclusion of the oblation, there should be an offering; one should present betel (tāmbūla). || 354 ||
Having worshipped it especially with incense and lamps, together with an image made of food and accompanied by a vessel for offerings (bali). || 355 ||
Having taken up the Astra-deity and observed silence, one should then perform the bali offering;
all those observing the vow of silence should dismiss the deities of the junctions.
Then, one should extinguish the lamps and cause a proclamation to be made for the duration of a watch;
one should perform a circumambulation of the village and cast the bali offering at the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha). || 357 ||
Having washed his feet, he should likewise enter the temple;
I shall now describe the Gaurī-yāga, for which one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during the first part of the night.

In the evening, having commenced the festival, one should likewise perform the circumambulation of the village around Umāskandeśvara, following the festival of the devotees without interruption. (359)
It brings merit for the welfare of the entire world, increases the prosperity of the whole kingdom, destroys all poverty, and augments the victory of the king. || 360 ||
The festival, which yields the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has thus been described in due order.
Thus ends the chapter on the Great Festival in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*. Om.
If a fault arises at the time of commencing an undertaking,
especially in the case of a festival, an expiation is prescribed.
Cut, broken, fallen, or seized by thieves and the like— such [defects] may occur regarding the banner, the flagpole, and especially the cloth. (2)
Having performed everything as before, perform the rite of re-awakening;
having offered oblations a hundred times with the Heart-mantra, perform the ritual bathing with the five products of the cow.
If one is deprived of the proper time for sacrifice, one should recite the root mantra a hundred times;
but if one is deprived of the sacrificial substances, one should offer a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra.
If the offering of the bali is omitted, deficient, or excessive,
one should perform a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra for the sake of universal pacification.
The trident-weapon (śūlāstra) has fallen, as has the eighth weapon, the throat (gala);
for the falling of the trident and indeed for all [these], there shall be a hundred oblations (śatāhuti).
If the image falls or is touched by those of other castes,
one should perform a ritual bath for it and offer oblations there with the root mantra.

If [the vessels] are broken or split through negligence, one should not observe the requirements of time—such as the lunar day, the weekday, or the auspicious moment—as was previously prescribed. || 8 ||
All the offerings of acceptance (adhivāsana) should be performed immediately;
the wise one should cause the ritual for each direction to be performed for all [deities] as previously described. || 9 ||
Alternatively, at the conclusion of a festival, the wise man should perform the consecration;
likewise in the event of a quarrel, the shedding of blood, or an attack by fire.

In a sacrificial hall or pavilion, or when there are thieves and the like; upon contact with a woman in her menses, a woman who has recently given birth, or a corpse—and especially upon seeing them—[one should not enter].
p.
246) Having discarded the previous vessels, one should then prepare new ones;
having performed a *śānti*-oblation, one should then sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). || 12 ||
Rituals such as festivals and the like are omitted for one day in the case of a minor transgression;
however, as before, one should perform the raising of the banner and conduct the festival again.
He saw Rudra’s women, female slaves, and devotees, along with instrumentalists and singers;
he saw those fallen and those afflicted by disease, as well as the flow of blood from the roots [of the trees].
At the time of the ritual action, one should sprinkle [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, for this shall be the rite for a woman. || 15 ||
At the time of the rhythmic beating of the musical instruments, at that very moment, one should perform the *chinnabhinna* [movement];
then, having again applied the instrumental accompaniment while pronouncing the *pavamāna* [mantra]. (16)
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for festivals and expiations in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Oṃ. Homage to the venerable gurus.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme installation of Śakti, for the benefit of all the worlds and bringing welfare to all living beings. || 1 ||
Sthāpana, and indeed Sthāpana itself, as well as Śaktisthāpana, Svasthāpana, and Pratiṣṭhā—thus Pratiṣṭhā is of five distinct types. || 2 ||
Installation (sthāpana) is said to be made of stone, while reinstallation (āsthāpana) is not of metal.
Re-consecration (sauta), the restoration of a dilapidated temple (jīrṇoddhāra), and the proper re-establishment (susaṃsthita) are likewise performed with the success of the original installation.
Thus, the installation mantra is to be joined [with the respective materials], and it is said to be fivefold:
[the image] made of stone, or made of metal, or made of plaster, or likewise made of jewels.
(248) Regarding stone for the house-form, the wise one should examine each stone;
the learned man should indeed distinguish the female stone from the male. || 5 ||
The preceptor, having had the astrologer determine the [auspicious] lunar day,
weekday, and moment, should perform the rite together with the artisans.
Accompanied by the sound of conch shells and adorned with full water-pots, the sight of Rudra’s wife for nine months [is like] seeing honey and milk. || 7 ||
Joined with two *vipra*s and accompanied by a *gaulī* on the right,
one should manifest [the mantra] at midday with the *ṛṣi* on the right side.
In the morning, however, the wise man should worship Janārdana with offerings from the left side for a muhūrta, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and kettledrums.

Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) joined with [the ritual] on the mountain peak, the wise preceptor, together with the artisans, should offer the bali-oblation in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (10)
Having performed the rites for the preceptor as before, the skillful artisan should then strike the image;
in the case of one made of metal, the wise one should apply beeswax to it during the process of gathering.

In the case of a palace, a wooden structure should be adopted; for the construction of a temple, a wise man should take one-sixteenth part, and then each subsequent part above that according to its respective proportion.
One should again place in the house a portion equal to one-twenty-fourth or one-eleventh of the total measurement, which may be without a specific measure or according to that very measure.
The measurement and height of the house should be thirty-three units;
likewise, the elevation should be eighty-four and sixty-two [units].
One should divide twenty-four by sixteen parts and add one part;
in this way, one should effect the initial rising by means of that measurement-finger (mānāṅgula). || 15 ||
The wise brahmin should subtract the squares from the products;
wherever the product multiplied by the multiplier is [found], it should be divided by eight in sequence.
That which is known as the "source of the learned" (śiṣṭayoni) is multiplied again by eight;
with two short vowels and twenty-seven, the remainder shall belong to the horse and the others.

That [product] is multiplied by the *randhra* (nine) and divided by the portion of the element (*dhātvaṃśa*) alone; the remainder shall indeed be the *karmādi* (the first of the actions), or it may be [calculated] by that same [number] multiplied by eight (*vasu*). || 18 ||
Having taken the portion by means of the sun's fraction,
the wise one [should calculate] the remaining portion multiplied by nine, according to the sequence of its tenth-parts.
The remainder is known as the expenditure (*vyaya*) by the Veda itself through its qualities;
that which is to be performed by the portion of Nandā is known as the remaining fractional part (*aṃśaka*). (20)
Excess of income, excess of wealth, excess of expenditure, and loss of wealth;
[the signs] named Goat, Balance, Banner, Lion, Elephant, Bull, and Cow-Wealth. (21)
The wise man should avoid the *nidhana* and the *śeṣa* [muhūrtas];
however, on the days of Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and Jupiter, they bring auspiciousness.
Likewise, other inauspicious things should be avoided with effort;
for each respective part, the specific power has been declared by its own lord. (23)
Wealth and proximity to kings bring prosperity and auspiciousness;
the remaining [planets] are also declared to be auspicious, and among these, [Jupiter] is the supreme bestower of good fortune. (24)
The king, the patron, and likewise the preceptor,
as well as the village and the banks of the rivers— one who is discerning should include these in the collection. (25)
Alternatively, without the king as the agent, there may be divine forbearance;
furthermore, for the practitioner, there is birth, prosperity, misfortune, security, the adverse point (pratyara), and death. (26)
Maitra, Paramamaitra, Janma and so forth again and again, Vipat, Pratyara, Naidhana, and likewise Candrāṣṭama shall occur. || 27 ||

Likewise, the doctrine of nihilism (vaināśika) must be avoided with great effort; however, that which is meaningful and superior should be accepted, while what is considered inauspicious should be rejected.
Having thus observed the limit of the image, the best of those skilled in ritual construction should perform the visualization;
here, that which is called "sakala" (with parts) is described according to the form of the primary liṅga.
Having fashioned the anthropomorphic form according to the measurement of the human *liṅga*,
and having fashioned the divine form according to the measurement of the *liṅga*, one indeed creates the image. (30)
Having indeed fashioned the *vāvaha* according to the measure of the Ṛṣis, one should initiate the power of all [the letters], which is unmanifest and in the form of a drop (*bindu*). || 31 ||
The goddess Dhātrī, Sarasvatī, and likewise Mahālakṣmī, as well as Mahāmoṭī, Durgā, and the group of the Seven Mothers (Saptamātṛgaṇa). || 32 ||
Arising from the totality of all purities, it is described as being in the form of a drop (bindu);
thus its characteristic has been declared, and it is established as having the nature of Śakti.

Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown and a basket-shaped headdress, his hands hold a lotus and a blue water-lily, and are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
(254) "The lotus-foot is well-placed and joined with the foot; thus, O Goddess, it has been fully described. Now hear the specific details. || 35 ||
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair, holding a water-pot and a rosary in his hands, and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. (36)
The right foot is in the svastika posture while the left foot is bent;
he is both lusterless and endowed with radiance, adorned with all ornaments.
Thus, O Goddess, it has been fully explained; now hear the specific details:
[he is] four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with a deer and an antelope horn. (38)
He is endowed with a crown of matted locks, granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
his left hand holds a ṭaṅka-axe, a discus, and a small bell.
Thus [is] the Goddess; now hear of Him joined with Her, having six arms:
first, He is endowed with the hands of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. (40)
One should especially have two lotuses, an axe, and a trident fashioned;
when these are worn, they are known as the "Chamber of Desire" (kāmakoṣṭha) for the reciters.
This form of Gaurī has been described; now hear how this should be installed, specifically on the top of the palace in the eight directions and the intermediate quarters.
The abode of Kāmakroṣṭhā has been proclaimed; one should especially install Manonmanī either on the left or on the right.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed in three ways: joined with eight times eight pillars, or equal to the number of the kalās and pillars, or joined with twelve pillars. || 44 ||
In the center, the best of those skilled in ritual procedures should fashion the [mandala] of Nanda;
likewise, the placement of jewels in the east and secondly the opening of the eyes. (45)
The third is the purification of the body; the fourth is the circumambulation of the village;
the fifth is dwelling in the water; and the sixth is the maṇṭapa.
Having established the seventh, the rite of oblation (homa) as the eighth;
the ninth is the placement of the water-offering (arghya), and the tenth is the supreme installation (sthāpana).
Construct a consecration pavilion for the temple or even within the city, either in the northeast, the southeast, the east, or the north.
One should cause a pavilion for the consecration to be constructed according to the Yamya, Rākṣasa, Vāyavya, or Vāruṇa directions; indeed, one should especially have it built.
One should specially construct or cause to be constructed a pavilion for the consecration (pratiṣṭhā-maṇḍapa),
measuring either twenty-five cubits or fifteen cubits.
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) should be twelve, ten, or even eight cubits,
resembling the smooth surface of a mirror; its width should be two cubits,
while the [inner] square should be two or four cubits.
Around [the central area], one should arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in order, joined with the secondary altars (upavedīs);
there shall be a yoni-pit in the four cardinal directions and a lotus-pit (padma-kuṇḍa) in the intermediate directions.
Between Indra and Īśāna, the wise one should fashion the primary circular pit; he should arrange nine fires, or otherwise, construct five fires.
p.
258) After verifying by means of the authoritative methods prescribed in the scriptures, he should dismiss the artisans.
Then, having smeared the pavilion, the sacrificial pit, and the altar here with cow dung— || 55 ||
In the northern part of the pavilion is the bathing-pavilion altar;
there one should feed the Brahmins and again [sprinkle] with cow-dung water.
One should smear everything with water that has been moistened;
then, beginning again from the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) rite, one should commence the Vāstu-homa sacrifice.
Or, O gods, having performed a special fire-oblation (homa) with rakshasas,
the wise one should offer the ritual sprouts (aṅkura) on the day prior to the installation.
For seven, five, three nights, or even for one night;
likewise, perform the immediate germination and the immediate consecration.
On the fifth day, the third day, or even on the first day prior to the specified date, the deposition of the jewels (ratnanyāsa) should likewise take place. (60)
In the center of the pavilion, or specifically in front of Śiva,
having smeared it with cow dung, prepare the sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) according to the prescribed rite.
Having placed [the seat] in the center of the pedestal, one should sprinkle it with water mixed with kuśa grass;
then, one should worship in its center the Anantasana (the Infinite Seat).
One should place the jewels there in sequence from the center to the northeast;
one should make ruby the central one, and likewise that of sapphire.
Vaiḍūrya is in the direction of Agni (the southeast), and likewise Vairava in the southeast;
Nīla is in the direction of Yama (the south), and Gometaka is in the direction of Nirṛti (the southwest). || 64 ||
A crystal should be worshipped in the western quarter,
a ruby in the northwestern quarter, a diamond in that northern direction, and coral in the direction of Śaṅkara (the northeast). || 65 ||
The placement [of the mantra] by means of the nine seed-syllables remains fixed for him;
he should thus establish each individual mantra so that it is smooth and very firm.
The artisan, with eyes as sharp as a blade, should perform the closing of the eyes;
the wise know that these procedures are to be carried out prior to the day of worship.
Three [units] joined with five, and the eye of the burnt cause;
therefore, one should emit [the seed-syllable] there when two eyes have been made on that day. 68.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice and place the vessel upon a pillar;
having taken the image (bera) into its center, one should install it with the heart-mantra.
The artisan should polish the image with his right hand using the weapon-mantra;
he should apply [the ointment] upon the circle of the eyes with a stroke of golden luster. (70)
In the center of the black circle, within the middle of the circle of light,
one should rotate that very silver [substance] according to the sequence of the seventh stage.
One should draw the line for the earth and the line for the eyelashes outside of that in succession;
having dismissed the artisan at this point, the wise one should cause the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be made.
Then one should perform the rite for non-attainment; one becomes purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Honey, ghee, and milk, each measuring one prastha, should be placed in a vessel. 73.
A golden lotus should be placed in the eastern thread-vessel; as before, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the east and place the image upon it.
The wise one should worship with scents, flowers, and so forth, using the *praṇava*, even a small amount of ghee, molasses, or ghee that has been consecrated by the long [syllable]. (75)
One should fashion three nails out of gold on the hand of initiation and in the palm;
one should not worship with the Netra-mantra, but rather perform the opening of the eyes.
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth state (turya), and that which follows the fourth—these five states beginning with waking exist; from among them, this divine waking arises.
At that time, the supreme preceptor should cause the opening of the eyes to be performed,
as well as the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), along with the leaf of the *śrī* tree and *kuśa* grass.
One should rub it with a bilva leaf and anoint it with sandalwood paste;
then, while recollecting the eye-mantra, one should display the dhenu-mudrā.
One should worship each pavilion with the [mantras] of the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
and there, one should likewise place clarified butter according to the sequence of golden flowers. (80)
One should display the armor with the *puṣpāvatī* mantra alone, and the cow and calf along with their limbs with the *godhenu-havya* mantra. || 81 ||
One should display [the deity] upon the pericarp with the mantra "brahmajajñānam";
then, having covered [it] with a cloth, [one should worship] with clarified butter and the deities resembling those materials and so forth.
Curd and milk combined with pieces of sugarcane, which are beautiful to behold, as well as grain consisting of rice, along with green gram and black gram; || 83 ||
Furthermore, having established a village adorned with all ornaments on the bank of a body of water, he should consecrate it with water alone. (84)

The wise one should first place the jar facing upward with its mouth toward the east, along with the jars of the world-protectors; then, he should arrange the eight Vāmā and other Śaktis and the *vardhanī* jar.
One should let it soak for a day and night, or for three watches, or for two watches;
or even at the very end of the night, or when the mother is seated upon the chariot. (86)
Or, having placed [the image] upon a palanquin, the preceptor, together with his disciples,
shall lead it into the bathing pavilion and place it upon the altar there.
The wise one should sprinkle the garment, the broom, and the hand along with the previously mentioned bath using the five earths, the five products of the cow, and bilva leaves.

The knower of mantras should repeatedly smear it with fragrant substances and the like, along with great torches; then, at the conclusion of the consecration with the water-jar, he should cover it with a cloth.
The wise man should cause a declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made there and worship with perfumes and other offerings;
the intelligent one should have the marriage-thread (*kautuka*) bound amidst the resonant chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*). (90)
Then the wise one should have a pavilion constructed;
he should worship the pavilion in due order according to the procedure previously described.
It was provided with a garland of *darbha* grass, hung with strings of pearls and blood, endowed with four doors, and adorned with four archways. || 92 ||
Having encircled the eighth neck, one should place it upon the altar;
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as before with eight droṇas of rice.
One should adorn half of that with rice and half of that with sesame seeds;
[the vessel] may be made of wood, or have five arms, or be made of hair, or from the feathers of a bird.
When they attempt to cross over, that bed becomes fivefold:
made of wood, consisting of planks, and likewise the *mukula* and the *kevala*. (95)
If these are not available, he should indeed cover himself with a cotton garment;
likewise, he may prepare a bed using wood and a wooden frame. (96)
One should worship the bed in the center, following the sequence beginning with Vāmā and the others;
starting from the Goddess’s seat, one should cover it over the bed.
First, the head and the face should be turned upward with the mantra beginning with "Praṇava" (Oṃ);
there, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the image as well as for the vehicle.
From Laṃbakūrca, there should be Vivaktra, joined with the [five] offerings;
one should worship him along with the Ācārya and the Putrakas using perfumes, flowers, and other [offerings]. 99.
One should perform the *puṇyāha* rite as before; fashion the [image's] characteristic features with cloth.
One should worship all [the deities] with perfumes and other offerings, and there, one should worship the Goddess by her own name. (100)
The wise one, standing facing north, should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the image with the five Brahma-mantras and show it the *surabhi* [mudrā]. (101)
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one becomes like fire;
then, through internal meditation, one should begin the image of the Lord of the Altar.
Then, having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should subsequently join each respective root mantra in its proper sequence, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ."
Having invoked [the deity] with the door-mantra, one should place the water-pots upon the principal [deity],
as well as perform the rites of installation (sthāpana), presence (sānnidhya), and confinement (sannirodha).
Having meditated with the *namaskāra-mudrā*, one should specifically display it;
thereafter, the wise practitioner should sequentially place the Brahma-limbs in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (105)
One should specifically display the mudrā of peace, as well as the lotus with its bud-like pericarp and moon, and the gesture of salutation that delights the mind. (106)

One should cause water for the feet and other offerings to be presented there; one should place the root-mantra at the very base, assign the limbs [of the mantra] to the limbs [of the deity], and worship according to the prescribed rite.
The wise practitioner should then install the eight powers, beginning with Vāmā;
thereafter, he should install the mantra and worship with perfumes and other offerings.
Having likewise bound the vajra-mudrā through a specific salutation, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa); its procedure is now described.
One should purify the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) there, and immediately thereafter perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*).
One should then install the presiding deities, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise. (110)

Likewise, one should perform the entire rite of the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya), beginning with the placement of the fire, according to the instructions for the primary [fire], including the eight circular pits (kuṇḍala) starting from the left. 111.
Then, having gone forward again, one should begin the ritual sprinkling with fuel-sticks,
clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees are [to be used] in order starting from the east;
likewise, Apāmārga, Arka, and Khadira are [used] in the directions starting from the southeast (Agni).
One should likewise use *palāśa* wood in the primary and other sacrificial pits; indeed, it should be used in all the various types of rites, and in its absence, one may use *palāśaka* wood.
The oblation of clarified butter is offered with the mouth by means of the root-mantra of the fuel-sticks;
the sacrificial porridge is offered with the *ghora* mantra, and the parched grain is offered with the *vāma* mantra. || 115 ||
Having offered mustard seeds with the *sadyojāta* mantra, barley oblations with the *hṛdaya*, and palm-fruit with the *śiras*, one should offer each of these various eightfold sets individually.
In this manner, one should perform the rite of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the oblation (homa) everywhere in due order;
at the conclusion of the materials, having offered the Vyāhṛtis, one should touch the image with the Vardhanī vessel.
One should touch each respective portion together with the mantras for those specific oblations;
these are the substances for the oblation of all materials, corresponding to the various fire-pits (kuṇḍas) of the deities' forms.
The wise practitioner should perform the oblation with the respective mantra according to his own spiritual lineage;
he should offer a hundred oblations of honey and milk, and a hundred of sugar and other such substances.
And in the sacrificial pits in the four directions, perform the recitation slowly;
recite the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and the study of the Atharvaveda. (120)
The preceptor should recite the Umā-sūkta and the Śrī-sūkta;
he should especially offer betel-leaf to her.
The expression "adhivāsa" (consecration) is used for the remainder of the night;
furthermore, there is "sadyo'dhivāsana" (immediate consecration), which is especially dependent upon direction and time.
At dawn, when it was clear, the preceptor, together with his disciples,
performed a special bath and carried out his daily rites.
Then, having put on a white upper garment and being adorned with ornaments on the five limbs, one should worship the Goddess at an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction.
One should kindle the fire and begin the ritual sprinkling;
having offered oblations of the excellent substances, one should offer one hundred oblations for each of the respective forms. (125)

One should offer each individual oblation with the mantra "sarvātmanā"; then, one should perform the Jaya and other offerings, the rekindling of the fire, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt and Śakra oblations in their proper sequence.
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the heart-mantra, one should begin the sprinkling (pariṣecana);
thereafter, one should accomplish the installation of the image and spread the enclosing sticks (paridhi).
Then, having placed the seats for all those wandering mendicants from the householders in due order,
the preceptor should rise and cast them into the midst of the fire.
Having adorned him with new garments, a turban, and an upper robe;
equipped with all the leaf-hand gestures and decorated with white garlands. || 129 ||
The wise and discerning practitioner should cause the image to arise by means of the heart-mantra;
however, one should especially avoid using garments or a *kūrca* in all instances. (130)
One should perform the study of hymns and knowledge within the family circle through dance, song, and so forth;
then, one should present the image upon the pedestal in the center of the bathing pavilion.
Having performed purification, the preceptor should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
then, having known the Goddess and Tryambaka, he should perform the rite five times with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should worship the Māyā-mantras with this mantra for Gaurī:
"Gandhodakodanaṃ sthānaṃ haridrāmalakaiḥ saha. (133)
Having firmly established the Goddess upon the pedestal, one should perform the consecration;
there, one should dismiss the artisan and sprinkle [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Furthermore, beginning from the auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should perform the *vardhinī* consecration;
there, one should cause the consecration to be performed with pure water and [images of] the deities (*bera*). || 135 ||
One should likewise absorb the Brahman into the self and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once more;
having offered the respectful oblation (arghya), one should especially cause a flower to be placed upon the head.
Then, having lifted the sleep-pot (nidrākumbha) together with the image-makers (mūrtipās), the preceptor (deśika),
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the image, should install it according to the previous sequence.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should gaze upon it at an auspicious moment;
then, by means of the syllables and the Brahma-aṅga mantras, the Vidyā should again enter the form.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the *vardhanī* vessel and lifted up the handful of clay,
one should meditate with a concentrated mind upon the moon-mantra situated in the center of the heart.
(275) When the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been obstructed, the teacher, having performed the *kumbhaka* (retention),
should recite the mantra "Ghaṭe ghaṭe" while the *jayaprāṇa* is being fashioned. 140.
Therefore, having recited the root mantra, it is said that [the water] produced from the heart-lotus should be poured by the preceptor into the vardhanī vessel using only that much [of the water].

Having extracted [the image] with the mantra "re sā mastrīvastrakūrca," and having placed the image within the heart while it remains in the house, one should then perform the consecration with the water-pot (kumbha). || 142 ||
One should perform the consecration by means of the Sahasrākṣarī mantra in due order;
or else, using the Saṃvatsarākṣara mantra, on the right or on the west.
One should place Vāmā and the others upon the seat with the *kuṃbha* [vessel];
with that water, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the Goddess. 144.
One should place [the seed-syllables] at the root of the feet and perform the placement of the limbs with the auxiliary mantras;
the wise practitioner should then perform the placement of the Mātṛkā using the Gaurī-Gāyatrī mantra.
Thereafter, one should worship with perfumes and other offerings; then again, with that which is especially excellent.
One should again offer water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, incense, clothing, ornaments, garlands, and the incense-lamp. (147)
Having offered the oblation, one should then cause the offering to be given to the goddesses beginning with Vāmā;
all such offerings as these should be caused to be presented with the *hṛdaya* mantra. || 148 ||
In this manner, one should indeed have [an image] made either of stone or even of metal;
having first established the stone image, one may then install the metal image, whether it be movable or immovable.
Or, in brief, [one should perform] the circumambulation of the village from the iron [image];
there, at the outset, one should again perform the festive rite and the auspicious ceremony. (150)
Likewise, the immovable [images] are consecrated without the water-rite;
for the bed, one should follow what is prescribed for the bed; they know all the rest to be of this same nature.
One skilled in the root of the trident should likewise place the jewels and other items;
one should place the nine gems with the root mantra "śailajā."
