But in the case of the Citrabhāsa, one should place the variety of those [deities] mentioned there; therein, the ritual of immersion in water (toyādhivāsana) is performed, followed by the ritual of resting (upaśayana), excluding [the specific rites for] Vināyaka.
Having understood this procedure in this very way, the wise man should cause the consecration to be performed;
for that which is made of stone, it should be done with wall-painting at the tip of the pedestal, measuring one cubit in height.
One may fashion either a pedestal (*pīṭha*), or a base (*pāda*), or even an image (*bera*);
it is taught that the form is indeed for ritual worship (*karmārcarūpa*), and one should perform everything right there. (155)
Now listen to the installation of Kāmakroṣṭha and the installation of all [deities].
Homage to the venerable Gurus; homage to the venerable Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the installation of Kāmakroṣṭha in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* of Yogaja.
One should tie an amulet made of jewels upon the left hand of the Goddess with the mantra "Gaurīmimāya," and perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites while reciting it. || 1 ||
Having established [the deity] with the root mantra, one should perform the fire offering (homa) as before;
one should display the bud-gesture (mukula-mudrā), the lotus-gesture (padma-mudrā), and the seed-syllable-gesture (bīja-mudrā). || 2 ||
(279) One should perform the study during the ten periods according to the previously mentioned rule. I, Gaurīkalākṣa, shall now declare that which originates from the seed-syllable of Gaurī. (3)
Tārā is to be known as a portion of Īśa, and Vidyā is remembered as a portion of Vastra (Umā). Mṛtyuñjaya is [the portion] of Raudra, and Svasti is the portion of Varman.
One should install Bilinī, Jvālinī, Matimatī, Māmativrajā, Śānti, Bhṛti, Kriyā, Kṣānti, and Ghorā as the left-hand digits (vāmakalā). || 5 ||
One should place Dānti, Śānti, Dayāsūti, Dviti, Sandhyā,
and Sadyajā upon the body of Gaurī outside the twenty-sixth [circle].
One should place the *tāra* (the syllable Om) on the head, and one should place the [syllables of the] Vidyā upon the faces;
[then] on the heart, the throat, the two arms, the belly, and the region of the navel.
p.
280) These are indeed the digits (kalās) of Aghora, located in the womb, the secret region, the two thighs, the two knees, the two backs, and the two sides. (8)
One should indeed place these goddesses, who are the digits (kalās) of Vāmadeva, upon the deity:
on both feet and also on both hands.
One should place the Sadyojāta-kalā on both breasts;
then, having joined it to the base of the staff, it should be provided with a new cloth.
In the Prasāda, in the Maṇṭapa, at the Gopura, and during the lighting of the lamps, as well as at sunset, the sounding of conchs and drums must be performed. || 11 ||
One should begin the lighting of the lamps with the mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ).
The water of Kṛttikā should be prepared; Kṛttikā shall be the primary [constellation].
Since the rites pertaining to fire and the constellations must be performed, one should therefore practice the Kṛttikā rite;
by means of the procedure for the lamp-mechanism, one should fashion a great lamp. || 13 ||
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a festival; it is prescribed that [an image] made of śāli rice be used.
One should worship the deities beginning with Umā and Skanda in a single form.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should place the sacrificial offerings (bali) starting from the east.
On the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), at the conclusion of the seating, one should cause the offering of oblations (bali) to the deities of the directions;
there, one should worship the preceptor (ācārya) with garments, sacrificial fees (homa), and finger-rings.
One should especially offer cakes or rice-flour preparations,
having given abundant sacrificial oblations accompanied by side dishes.
There, one should cause betel-leaf to be offered, accompanied by all the ritual services.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Ritual for the Lamp of Yoga on Kṛttikā" in the *Yogaja-pīṭhatantra*.
Now I shall specifically describe the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the rite of offering the sacred thread).
That which is called *pavitra* is designated as "pure."
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas, as well as all the hosts of sages and the multitudes of those dwelling in sacred fields (kṣetra). || 2 ||
For the sake of pleasing everyone, indeed perform the Pavitrārohaṇa rite;
one may do so in the month of Āṣāḍha, or Śrāvaṇa, or even Bhādrapada.
In Āṣāḍha it is declared to be excellent; in Śrāvaṇa, one should place it as middling;
in Bhādrapada, it should be known as inferior—thus it is proclaimed according to these three months. (4)
In this manner, it should be performed every month, especially on the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
or else, on the thirteenth day, one should then offer fragrant purificatory threads (gandhapavitraka).
The best [cord] is one made of gold thread, the middling is of silver, and the lowest is of copper thread; if these are unavailable, it may even be of cotton.
Kusha grass and bark garments, as well as the collection of [implements] belonging to the sages, the eye-cloth, and the excellent lotus-thread. (7)
If [cotton] is not available, it is said that one should make [the thread] very firm with cotton;
this is the rule for the thread known by the knower of threads regarding the daughters of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
One should prepare it with fine threads and avoid the appearance of hair;
having sprinkled it with pure water, one should wash it according to the prescribed rule. (9)
Having beautifully decorated the pavilion with fine silk cloths and divine garments,
one should adorn the earthen vessels, the full water-pot, and the mirror.
One should perform the offering of the sprouts there according to the previously mentioned procedure,
using twelve, sixteen, or twenty-five [sprouts].
One should place either fifteen, eighty, or one hundred and eight [vessels],
together with the materials for the ablution, according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), which is covered with cloth and provided with a lid, and endowed with gold and jewels, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Thereafter, having prepared the fire-oblation (homa) either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon an altar (sthaṇḍila),
[one should offer] fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds, or sesame seeds. (14)
All the materials for the oblation are offered in their proper sequence;
specifically, following the order of fuel-sticks and clarified butter, the clarified butter is offered with the left hand.

Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and the parched grain (lāja) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra; one should offer all the substances and the clarified butter (ājya) to Īśāna with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should offer sesame seeds with the *śiromantra* at the crest, and likewise a handful [of them]; having offered parched grain with the *kavaca*, and cakes with the *astra* mantra. (17)

Having specifically offered unbroken grains with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) in sequence, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in this manner, concluding with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) using the root-mantra (mūla-mantra). || 18 ||
One should worship either the *liṅga* or the *kautuka* at a pure location;
one should also worship the sixteen images with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (19)
One should worship the image in due order, either in its place or in a pavilion;
thereafter, one should offer a great food offering (mahānaivedya) and betel leaf.

With hymns and the recitation of auspicious texts, with the sounds of Vedic study, with the resonance of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, and with auspicious cries of "Victory! and the like; || 21 ||
In that place, however, the Geya should be performed;
one should consecrate the sacred thread and, through the yoga of meditative concentration, bring about the breaking of sleep during the night.
Having performed the ritual of placing the sacred grass (pavitra) upon it according to the prescribed rules,
one should subsequently perform [the recitation] one hundred and eight times, or fifty, or twenty-five times.
They are proclaimed as being superior, middling, and inferior;
for the sake of auspiciousness, twenty-five purifiers (pavitraka) should be prepared. (24)
One should perform the binding there using a measurement of two finger-breadths or else one finger-breadth; one should bind it with a thread in due order.
One should fashion the saffron with saffron and the musk with turmeric; then, having performed the tying of the knot according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
Uśīra, haribera, the flower named taraṅga,
and the fragrant leaf called kallola— their knot is prepared.
Then one should make a knot; the number of threads shall correspond to the [prescribed] count. One should tie it with a measurement equal to the circumference of the linga. (28)
One should thus diligently fashion the Gaṅgāvatāra-ūṣṇīṣa out of a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal. (29)
Endowed with all auspicious marks, vast and most beautiful—this should be placed in the center and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (30)
A new garment, well-fitting in every respect, should be put on;
upon that, one should place a *kūrca* (grass mat) and install it in the pavilion in due order.
Having performed this, one should wait for the morning time and then perform purification, sipping water, bathing, or the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana). || 32 ||
On the preceding day, one should perform the ritual installation of the deity according to the prescribed rule;
then, having offered the thread for the mounting of the Lord, one should present it to Caṇḍeśa.

Having placed the water-pots all around in a distinguished manner, and having caused those who recite auspicious blessings and benedictions to proclaim a "day of merit" (puṇyāha), [one should proceed]. (p. 289) 34.
Accompanied by shouts of victory, songs, and dances, as well as the chanting of the Vedas and other sounds,
along with the beating of kettledrums, clay drums, cymbals, trumpets, and bronze bells.
Adorned with all ornaments, it was accompanied by jhallarī cymbals, mṛdaṅga drums, kartarī cymbals, tāla-clappers, flutes, conchs, dundubhi kettledrums, and other musical instruments. || 36 ||
He is clothed in new garments and his head is wrapped;
his head is adorned with golden flowers, and he wears a golden sacred thread.
Adorned with golden rings and bracelets, beautified by ear-pendants, endowed with all ornaments, and graced with flower garlands. || 38 ||
All these [elements] and others have been fully adorned by the teachers;
having thus adorned them for the sake of the practitioners, one should extract the *pavitra* in due order. (39)
Adorned with all ornaments, one should circumambulate the Ālaya;
then, having gone to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should place the sacred thread (pavitraka) upon it.
Having worshipped it especially with the sequence of incense and lamps,
one should then exit that house, which has been encircled by threads.
An offering (naivedya) should be presented, especially milk-rice (pāyasānna);
there, one should honor the preceptors according to one's means.
Having fully worshipped the practitioners, he should satisfy the devotees in due order;
then, with the worship of the attendants, he should feed the Brahmins.
One should daily feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity and suitability,
beginning with the Āgamas and including the Śivadharma Purāṇas. (44)
Having honored those who recite the Purāṇas, one should also worship the sacrifice to the gods;
having invoked all the deities, beginning with Parā, with the sacred pavitra threads.
The offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) should be performed by the attendants for the devotees;
the sacred thread, along with its central ring (karṇikā), must be bestowed upon all the people.
For twelve days, eight days, five days, or even three days,
one should perform the Pavitrārohaṇa rite and worship there at the time of twilight.
Then, accompanied by his wife, he should perform [the rite] adorned with all ornaments. || 48 ||
Taking the previously consecrated water, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa;
there, one should perform the ritual bathing and worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (49)
Afterwards, having honored the ascetic and clothed him, one should attend to him;
one should provide the yogi with a loincloth, an upper garment, and a companion.
One should avoid shaving the hair and so forth, initiation, purificatory rites, receiving gifts, needlework, and the like, as well as staying awake at night, on these aforementioned days. (51)
One should first avoid a circular mandala, or one arising from a creeper or a liṅga;
likewise, it may be a lotus mandala or even a half-moon.
One should honor the teacher’s satisfaction of mind during the first part of the night;
one should worship the mandala there at the conclusion of the ritual worship.
Having adorned the pavilion, one should prepare all the ritual materials:
a mirror, a fly-whisk, a palm-leaf fan, and paintings. (54)
Then there is the growth of body hair, followed by the cutting of nails, hair, and so forth;
[the wearing of] ornaments, the carrying of a bowl, the application of ashes, a water-pot, and the sacred thread.
The wrist-band, the belly-band, the support, and the loincloth;
as well as the collyrium, the vessel, and the two applicator-sticks for the collyrium. (56)
The yoga-band, the staff, the girdle of muñja grass, or the black antelope skin;
the conch-shell vessel, the five-metal alloy, and the weapon of the eight auspicious signs. || 57 ||
One should place the tortoise-posture for all [the deities] and construct the pavilion;
[one should also depict] the black antelope, the axe, and the alms-bowl placed below.
The divine weapon, the divine bracelet, the sun, the moon, and fire;
the Gaṅgā, the armlet, and the garland, along with the eight types of serpents. (59)
There were garlands of rudrākṣa beads, garlands for the head, and garlands for the uṣṇīṣa; there were garlands for the forehead, garlands for the neck, and those bound as ornaments upon the ears.
Perform the recitation with a garland hanging from the heart down to the navel;
likewise, use a garland on the arm or a garland on the hand [reaching] to the elbow.
Taking the vessel with various [substances], one should place it before the maṇḍala;
in this very same sequence, one should likewise establish each of the ritual substances.
One should worship [the deity] from the beginning until the conclusion of the Pavitrārohaṇa rite;
the mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain a meritorious state. || 63 ||
Just as the preliminary rite should be performed for the purification of the *pavitrāroha*,
so too, according to the scripture, is the *pavitrārohaṇa* rite joined with the Goddess. (64)
Thus ends the chapter on the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Now I shall speak specifically of the form of the mandala;
the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) is divided into four parts, and the altar (*vedikā*) occupies one part.
One should draw a mandala in the center measuring five tālas in height, with a projection of one tāla and a surface like the belly of a mirror.
Having drawn a grid of eight times eight squares, one should draw four central compartments upon a lotus pedestal, colored white, red, and black.
Having drawn the yellow and dark paths for all [the deities], the wise one should then arrange the white ritual procedure on the exterior of the lotus pedestal. (4)
In that interval, one should likewise fashion the path, the red and dark-blue [sections], the black, and the yellow,
as well as the four gates according to the proper rule.

One should make the *ardhamāraka* at the door; it is said that there is a *pa* (pillar) at every corner (*karṇa*). One should make the *kapola* at the cheek; here, these are outside the *brahmasthāna*.
The petal should have a width of three finger-breadths; the crescent moon should be three finger-breadths;
the lotus should likewise be three finger-breadths; and the svastika should be three finger-breadths.
The Śrīvatsa foot, measuring three finger-breadths and square in shape, should be placed;
it may be white, red, yellow, black, or dark blue.
The *pada* is desired to be auspicious in every respect and free from all defects.
297) It should be white with rice flour, and the *sindūra* is a red mineral. || 9 ||
Turmeric is yellow powder; black and dark [pigments] make five [types].
Charred *lī* wood is black; "pāda" refers to a replica or a crafted image.
Having drawn the mandala in all [the aforementioned cases] in reverse order, listen now to the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] arising from the entwining of creepers. || 11 ||
Having laid out eight times eight squares, one should especially draw a four-square lotus in the center with five colors upon its eight petals.
One should fashion a lotus with a width of four [units], nourishing it with the part belonging to Kauśika;
one should make the pericarp with the part of Vyoman, and the filaments with the part of the wings.
One should fashion the *śeva* and *dara* measures according to half the size of the *karṇikā*;
the walkway (*vīthikā*) outside the lotus, however, should be white in color and occupy half of a quarter-part.
It should have four gates aligned with the street and be supported by beautiful gateways;
its side-faces (kapola) should be equal to those, and its subsidiary ornaments (upaśobhikā) should be equal to the beautiful gateways.
In the four directions starting from the northeast (īśāna), red, reddish-brown, white, and black powder is prescribed; this is especially [applied] to the cheeks.
From Indra to Soma, the four directions are conceived as the liṅga;
having fashioned the liṅga as seven steps, the outer pedestal is four steps.
The three-word *liṅga* beginning with "ūrdhva" and ending with "puruṣa" serves as the coloring for the faces;
from Indra up to Soma, there shall be twenty-eight words.
The wise one should conceive the meaning of the gender so that the word may correspond to its number;
likewise, he should visualize it as yellow, black, white, or blue. (19)
In the center, one should fashion [the design] with five colors joined with red;
in each corner, one should fill in the fourth [color], which is the opposite [of the adjacent one]. || 20 ||
Thus, one should mentally conceive the preceptor as the Liṅgodbhava;
I shall now describe the preceptor as the Manobhava—listen with a one-pointed mind.
Having made the ground level, resembling the surface of a mirror,
one should likewise [draw] a thread with its tip pointing east and another with its tip pointing north.
In the center, there should be a nine-square lotus with eight petals and filaments;
in the four directions, there should be nine divisions, and the wise one should have the temple constructed thus.
Provided with the six groups [of deities] and adorned with the nose and other features,
one should construct the temple as before, having divided it into eight equal parts. (24)
The base (bandha) or the pedestal-base (pādabandha), fashioned with a decorative motif (pariliṅga),
is joined with a pedestal (liṅgapīṭha) and extends to one-third of the height of the plinth (pādavarga).
In the corner, a svastika is prescribed according to the specific ninefold division;
it consists of five powders and five faces, specifically for Puruṣa and the others.
One should gradually arrange the temple facing that [direction],
and one should place the eight Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, all around it.
One should perform the worship in sequence by means of the path of the five obstructions;
one should draw the mandala all around with three hundred and sixty [squares].
One should visualize each one individually and in reverse order with five colors.
One should cut the plantain fruit, the mango fruit, and the jackfruit into pieces. (29)
Having placed [the image] facing the mandala, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
[one should give] a gold coin, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should fashion an utpala-flower mandala and arrange it; [the materials] such as a hundred niṣkas or more, or even a mountain, according to whatever is available in a secluded place.
To the eastern part of the mandala, a mountain of gold is prescribed;
for the reciter (vācaka), however, there is a mountain of silver, while to the south is a mountain of copper.
Having placed a jewel in the Rākṣasa [direction], one should place a mountain of *śāla* wood in the west;
in the Soma [direction] a mountain of mustard seeds, and in the Śāṅkara [direction] a mountain of sesame seeds.
Thus all these have been stated, either individually or as a collective burden.
One should perform the rite according to one's means and fashion a mountain;
the wise practitioner should offer oblations of Jaya and the others, accompanied by the five Brahmans and the six limbs.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth by means of his own name,
the knower of mantras should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with śāli rice on the northern part of the mandala.
In the midst of that, the wise one should prepare a bed with red cloth;
then he should perform the binding of the eyes and wrap [the disciple] with a new garment.
One should tie the protective amulet there; for women, make it two-eyed.
A night-oblation must be performed, and one should offer oblations to all the gods.
Perform double the number of all ritual services for the God of gods.
At the clear dawn, one should release the blindfold there. (39)
Having offered a golden flower, one should cause its name to be bestowed;
one should then have the Lord bathed fifty or twenty-five times.
Or one should offer oblations to the God of gods one hundred and eight times;
one should cause a golden auspicious thread and a new cloth to be given.
Having offered abundant oblations, he should propitiate the God of gods;
having worshipped all the deities, he should show them the mandala.
One should cause all the implements for the sacrifice to be offered to the preceptor;
one should bathe [the image] with coconut water after the consecration with ghee and milk. || 43 ||
One should offer the deity, accompanied by Umā and Skanda, abundant sacrificial oblations;
there, one should cause betel-leaf to be given to the devotees along with their attendants. (44)
One should feed the Brahmins there according to one's capacity and cause gifts to be given;
one should worship the preceptor there and observe the vow until death.
Then, having honored the preceptor who has bestowed the instruction of the Śiva-mantra,
the wise disciple should proceed ahead and enter his own home.
Thus ends the chapter on the Maṇḍala in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the ripening of fruits:
"That man who, having seen the peak from afar, bows down to Śiva... (1)
One is liberated from all sins, just as snakes are freed from their sloughs, by performing circumambulations of the temple of Śiva with a resounding *murumuru* sound and vigorous strides. (p. 305) 2.
May that Māyā, who is auspicious at the end of those afflictions and the destroyer of the evils arising from existence—when touched by people in this world of mortals—cause them to live well. (3)
During a festival or at the time of an offering, a person who performs a circumambulation obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
Having performed the salutation in this manner, one should likewise honor [the deity] in the world;
one should offer water, a flower-stand, and flowers, dedicating them to the God.
That man who has established a grove for the God of gods upon the earth enjoys various enjoyments, having adorned it with diverse flowers.

Thus, one who possesses wealth and is illustrious is highly honored in this world; [he is even more so] when he is exceedingly endowed with yoga and is a learned Vedic scholar who has mastered the Vedas. (7)
Having bathed the Lord Nāyaka with milk at Gośṛṅga, one should [worship] him with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water from kuśa grass. || 8 ||
A man who, filled with devotion, performs the ninefold ritual bathing of the Lord of the Gods, obtains a reward equal to the merit of giving ten million gifts.
One should enjoy various enjoyments and be honored in the world of Śiva;
for whatever action exists on the ninefold path, it likewise becomes ninefold in its enjoyment.
Having prepared the oblation in nine ways, [one obtains] that fruit according to its weight;
however, he who gives a bell for incense is liberated from Nirṛti.
One should cause garments, ornaments, and so forth to be offered to the God of gods;
having worshipped him with various cloths as well as various ornaments. (12)
But when worshipped here in this world, his power is indeed without distinction;
even on a piece of ground only as large as a cow's ear, he becomes as fickle as Umā’s husband.
Even one who is a lord of villages is especially honored here;
however, in the presence of the God of gods, he becomes like a single Rudra among the Prajāpatis.
One should cause a lamp to be offered to the God of gods even once at the proper time;
he too is remembered as being like a lamp in the worlds, for his light causes all activities to flourish.
One who undertakes [the work] with Śiva in mind shall again partake of heaven;
by performing all acts of charity, austerity, and sacrifice, one shall obtain their fruit.
Therefore, one shall obtain that great fruit in the supreme heaven;
by that, one will be protected for seven successive births. (17)
Whatever a man constructs with bricks,
stone, or metal, he is honored in the world of Śiva by means of a golden celestial chariot.
Established by a Siddha in a celestial chariot and traveling through the path of the sky, he reaches the world of Śiva while being honored by men. (19)
Thereafter, they shall obtain the fruit of proximity to the Śiva-liṅga;
indeed, they shall become of the same form as the image that was installed.
When the Śiva-sacrifice was completed and the ritual worship had been performed,
[he honored] the twenty-one gurus as well as his own lineage-holders.
They desire the Darśa sacrifice first;
for those born on the mother's side during the state of union, that world is held to be their place. (22)
For those who serve [the teacher], there shall be no separation from sons, brothers, and wives;
indeed, they shall dwell forever in the world of Śiva, surrounded by all the gods.
Then, having offered extensive oblations when the dissolution has arrived,
and having attained the yoga of knowledge, he is liberated right there.
By constructing walls and pavilions as desired, one shall attain heaven;
likewise, by diligently constructing step-wells, wells, and tanks dedicated to the deities. (25)
By performing this, one becomes possessed of abundant wealth, and at its conclusion, one shall attain Śiva;
moreover, there will be even more for him, and his attainment of heaven is certain. (26)
Having understood the true nature of sitting upon the seat, one should worship Śiva;
for indeed, [one attains] sālokya, sāmīpya, and sāyujya. (27)
For the fourth [type] is conformity (sārūpya), which is superior, middling, or inferior. The middling is a square pillar, representing the deities of Dharma, Jñāna, and so forth. (28)
Externally, for the twelve pillars, the deities are the twelve Ādityas;
for the twenty external pillars, they are the Vasus and likewise the two Aśvins.
Having wrapped the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara), Viśva, and the deities who are the pillars of the universe with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned them with flower wreaths; || 30 ||
Having wrapped that [image] in a cloth and likewise enveloped it with a pillar-covering,
one should cover it from above with white cloths and adorn it with eye-cloths.
A coconut fruit adorned with flowers and strings of pearls,
and an Aśvattha tree decorated with red leaves and cakes; (32)
Having prepared a ground smeared with cow dung, adorned with incense and lamps, and provided with perfumes and flowers, one should sprinkle it toward the surface of the earth.

Just as the preliminary dance was performed previously at the time of the offering of the sprouts, so too should the pavilion be prepared as previously described; now listen to the time for the dance.
In the permanent place, the dance is performed until the end of the worship,
likewise during the bath with milk, the bath with ghee, the bath with honey, or even in water.
Or on another auspicious day, he should perform that dance;
before the commencement of the dance, he should first administer initiation to the women.
Likewise, for one who has been initiated at the commencement of the Gāndharva [rite].
The trumpeter, the one who beats the drum, the singer, and likewise the flute-player. || 37 ||
Indeed, he bestows the Śiva-initiation upon the wives of Rudras present there, [making them] endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with all ornaments. (38)
One should commence the pure dance (śuddhanṛtta) when endowed with these characteristics;
however, one who is deficient in limbs, lacks a nose, or is a child or likewise an old man [should not do so]. (39)

One who is diseased, one with deformed limbs, one afflicted by consumption or leprosy, a drinker of forbidden liquids, and a heretic—one should avoid such persons, as well as women [who possess these defects]. (40)
Until nightfall, the wise man should offer worship, perform the rite with ashes,
circumambulate the village, and then enter his own dwelling.
In the evening, one should especially perform [the rite] without the *homa*;
afterwards, one should offer the *homa-bali* accompanied by the deity of the weapon (*astradeva*). (42)
One should offer the inner-liṅga oblation, the vessel, and to Candraśekhara himself;
or one may perform the oblation at night, performing the oblation for all [the deities].
One should perform a circumambulation of the village and enter one's own abode;
then, on either the eighth or the ninth [day], follows the sequence for the ritual of the Gandhotsava festival.
The offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) should take place on that day, or on the third, or even on the second;
however, on the night preceding that day, one should [install] Naṭeśvara in the *kautuka* [vessel].
The *bhujaṅgalalita* and the *bhujaṅgatrāsaka*;
this dance has been described, and therein one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*).
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva, as well as an assembly hall;
there, upon a pure surface smeared with cow dung, one should prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila). (47)
With eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice and half that amount of husked rice (*taṇḍula*),
along with half of that again combined with sesame seeds, one should likewise prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity.

Having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, and adorned it with parched grain and blossoms, there should be rice for the sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) of the Tripāṭhins in its center. (49)
A golden thread, and especially a cotton thread; in their midst, one joined with a strand, as well as saffron and sandalwood. (50)
One who possesses a long beard and is equipped with the sacred thread should perform a circumambulation around the enclosure wall,
keeping it to his right, while standing upon the head of a servant.

With the sounds of conchs and drums, and by those reciting hymns and auspicious words, one attains the presence of the deity; one should then cause the proclamation of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) to be made in due order. (52)
Therefore, the fire-ritual should be performed on a sacrificial mound or likewise on sand;
one should draw three lines toward the northeast with the mantra "brahmajajñānam. (53)
With the *suvarṇa* mantra, one should likewise [place] the thread on the south;
with the *āpyāyasva* mantra, one should gradually draw the line on the north.
One should draw the first line with the mantra "yo rudraḥ," place [the deity] in its center, and then perform the circumambulation from left to right.
One should worship Vāgeśvara and Vāgeśī along with their mantra in due order, accompanied by the three deities, joined with the *kūrca* [mudrā], and provided with flowers and perfumes. (56)
Having worshipped [the deity] especially with incense and lamps,
one should then prepare the vessel for the fire on the left side in the proper sequence. (57)
Having prepared the seat to the north, as well as the praṇītā and prokṣaṇī vessels,
he should duly prepare the ghee-pot, the caru-pot, the sruk, and the sruva ladle in their proper order.
Having taken the fuel-sticks joined with the sacrificial materials, the three enclosing sticks, and the sprinkling-vessel filled with water, in due order; || 59 ||

One should prepare the *prokṣaṇī* water in due order, joined with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*). Then, taking the *praṇītā* vessel, one should fill it with water, flowers, and unbroken rice.
Having likewise resolved upon Janārdana in the north, one should worship Him;
having filled the vessel for clarified butter with ghee, [one should prepare] the *kūrca* of three-fold touch.
Then, having released the tuft-knot (kūrcagranthi), he likewise places [the materials] in the midst of the fire;
likewise, the sacrificial grass (darbha) arranged with clarified butter and the southern fire. (62)
One should offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis and perform the rite with the Brahmajajñāna mantras, having strewn darbha grass around the fire.
And on both sides, they stood [arrayed];
meanwhile, the great sound of mṛdaṅgas and other instruments resounded in the eastern direction.
Other devotees likewise stood outside of that [inner circle];
having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) as before with hymns and auspicious recitations, || 65 ||
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
likewise, the Nardaka and Mardaka should be honored with a niṣka of pure gold.
The singer and the flute-player should be honored with garments, gold, and rings; likewise, the drummer should be honored with sounds, and one should cause a pair of garments to be given. (67)
One should also offer betel leaves to these deities of other classes; [one should perform] song, the production of instrumental music, and musical instruments arising from rhythmic timing (tāla). 68.
The origin of these is recorded as having arisen from rhythmic clapping and dance;
furthermore, there is the determination of the movements and hand gestures used in the performance on the stage. (69)
With both eyes, one should visualize the support of the *bhāvapāda-tāla*, joined with the head, hands, waist, chest, and sides. (70)
These six, joined with the major and minor limbs, constitute the characteristics of dance;
one should perform beautiful dancing through the proper application of tempo and rhythm.
If the *geya* (singing) is deficient, there will indeed be drought; if the *vādya* (instrumental music) is deficient, there is loss of wealth;
if the *nṛtta* (dance) is deficient, there is poverty; and if the *tāla* (rhythm) is deficient, it is terrifying. (72)
The navel-base is surrounded by the Bindu, Nāda, vowels, and consonants;
the heart is pervaded by the letters ending in the throat [M] and by the teeth and the tongue. (73)
Between the semen and the blood is Śiva, born from the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
in his center resides the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the form of the *bindu*, which is higher than the highest.
Mā, pā, dhā, nī, sā, rī—this is declared to be the sequence of the seven notes (saptasvara) according to the entire ritual procedure. || 75 ||
Ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, and daivata (niṣāda), as well as niṣāda without its parts (niṣkala)—these constitute the notes (svara) for the one with parts (sakala). || 76 ||
For that which is partless (niṣkala), the supported must be the possessed (sakala).
320) The possessed would be of the nature of power (śakti), while the partless is of the nature of the individual soul (jīva). || 77 ||
The support for the utterance of the tone should be equal to the vital breath of the *praṇava*;
the wind, having reached the lotus-stalk, is joined with the power of generation. (78)
As is space, so is wind; its sound should be of that same measure.
They say the syllable *a* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and likewise, the syllable *a* is fire (*anala*).
When the union of two syllables is perceived as a single vowel, that unifying [rhythm] is called the fourth *ardhamarda* in the world. (80)

Having fashioned the seven notes, the three scales (grāmas), the twenty-one melodic modes (mūrcchanās), and the resemblance of syllables, the singers [should perform] the limbs of the musical meters (varṇa).
[He saw] his own master and the author of the Śruti, adorned with the seven musical notes (saptasvara),
existing in the Saugrāma [scale], combined with the pure Ṣāḍava [scale]. (82)
Endowed with these characteristics, specifically those of the *vaṃśaka* meters:
first, there are eight long syllables (*guru*), and in the middle, sixteen short syllables (*laghu*). (83)
The wise one should also quickly cast thirty-two drops; certainly, by means of the other [deity], he binds Tiṣya and brings about creation. 84.
Thus is known Kāyapatitā, and she is indeed the eighth; she is the instructor of the garland of petals for the fifth finger of that hand. 85.
Gāndhāra and Mayākuṃbha—these are the sixfold types of rāgas.
The parīcāra, madacārī, and gacārikā are the movements of the festivals.
These are known as the four *mahācārikas*:
*dhruva*, *ākṣipti*, *lava*, and likewise *vardhamāna* and *triya*. (87)
The maṇḍala, the kuṇḍita, the vikṣepokṣita, the āveṣṭita, the veṣṭita, the urveṣṭi, and the tantu. || 88 ||
The Bhramarī, Rasacārī, Karaṇa, and Aṅgahārikā. || 89 ||
Accompanied by its various modes, with aesthetic flavor (rasa), and including bracelets and earrings, pure dance (śuddhanṛtta) is prescribed as being endowed with sattvic vision.
With *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *asuras*, hosts of *gaṇas*, and *rākṣasas*, the ear would encounter a terrifying sound, filled with many cries of dancing. 91.
And even that which has reached the ear through song suddenly goes outside;
for thus it brings peace to the world and increases the prosperity of kings and kingdoms. (92)
The increase of one's position has thus been described, as well as the augmentation of wealth and grain;
now follows the crushing of crookedness and the breaking of obstacles by the one with the tawny matted-hair crown.
The yellow-clad one, who holds the crescent moon, whose death is the water of the Ganges, the god of the thirty [deities], whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods and asuras. 94.
The sprouting of the primordial sound, the destroyer of the suffering of all worlds seeking refuge, cast down by the dance at the feet of Vaidyanātha, and possessing the gait of a white bull. 95.
One should place many young girls upon that small portion of the body which bears white ashes and the white water of the Gaṅgā. 96.
Having performed the *pāṇinaukṣāsana* with the *puṣpāñjali-sumudrā*, [one performs] the *noroga*, the *sahānṛtta*, and the *nṛttākṣipta*. (97) p. 324)
With the speed of a whirling bee, with the strength of a bee’s wing, with the measure of a great day and night, he who possesses the power of truth,
with slow-moving limbs and the grace of a perfected one, is this very one-faced Lord.
The two wrists are contracted and devoid of movement;
with the hands raised halfway upward, the *vartana* gesture becomes the *kamala*. || 99 ||

With his mind fixed upon the pair of eyes of Samyāva, which resembled the throat of a cuckoo amidst the humming of bees intoxicated by honey, he entered the forest of Vratagandhavāna like one entering a well-prepared sacrificial arena. 100.

O playful one, sporting with graceful movements, as the lotus-like breasts of the beautiful woman tremble with the gentle breeze of her sighs, even the reflection of the moon does not enter [her heart], held back by the slow-moving currents of her deep longing.
With various fragrances filling the air with *mandāra* flowers,
accompanied by songs like the honeyed humming of swarms of bees,
and with glances graced by various graceful movements of the limbs;
Seated upon the lotus throne, offer this handful of flowers:
Victory, O bearer of the Gaṅgā! Victory, O moon-crested one! Victory, O wielder of the sword-like trident! Victory, O destroyer of Tripura!
Victory, O you whose feet are worshipped by the forest of the three worlds! Victory, O you who travel upon the excellent white bull! Victory!
O Lord of Physicians, God who destroys old age and disease, I take refuge at your feet—

O you who dwell in the abode of the multitude of lotuses from the pure Kamalākara, who are united with the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā), whose white and dark eyes are worshipped by the lotus-born (Brahmā), and who delight in song and instrumental music.

O Goddess Sarasvatī, abode of virtues and non-virtues, fashioned by the gods, who art praised by all; O thou who grantest the choice of excellent qualities, accompanied by Gaṇapati, victor! In that place where the multitude of sins has been destroyed, where the lotus-like face of Nala shines with a luster that is not red, and where the moon is present upon the lotus that delights in existence—there, as the sun’s rays enter, as if into a cave swallowed by the mass of wind and fire, and filled with the sweet sound of the songs of swarms of bees and the cries of cuckoos, the supreme light of the gods enters.

The *nṛttākṣipti* (dancing gesture): As the sound of the songs of Kinnaras, who are delighted by the sweet warbling of intoxicated cuckoos and bees, enters—[a sound] slow with the arrival of the gentle breeze from the mountain of separation—the Lord of Elephants (Gajapati) [is perceived] on the peak of the mountain that is his abode. This is established by the following: by the thickets of *punnāga*, sandalwood, lotuses, and creepers; and by the intoxicated bees, *tāla*, *yogavakula*, blue lotuses (*utpala*), and *karṇikāra* flowers.
May he who dwells upon the lotus seat accept my handful of flowers with glances endowed with various and manifold expressions.
The Flower Offering:
Prostrate before the form of Bhairava, who wears a garland of skulls and severed heads dripping with the blood of blossoming trees, and who brought about the destruction of half of Kandarpa.
The departure—namely, the fivefold purity:
the deity bearing a divine skull-bowl and trident, adorned with a skeleton as his ornament;
having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, assuming a form that inspires awe, and possessing the terrifying jewels of the hoods of Vāsuki.
O Rūpa-Rudra, the one-eyed one, the God of gods who is like a Guru— homage to you, who are worshipped by the three worlds!
O Prāvīśika, you who cause the Guru and Jamala to become collyrium and ashes, and who destroy the pride of the poison-bearing serpent.

Bow down with your head to Keśava, the Lord of the three worlds, who destroys [the cycle of] death through that which is not a means of destruction, who bestows the earth, who fulfills the desires of Hara, who removes the pride of the king of gods and Madhu, who lifted Govardhana, who rescued the people from the mountain, and who, having seen the essence of the world, bears white ashes. [The *nṛttākṣipti* gesture: The *mālākṣipti* gesture signifies the lifting of Govardhana; the *janākṣipti* gesture signifies the lifting of the people from the mountain. Having beheld the Lord of the three worlds, who wears white ashes, I bow my head to him.
With incenses—
those produced from the lotuses of that very lake,
which cause bees to wander within and make the pericarp appear as if it were a sacrificial blade (kṛttikā).
May he who dwells upon the lotus throne, with his circular range of vision and glances, accept from me this handful of flowers.

The Handful of Flowers (Puṣpāñjali): O Fish, Tortoise, Boar, and Man-Lion; O destroyer of the great asura Kaṃsa and of the gods and dānavas, who wears a crown with a frowning brow; O destroyer of Tripura, who cast down Māyāmoha; O you who dwell in the water-palace and consume fire, whose hands and belly possess divine power!
The ageless, supreme bliss, the ultimate victory of Viṣṇu, the wind.
Homage to the one who brings about freedom from desire; homage to the one whose passion is logic; homage to the bearer of the half-moon; homage to the divine river of the lordly elephant;
homage to the one adorned with ornaments made of serpents; homage to the Goddess accompanied by Umā; [homage] with the introductory verses.

The forest, with its canopy of flowers and the sweet sound of songs from the circling bees among the various trees, enters that [place] gently like a bridegroom; it is a grove where the trees are bent low by the wind, which is softened by the sweet humming of intoxicated bees.
When the sun, the mountain of rays, had ascended the sky from the mountain of the eastern horizon and was moving upon the feet of the lordly elephants of the quarters,
the assembly of Vandyaghaṭīya and others resounded with the humming of bees attracted by the exquisite fragrance of fully blossomed *karṇikāra* flowers and other varieties.
May he who dwells upon the lotus-seat, with his hands full of complete glances, offer a handful of flowers from me there.
The Flower-Offering:
The bow, gracefully held in the hand of the Lord who bears the weight of the King of Serpents, is drawn to a half-moon.

If there is the departure on the excellent bull, the beloved burner (fire), the deer-lord (lion) garment, the half-moon-adorned crown of matted hair, the feet of the Lord worshipped by Vāsudeva, the pair of deities worthy of worship and salutation, and the Guru—this is the constant [practice]. In the *naiṣkrāmaṇa* [rite] for the purification of the silk cloth:

the person who is like the sun, who has long been purified by the heat of the child (the fire), accompanied by the most profound essence of the people, having seen the form of the Lord, [he is] Hara, struck by the feet of the drinker of the beast (Śiva).
With introductory verses: In the Malaya forest, fragrant with sandalwood, she wanders with the hue of a lotus petal;
weary from the fatigue of amorous play, she enters the palace with the grace of a rutting elephant.
Nṛttākṣipti (p. 332):
The foot worshipped by the lotus-born Brahmā and adorned with the crest-jewel of Śiva; the foot served by sages, seers, and gods upon the pair of lotuses; the foot honored by the three worlds.
In the circle illuminated by the slow-moving Vedas of the Siddhānta, refined by the grace of Śiva, salutations with constancy to that which is measured by the yogins and the supreme yogis;
it is praised by the hymns of the divine bees amidst the pollen of the lotuses created by Cilādi and others.
May he who dwells upon the lotus-seat, through the movement of his hands, the shifting of his gaze, and the casting of glances, accept this handful of flowers from me.
The Flower-Offering (Puṣpāñjali)—p.

The Fish, the Tortoise, and the Boar; the Man-Lion with his brow furrowed like a diadem; the Destroyer of the great Asura Kaṃsa and the gods; the one who struck down and cast away the Tripura of the Dānavas.
Punarukti—The water-born fire, the divine one from the womb of Śaṅkara, the ageless, the supreme, the most blissful, the victorious wind;
the bestower of freedom from desire, the passion of logic.

Salutations to the one who bears the moon upon the earth; salutations to the one whose path is the divine lord of elephants; salutations to the one adorned with ornaments made of serpents; salutations, O Goddess, to the one accompanied by Umā. (With these) introductory verses.

A song is heard, half of which was composed while dwelling upon the very peaks of mountain summits: "Bow down to Keśava, the destroyer of sins, the slayer of the Dānava Gaja, and the remover of Tripura!
[He who is] tossed by the movements of his dance...

In the spotless groves of the Malaya mountains, which laugh with the blossoming of excellent trees like the gods, as the lion enters the thicket of creepers— [a place] where the beloved’s necklace is crushed by the contact with lotuses and *vakuḷa* flowers—
the lioness, whose fame is like the blue lotus of the water-born, [is accompanied] by the splendor of swarms of bees garlanded with special honey. (Dhruva)
May the handful of flowers offered by the one seated upon the lotus throne— by means of glances like the lotuses of the Ālīla-maṇḍala— remove my [obstacles].

This handful of flowers belongs to the son of Aja (Viṣṇu), whose single form possesses manifold aspects, whose jeweled feet are worshipped at the five sacred sites and at the ear-petals of the flute-player, and who is celebrated for his generosity through many paths such as the hand.

I bow to the twelve-fold Śambhu, who consists of sacrifice and whose form is Śiva; the casket containing the entire lineage of the Ṛṣis, the bestower of boons through the supreme Veda. [This is] the *naiṣkrāmaṇa*.

Mounted upon fragrance, having been caused to enter by means of the *utthāpanas*, and having been drawn forth and delighted by the *parivartaka*, there is the application of the *sruva* ladle. And at the entrance of the stage, there is the essence of the Sun (*saurasa*).
And the release of flowers occurs through the great practice of the lord of practitioners, by means of the Śaikra-maṇa.
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta),
to be performed at the time of dawn and after worship, devoid of singing and dancing.
At midday, during the time of worship, one should perform twice the amount of dance;
however, when the dances for the two junctions [of day and night] are omitted, it should be performed until the end of the evening worship.
Having commenced with dance and song, one should perform dance and song;
however, if there is an absence of dance for a single day, there shall be twenty-five ablutions (snapana).
One should perform the *śānti* oblation according to the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures;
having offered abundant sacrificial oblations (*havis*), one should also cause betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) to be presented. (4)
It is recorded as occurring on the second, third, or even the fourth day, or indeed the fifth;
or on the sixth day, or even the seventh, eighth, or ninth.
Having taken from three to a hundred [leaves], according to the extent of one's means,
the Guru should plant the lineage [of the disciple] upon the Śaiva [deities] beginning with Hāṭaka.
One should give land consisting of water, dry land, gold, and grain in succession; having established as many images of Śiva as there are [units], one should likewise honor as many ascetics.
There shall be that same number of musicians, that same number of courtesans,
that same number of potters, and that same number of flower-keepers.
There were as many temple-maidens (devadāsīs), as many washermen,
as many carpenters, and likewise as many cowherds. (9)

One should cause those who live by other occupations to bring [the offerings] according to their means; as much wealth as they possess, so much sacrificial oblation (havis) should one cause them to offer. || 10 ||
One should offer half of the power-substance (śakti) and the oblation (havis) according to one's capacity, as well as the enjoyment of worship;
likewise, there should be the enjoyment of lamps and the enjoyment of half the fragrant substances.
Half of the flowers are for enjoyment, and likewise for the purpose of the ritual bath;
there is also enjoyment for the festival, and indeed enjoyment of the flowers. || 12 ||
The enjoyment for the sake of expiation, the enjoyment of the Kṛttikā lamp, the enjoyment for the sake of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, and the enjoyment when there is deficiency or excess. || 13 ||
One should cause the sacrifice to the gods, the provision of enjoyments, and the inscription on stone to be made;
likewise, the service to the deity and everything pertaining to the rites for the gods. (14)
One should not cause the king to perform any other work than that which is necessary for his mortal life, provided it does not exceed the certainty of his available wealth. || 15 ||
One should go to the temple as one's own home; another's abode is not to be looked upon with envy.
Having ensured that one's enjoyments are well-sustained, one should perform service for the king.
Having divided one's wealth and possessions into three parts, one part should be for the sake of Dharma, and two parts should be the remainder for the gods. || 17 ||
Whoever should practice in this manner in due order goes to the world of Śiva; thus ends the chapter on the certainty of power in the Yogaja [Tantra].
339) Now I shall describe in detail the supreme procedure for the food offering (naivedya): that consisting of golden rice, great rice, and likewise jewel-rice. || 1 ||
There are white and black varieties, distinguished in many ways;
there are all types of rice, as well as barley and wheat.
And for all those worthy of initiation, the remnants of the oblation are prescribed;
three hundred pearls and twice that number of grains of rice are desired as the arrangement.
For those who maintain two households, twice as much [as previously stated] is prescribed for each household;
two *vāris* are said to be a *prastha*, and two of those are a *caru*, which is an *āḍhaka*.
Two of those are called a *havir*; two of those are declared to be a *śiva*.
Two *śivas* are said to be a *droṇa*, and two of those are called a *khāni*.
Three *khāris* are said to be a *bhāra*, as is traditionally remembered in due order.
One hundred *bhāras* is declared the best [weight], while fifty would be the middle.
Twenty *bhāras* is the lowest [weight], ten *bhāras* is the lowest of the low;
five *bhāras* shall be the small, and likewise two *bhāras* is the base.
A *kalpa* is said to be a "burden," which one should carry by means of the power of dance;
one should prepare an *āḍhaka* of oblation, and half of that is called a *caru*.
Half of that is said to be the offering for Bali, as it is traditionally remembered;
this applies in due order to Gaurī and the other Śaktis, as well as to their attendants.
One should offer two *prasthas* of the sixteen types of food offerings,
and one should present four parts of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) divided into two portions.
One part shall be the remainder; that remainder is for the offering to the children and others.
Eight kinds of sacrificial food (havis) have been declared: rice with mung beans and rice with milk porridge (pāyasa). (11)
Kṛsarānna, gulānna, śībānna, yavānnaka, māṣānna, and śuddhānna—these constitute the eightfold oblation (havir). || 12 ||
One should avoid the husk and the mung beans, though they may be combined with coconut fruits;
[the dish should consist of] half rice and a small amount of mung beans mixed with salt. (13)
In this manner, rice with meat is said to be *udgānnam*, and likewise *kṛsarānna*;
it is combined with plantains, green gram, cumin, and black pepper.
Combined with coconut ghee and moistened with fresh leaves, it should be accompanied by mung beans, coconut, and jackfruit. || 15 ||
That which is renowned as *gulānna* is here called *apūpānna*;
one should cause *apūpānna*, as it is known, to be given at all times. (16)
And for all [of them], one should provide an offering accompanied by side-dishes and condiments, combined with curd and ghee, consisting of oblations of five colors.
One *prastha* of rice, one fruit as a side dish, and an equal amount of molasses, combined with black pepper and salt. (18)
Cumin and coconut, combined with all the various side-dishes (upadaṃśa), and ghee ground together, is called pure upadaṃśa. || 19 ||
Mango fruit, citron, and tamarind fruit combined—these, along with sour condiments, together with black pepper, salt, and ghee. (20)
One should especially avoid cumin, mustard, and fragrant grinding spices, as well as food that is overcooked or undercooked. (21)
The wise man should cook the mustard in three ways along with its accompaniments;
it becomes threefold: dry, fresh, and cooked, as well as cooked with sour sauce. (22)
The breadfruit, the plantain, the mango, the vṛhatī, the pumpkin, the white harīphala, and the vallīpanasa; || 23 ||
Regarding "the minor [ingredients]": either one, or even two, such as śigru, mārjāra, kāliñca, timisī, and mātuluṅgaka. 24.
The body is like a coconut fruit, and the blood is like the fruit of the agastya plant;
there is a creeper like the kārīśa tree in the forest region, as well as thorns and the black dūla vine.
Māṣa beans, along with māṣa-latī and accompanied by fruits for dipping—this other substance, when combined with devotion, should be known as such by the wise. || 26 ||
The root of the creeper is the primary root here, while the pericarp has a distinct root;
the wise man should provide the "group of roots" for these as having separate roots.
One should bring other root-substances under control by means of devotion;
however, one should especially avoid all those born of the Śakti class.
One should offer red rice mixed with *dhruva* to the devotees once a day,
along with a powder of *marīca*, mustard, cumin, and coconut.
For all types of upadaṃśa (syphilis), one should prepare this [remedy] equally;
having melted ghee, one should then combine all the medicinal ingredients.
The wise one should cause an offering of food consisting of the six flavors combined with ghee to be presented.
First, he should offer the fruits of his agricultural labor to the God of gods. (31)
One should place the food on a platter, but not on charcoal or husks;
one should especially avoid food that is overcooked or undercooked. || 32 ||
Having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis), one should place a leaf above the cloth—
either a plantain leaf, a palāśa leaf, or a leaf from another milk-exuding tree.
One should present the great sacrificial offering (havis) to other pure vessels,
along with the sacrificial food (havis), upward-pointing side-dishes (upadaṃśa), jaggery (guḍa), and plantain fruit (kadalīphala).
Having carefully poured in ghee, or curd, or even milk, the practitioner of mantra should offer it with the heart-mantra and the mantra "devasya tvā. (35)
One should cause water mixed with *pāṭalī*, fragrant [substances], *uśīra*, and *elā* to be offered, and afterwards present it to Caṇḍeśa. || 36 ||
Having performed the purification of the floral offerings (nirmālya), one should present betel leaf along with camphor,
nutmeg, cloves, oil, and kramuka fruits.
Thereafter, one should offer betel-leaf prepared with a small amount of lime-powder, along with sandalwood, camphor, and musk for the mouth. (38)
Accompanied by the singing of mantras, the articulation [of sound] should be touched upon the hollows like Rāma, joined with a gentle breeze and the Himalayas. (39)
When this is done, mortals shall indeed attain all sovereignty;
on Saturdays and Wednesdays, the wise man should apply scented oil to the earth.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the food offering (naivedya) produced through yoga.
I shall describe the fire-ritual; listen with a one-pointed mind.
A wise person should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed characteristics of the pit.
Alternatively, the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) may be prepared in another manner using sand;
for ten million oblations (koṭihoma), it should be eight cubits in size, while the characteristic measure for a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma) is as follows.

The fire-offering (homa) may consist of ten thousand oblations with five cubits [of ghee], or three cubits, or four cubits; it may also be two thousand oblations with two cubits, or five hundred plus one oblation with one cubit.
It should be one hundred [cubits] long with a width of one *ratni*, and fifty [cubits] wide with a height of one *dṛṣṭi*;
below the height of one *dṛṣṭi*, it should not exceed eight cubits.
p.
348) Construct the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the characteristics of a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), provided with two, three, or one girdle;
it should be one cubit in measure and augmented by three finger-breadths. || 5 ||
Having placed a lotus on the south, one should fashion the womb (yoni) on the north;
it should have three lines running from east to north, surrounded by a boundary and provided with a layer of sacrificial grass.
In the eastern and western sacrificial pits, the wise one, standing facing north, should fashion the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; in the others, having turned to face the east, he should do so.
The sacrificial altar consists of a spread of grass; in the middle is the mound, which is prepared with a cord.
Starting from the south, the enclosing sticks (paridhi) are placed extending eastward, though some omit the enclosing sticks.
Having placed the *kūrca* (bundle of grass) upon that, one should place two fuel-sticks with their tips pointing toward the full vessel;
then, one should arrange the *kūrca* bundles starting from the east using five, seven, eight, or nine blades of *darbha* grass.

One should fashion the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the fuel-sticks (*idhmaka*) with the measurement of the little finger; the wise one should have the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made twelve finger-breadths in length. (10)
The wise man should place the *brahmakūrca* with six finger-breadths, the *viṣṇukūrca* likewise, and the *rudrakūrca* in the middle— thus establishing the three forms.

One should fashion all the *kūrca* bundles with three, five, seven, or nine blades of grass; the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of four blades of *darbha* grass and eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length.
One should fasten blades of Palāśa, Aśvattha, and other leaves, as well as the *sṛk* and *sruva* ladles;
one should fasten the *pavitra* strainers made of Darbha grass in the sequence of one, two, and three.
Three, three, and two finger-breadths above that, there should be a binding in the middle half of that measure;
at the tip, the wise one should place the loop according to the measurement of a barley grain.
This is declared to be the *pavitra* [purifier] when joined to the base of the ring finger.
Having kindled the fire and performed the ritual movement (*viharaṇa*), one should then perform the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*). || 15 ||
One should sprinkle with the water of Śiva either fire produced from the charcoal of a Vedic scholar, or fire arising from a sun-crystal, or even the rubbing of the little fingers.
Having gathered fragrant wood and kindled the fire, the wise man should arrange the enclosing grass with its tips pointing eastward and then northward.
The wise man should generate the Śiva-fire and then mutter the Śiva-mantra;
[the fire] has two mouths, one heart, four ears, and two nostrils.
He has two faces and six eyes, is tawny, and possesses seven hands;
he has three girdles, three feet, and, in brief, seven tongues. (19)
Having thus visualized the Śiva-fire as having four horns, mounted upon a bull, and possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun, the preceptor [should proceed] with the Śiva-mantra. (20)
He has the form of an elder, three eyes, and four arms; he has reddish-brown eyes, and his vehicle is a bull;
he is red in color with a white upper garment; he is the bestower of boons, holding a spear in his hand, and is the very embodiment of Śiva and Agni.

One should meditate upon the Fire-god (Agni) seated upon a goat, resembling a mass of lightning, with four arms, three feet, four horns, and two round faces. He has blazing hair, seven tongues of flame, six beautiful eyes, and wears the supreme *mauñjī* grass girdle wound three times. In his right and left hands, he holds the *abhaya* and *varada* gestures; in the other [two] hands, he holds a *sruk* and a *sruva* ladle. One should meditate on this Fire-god, established in the *Gārhapatya* fire-hearth, adorned with a crown of matted locks, resembling the rising sun, holding a *sruk* and a sword, displaying the *abhaya* gesture in his right hand and resting his left hand upon a seat of *kuśa* grass (*kūrca*).
Sakerava,
Parātparatriḍviṣa, Sunetra, Abhuja, Athārṣaka, Sarvālaya, and Gārhapatya above.
I shall describe their respective forms: for the householder ancestors it is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, and for the gods it is the Āhavanīya fire.
That fire is proclaimed to be of three kinds: the child-fire, the youth-fire, and the old-fire.
The child-fire is for consecrations, and the youth-fire is for festivals.
In the Vṛddha fire, there should be the daily oblation (nityahoma) performed by way of both the Savya and Apasavya paths;
[the deities are] Kālī, Karālī, Manoramā, and Sulohitā.
Dhūmravarṇā, Puligā, Viśvarūpī, Vilohitā, Devī, Lolā, and Asyabhāvā—thus are the Śaktis proclaimed. (25)

For the *jihvāhasta* (tongue-hand), the handle of the *nāha* should be six finger-breadths long, with the base and tip of the *puṣkara* (bowl) being equal in form. The strengthening rite (*balikarma*) should be performed at the center and both sides; it should be filled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

This staff should be near the cowherd (*gopāla*); "vaṃ" should be at the tip, and the Brāhmaṇa should be on the right. One should fashion a well-crafted bundle of grass (*kūrca*) for the clarified butter.
Having indeed placed Viṣṇu on the left, one should place the praṇītā vessel;
and Bhava and Ugra should be placed in the fire-pits starting from the east and extending to the southeast.
One should worship Śarva in the southern pit, Grāmadeva in the southwest,
Rudra in the western pit, and Bhīma in the northwest.
One should worship Paśupati in the northern pit and Īśa in the northeast;
and the three-eyed, four-armed [deity] in the central pit during the rite of oblation.
Having worshipped all the gods, it is remembered as the "excellent oblation" (śreṣṭha-homa);
however, when the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapāla-astra) are omitted, it is the "intermediate oblation rite" (madhyama-homa-karman). (29)
One should install all the presiding deities of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the center of the pit;
fuel-sticks (samidh) are offered with the Sadyojāta mantra, and clarified butter (ājya) is offered with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Having offered the *caru* oblation with the *aghora* mantra and the parched grain (*lājaka*) with the *puruṣa* mantra,
one should offer all five [grains] in the northeast and offer sesame seeds with the *kavaca* mantra.
Having become [the oblation], we are offered with the heart-mantra and the seventh mantra;
[using wood from] the Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, and the Vaṭa tree.
The nyagrodha, the plakṣa tree, the apāmārga, and likewise the śamī;
the bilva, the kapittha, and also the jambu and vakula. || 33 ||

Thus has been described here the sacrificial fuel of the *palāśa* wood for the primary rite, as well as the preparation of the altar, the ritual scraping, and the sprinkling of water around the established fire. (34)

The materials for the strewing, the vessel, the sprinkling, the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), the praṇītā water, having worshipped Viṣṇu, and the brāhmaṇa along with the kūrca grass-bundle; || 35 ||
The first [rite] consists of three blades of darbha grass placed upon the fire, as well as the sacrificial ladle and the enclosing sticks;
having then performed the sprinkling of water, one proceeds clockwise starting with the invocation (āvāhana).
One should place pure rice, ghee, and all other ritual substances; then, one should perform the sprinkling with the mantra beginning with "adite 'nv" and ending with "adi. (37)
One should prepare the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) with the *yuktovāha* mantra and so forth;
the worship of the deities, such as the Mūrtis and others, should be performed with their respective mantras. (38)

At the conclusion of the ritual action, one should perform the mental oblation (*cittāhuti*) consisting of the fires, the elements, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* [mantras]. After all the general rites have been performed, one should contemplate one's own specific practice. (39)
One should perform another sixteen-fold rite beginning with union according to the seasons;
one should offer oblations for the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the purificatory rites of Śiva.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) arising from yoga.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
One should divide the center of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) into nine parts.
In the middle portion, a sacrificial altar (vedī) should be made with a height of one cubit;
an intermediate altar (upavedī) should be constructed with twice the width and four finger-breadths [in height].
The height should be exactly that same measure, or else six finger-breadths;
the eastern [pit] should be square, while the southeast should have a yoni-shaped pit.
In the south there is a semi-circular pit (ardhakuṇḍa), and in the southwest a triangular one;
in the west there is a circular pit, while in the northwest it is hexagonal.
In the north, however, there is a lotus-shaped pit, and in the northeast, one with eight corners; between Indra and Īśāna, construct the primary circular [pit].
For all fire-pits (kuṇḍas), the shape is like a swan or a square;
their measurement is proclaimed to range from eight cubits down to one fist.
For all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the measurement for the hand-digging (khanamuṣṭi) should be provided;
they should be equipped with three girdles (mekhalā), or even just a single girdle.
Starting from the lower girdle (mekhalā), measuring two or three finger-breadths [in width],
with a height equal to its breadth, there is one girdle six finger-breadths [in height]. (8)
One should not fashion a womb within a womb, nor should one cause Padmanābha to be made;
having condensed [the space] to the measure of a palm, one should arrange the ritual procedure (kalpa) in the center.
One may fashion it with six finger-breadths, or even four finger-breadths;
its height should be one finger-breadth, or even two finger-breadths.
Having thus performed the lotus-arrangement, one should place the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in its center;
above the girdle (mekhalā), the womb (yoni) should be four finger-breadths in measure.
The width of the foremost finger [of the base] is one finger-breadth, and its height is likewise one finger-breadth;
having divided the square into five parts, one should place one part at the front.
Having taken half of a corner, one should exclude it from the outside;
from that corner, one should rotate another [line] into the shape of a womb (yoni), joined with two threads.
Having divided the width into nine parts and having placed a portion sequentially from top to bottom,
one should drop a thread and then rotate it to form a half-moon shape.
Having placed the Lord of Wisdom (Buddhīśa) at the side of the field-dwelling, the wise one should cause [the site] to be prepared;
he should stretch three lines, and it is declared that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is triangular.
Having divided a square into nine parts, one should place a portion in the outer direction;
one should then rotate it to form a circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa), which is suitable for all ritual acts.
Having first performed the preliminary rite, one should cause it to be made in the shape of a lotus, endowed with a pericarp and eight petals; the height of the lotus should be greater.
One should divide the width of the square into six and four parts;
having set aside one part, the wise [practitioner] should apply the measuring cord. (18)
It is known as the circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa); one may also rotate it by a tenth part [of the side].
Thus the characteristics of the pit have been declared; one should not [apply these] to the square pit (caturaśra).
Having taken half of a corner, one should form it with that very corner;
thus the triangle-shaped sacrificial pit (śrakuṇḍa) is produced, which is honored in all rites.
The fist, the cubit, and the forearm [are used] up to the limit of eight cubits;
[the shapes are] seven-sided, nine-sided, lotus-shaped, and sixteen-sided. || 21 ||
The wise one should apply this through reasoning and fashion all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas);
indeed, for all the pits, the interior is said to be the same.
p.
361) "Whatever is the measurement for the girdle, that is remembered as the measurement.
Thus ends the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the *Yogaja* [treatise].
I shall now describe the propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa); listen with a one-pointed mind.
[This applies] to Sadāśiva and the other deities, as well as to their retinues.
Within the enclosure wall, one should perform oblations with the names and other attributes of the deities;
there, one should worship them twice as much, following the sequence prescribed for the ritual of worship.
This is declared to be the *śānti-homa*; one should offer oblations to all the deities.
This is called the *śānti-homa*; now listen to the *mūrti-homa*.
p.

362) Within the inner pavilion of the temple, the wise one, having prepared a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the four directions and a circular sacrificial mound in the northeast (īśāna), [should proceed]. || 4 ||
Following the sequence of the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should likewise prepare the mouth of the fire;
Sadāśiva with his mantra in the northeast, and the mantra of Īśa in the east.
One should perform the fire-oblation according to one's capacity with the Rudra-mantra in the south, the Viṣṇu-mantra in the west, and the Brahma-mantra in the north.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering and cause Śiva to be bathed;
there, one should worship him twice as much and present a great sacrificial offering.
The "Form-Homage" (mūrtihoma) has thus been explained; now hear about the "Directional Homage" (diśāhoma).
The deities of the eight directions are situated from Indra to Īśāna.
Having fashioned a square altar out of sand on all sides,
one should perform all other remaining rites as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya). || 9 ||
One should worship the deities of the directions there and perform the oblation for the directions (diśāhoma).
This is declared as the diśāhoma; now hear about the vāstuhoma.
In the center of the pavilion, prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice;
having placed the Vāstu-pitcher upon it, one should worship the deities of the Vāstu site.
Having made it square and level, measuring one cubit in size,
it should consist of either sixty-four squares or nine squares.
Having delineated [the mandala] with a thread made of flour, one should worship the deities beginning with Īśa;
having worshipped the deities beginning with Brahmā, one should then worship [the deities] beginning with Cakrī.
One should worship these forty-five deities of the site (vāstudeva).
Having worshipped the deities of the site, one should cause the offering to be presented with the bali-mantra. || 14 ||

Then, having performed the ritual for the deity of the site (vāstudeva), one should offer oblations to the gods in due order and likewise perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) with fuel-sticks using the mantra beginning with "svadhā."
At the conclusion of the Vāstuhoma, perform the paryagnikaraṇa rite;
likewise, perform the Vāstupunyāha ceremony with the water from the Vāstu-pitcher.
This is declared to be the Vāstuhoma, which is to be performed first at all times;
thus the homa has been described, wherein oblations are offered with their respective mantras. (17)
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the Vāstu-homa, including the propitiatory oblations (śānti-homa) and so forth, within the Yoga-ja [tantra].
Now, I shall explain specifically the characteristics of the initiations (dīkṣā); listen.
But the knowledge of Śiva is bestowed, and the three impurities are destroyed. || 1 ||
This word *dīkṣā* is proclaimed as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
seven types of Śaiva [initiation] have been indicated—listen now to them according to their respective systems.
The first is Anādiśaiva; the second is Ādiśaiva;
the third is Mandāśaiva; and the fourth is Śaivaka.
The fifth is Antaraśaiva, the sixth is Pravaraśaiva, and the seventh is Antyaśaiva; these are proclaimed as the divisions of Śaivism.
The Śaivas are said to be of seven kinds; now hear their distinctions:
the Ādi-Śaiva is traditionally held to be among Brahmins who have been initiated by Śiva.
First, among the twice-born, those initiated into the five faces were Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Maitri. (6)
And Parāśara—these five were consecrated in the five faces;
and their mother was Śivadvijā, O twice-born ones.
One who is known as an Ādiśaiva shall not undergo initiation again;
having been initiated from the beginning, he need not perform the worship of Śiva according to the four Vedas.

O twice-born ones, one who is devoid of initiation should not, out of delusion, perform the rites for the supreme Lord Īśāna; rather, for Brahmins and the other castes, it must be performed through initiation by one who follows the primordial Śaiva tradition.
One who has not been initiated, even if he is learned in the four Vedas, should always perform worship for his own sake;
however, at the time of the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana), one should perform the worship of Śiva.
The twice-born devotee of Śiva should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed for the sake of purification.

Among Brahmins, only one who is a great Śaiva and endowed with Śiva-initiation may perform worship for the sake of others; one who is uninitiated, even if he has mastered the four Vedas, must not cause such worship to be performed.
O Kuru, once initiated, one should worship the Brahmins for six months;
O God of gods, after six months, those who have been consecrated by a mere fraction [of the rite] fall from their state.
If a Brahmin remains for three years for the sake of service, maintaining his outward marks [of a religious student] through initiation, he becomes a "devalaka" (temple-priest) toward all gods.
They never perform the installation or the worship of these [deities], which are endowed with their respective characteristics and located everywhere in Alakā. || 15 ||
The Kṣatriyas and the Vaiśyas are likewise remembered as followers of Śiva;
indeed, Rudra and Avāntara follow in succession according to each respective caste. (16)
"A gold thumb-ring, an axe, or a cloth for the waist"—such are the [marks] of the foremost Śaivas; now hear those of the lowest Śaivas. || 17 ||
Among other castes as well, those known as the Antyaśaivas must have all rites—
from the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) down to the daily worship (arcana)— performed by an Ādiśaiva.
But if one should cause it to be performed otherwise, he shall obtain that which is fruitless.
