Those who know the truth of the Vedas and Vedāntas are remembered as the Ādiśaivas. (19)
The divisions of Śaivism have been fully explained; now hear the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā).
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Viṣṭi, and the three Uttarās—these are the [auspicious] constellations.

Puṣya and Śatabhiṣaj are declared to be the asterisms for initiation (dīkṣā). It should be performed during a fixed zodiac sign, or during both [fixed and movable], when there is an auspicious rising. (21)
Having commenced the rite of initiation (dīkṣā), one must avoid all houses situated in the eighth position therein, especially in the absence of the rising of the moon.
One should avoid the empty days, the eighth, the ninth, and the new moon;
first perform the ritual of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having washed the feet of his disciples— who have fasted, bathed, performed their purifications, and conquered their senses— he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.
There, in front of Śiva, the wise one should decorate a mandala endowed with the characteristics previously described; he should construct it like the pavilion for the consecration ceremony.
In the center of the pavilion, however, one should construct an altar measuring one, two, or three cubits according to the prescribed rule, for either a Śiva-liṅga or a maṇḍala. (26)
There, a mandala should be prepared— either the Ācārya, the Manobhaṅga, the Sarvatobhadra, the Svastika, or the Ardhacandra.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center with eight droṇas of śāli rice—
or half of that, or half of that again— he should fashion it with eight corners and with a rim.
One should offer oblations with half that amount of rice, and with half that amount of sesame seeds as well;
one should especially move about [performing the rite] with parched grain, flowers, and *darbha* grass.
A new water-pot and a *vardhanī* vessel, both covered with lids made of cloth, gold, and precious gems, and filled with fragrant water; || 30 ||
Having covered the thread with sprouts, one should place the *arghya* flower;
the wise practitioner should then install the Śiva-pitcher, the Vidyeśa, and Manonmanī. (31)

Whether it be a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), measuring one, five, or nine [cubits], one should perform all the rites beginning with the taking up of the fire as prescribed for the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya). || 32 ||
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the north and encircle it with a blanket;
then, having sprinkled the body of the disciple with water while reciting the preliminary mantra, one should apply the protective thread (kautuka).
The wise one should bind [the image] with the Ādi-Śaiva [mantra], perform the consecration (adhivāsana), and provide entertainment accompanied by dance and song.
Oṃ!
Salutations to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul.
Salutation to the one of beautiful form, to the universal one, the lord of dreams. || 35 ||
Having thus recited the mantra, one should meditate upon Sadāśiva;
at the clear dawn, with the rising of the sun, one should perform [the rite].
Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, the wise one should perform the binding of the eyes with the mantra of the heart.
It may be made of *dukūla*, silk, fine cotton, or even ordinary cotton;
the best is twelve cubits in length, while the middling is ten cubits.
The smallest [liṅga] should be nine cubits in length and four tālas in measurement;
it should be wrapped in nine cloths, and one should avoid those that are worn out or cracked.
One should immediately cover the disciple's hands with a cloth and cause the binding of the eyes;
one should bind the eyes with a cloth while reciting the Netra-mantra. (40)
There, one should mutter the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra conjoined with the *Tatpuruṣa* [mūla-mantra];
the *Netra* and *Bala* [mantras] should be performed together with golden flowers. (41)
The best [image] is worth ten niṣkas, the middling eight niṣkas, and the lowest five niṣkas; its characteristic is that it resembles a lotus flower.
And the wise one, facing northward with a single-minded focus, should cause all those who are poor to obtain their gains. (43)
One should place a flower in the hand with the Īśāna mantra,
and having performed three circumambulations with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Having meditated upon the supreme Lord Śiva with the Śiva-mantra,
the wise one should scatter flowers upon the mandala while reciting words of auspiciousness and benediction. (45)
In whichever mantra a flower dwells, that mantra— being of the same nature as its name and lineage— is sprinkled with it and likewise bestows grace.
In the petal of Īśāna is disease; in the southeast (Āgneyī) is grief or a living being;
in the southwest (Nairṛtī) it is said to bring fortune; and in the northwest (Vāyu) it is a human being. (47)
O best of Brahmins, that which was performed by Śrī in the four directions is known as *tacchrīkṛta*;
when the flower falls upon the pericarp, then indeed there shall be happiness.
On the petal of Īśāna, the number of eyes is stated here;
one should apply ashes mixed with water upon the head. (49)
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, especially with mantras,
one should sprinkle the head of Śiva with water from the Śiva-pitcher. (50)
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should place the Armor-mantra between the breasts.
One should place the Astra-mantra on the region of the hands and the Guhya-mantra on the left; one should assign Sadyojāta to the feet and thus perform the placement upon the body of the disciple.
Having placed the Heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the Head-mantra on the head;
having placed the Crest-mantra on the crest, the Armor-mantra is placed between the breasts.
One should place the eye in the region of the hand holding the weapon,
and the [other] eye on the right side of the deity, joined with a Palāśa leaf.
That mental [recitation] is prescribed as being joined with the *kūrca* [mantra].
Then, the disciple, seated upon his seat and facing eastward, [should be addressed]. (55)
Joined with the seed-syllable of fire, the triangle situated within the mandala should burn [the body],
starting from the big toes up to the end of the head.
There, the wise one should indeed place with a single-pointed mind the syllable *ma*,
which resembles the lunar disc and is born of himself.
The *vidyā-tattva* is the letter *u*, while the *śiva-tattva* is the letter *śa*.
With the single syllable *oṃ*, one [visualizes] the lotus, the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), facing downwards.
One should contemplate that [light] there, within the *suṣumnā*, up to the head;
by means of it, one should contemplate oneself as being flooded, becoming unprecedented. (59)
Whoever constantly practices this samādhi that destroys death, for him death does not arise; such is the certainty of the scripture. (60)
Thereafter, one should specifically perform the deposition of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) upon the body of the disciple:
the path of mantra, the path of words, the path of principles, and the path of worlds.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the path of kalās—thus, these twenty constitute the state of Śiva;
as well as sattva, rajas, and tamas, and the self (ātman) together with the inner self (antarātman). 62.
One should meditate upon these as the Supreme Self, the very essence of the self;
one should then place the three mandalas of fire, the sun, and the moon.
Having first placed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, one should then place the Śaktis, as well as Bindu, Nāda, and Śivā.

One should then place the temple of Sadāśiva, together with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva, upon the body of the disciple there, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the word "namaḥ. (65)
Having recollected the respective mantra, one should apply it to the body of the disciple;
one should place honey and the other substances on the head, or indeed on the mouth or the half-mouth.
Having placed the path of the principles (tattvādhvan) in the heart, the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) in the navel;
the path of the vowels (svarādhvan) in the region of my heart, and the path of the letters (talādhvan) in the feet.
Furthermore, one should apply the path of the *kalās* from the base of the feet to the end of the head:
Sadyojāta with eight *kalās*, and Vāmadeva with thirteen.
One should assign eight digits (kalās) to Aghora, four to the face itself, and five digits to Īśāna; thus, one should assign thirty-eight digits in total.
There are eight Vidyeśvaras and likewise an octad of Gaṇeśas;
the presiding deities of the ten worlds are recorded as the tenth [group] of weapons. (70)
Having thus laid out the path of the words (padādhvan), one should then lay out the path of the principles (tattvādhvan):
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
and speech, the feet, the hands, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth. (72)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
likewise, mind, intellect, ego, primordial nature (prakṛti), and the person (puruṣa). || 73 ||
The Nāgamāyā-vidyā, as well as Kalā and Niyati,
and likewise the Śuddhamāyā along with all the [other] principles (tattvas) up to Vigraha.
Śuddhavidyā, Śuddhakalā, Sadāśiva, and supreme Śiva—
one should thus place the thirty-six principles (tattvas) in their proper sequence. (75)
Then, having projected the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā), one should project the path of the kalās from Diśī to Kānta;
thereafter, one should project the path of the worlds again according to the sequence starting from the base of the penis (meḍhramūla).
The knower of ritual procedures should visualize the heart and other centers below;
[therein are] the Kalās, Niśas, Andhakārāndhas, and twenty-one Narākas.
Raurava, Kumbhipāka, Yantraka among them,
Kṣura, Atitāla, Jala, Sītala, Uṣṇasantāpana, and likewise Lohatapta. || 79 ||
The *kṛka-śalmali* well and the machine among the Nilayantras;
the bow, the fire-sound, the thunderbolt, and likewise the trident-restraint. (80)
There are Pāṣāṇa and Pāṃsu, as well as Vaitaraṇī;
also Tala, Vitala, Nila, and Talātala. (81)
Sutala and Tarātala, and Rasātala above that;
likewise Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and Svargaloka. || 82 ||
And one should know the Mahāloka, as well as the Janaloka, the Tapoloka, the Satyaloka, the Gāndharvaloka, and the Yakṣaloka. || 83 ||
And the world of the Vidyādharas, and the worlds of the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Lohakas; and the world of the Asvaras, and the world of the Kinnaras. || 84 ||
The world of Indra, the world of Agni, the world of Yama, the world of Nirṛti,
the world of Varuṇa, the world of Vāyu, and likewise the world of Soma. (85)
The world of Īśāna and Devaloka, and likewise the world of Brahmā;
and above the world of Brahmā, the world of Viṣṇu beyond that.
Beyond that is the world of Ananteśa, and after that the subtle world;
then the world of Śivottama and the world of Ekanetra.
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkhaṇḍa, and Śikhaṇḍin;
the world of Maheśvara and the world of Sadāśiva. 88.
Lokāloka and Śivāloka have been proclaimed in succession;
however, there exists no other world above the world of the dogs (Śvaloka). || 89 ||
Beginning from the root of the navel up to the region of the heart,
one should deposit these paths of phonemes (varṇādhvan), extending even from the head down to the feet. (90)
Having placed the letter *a* on the crown of the head, the letter *ā* on the forehead;
the letter *i* in the right eye, and the letter *ī* in the left eye. (91)
The letter *u* is on the right nostril, the letter *ū* on the left nostril;
the letter *ṝ* is on the right ear, and the letter *ṛ* on the left ear.
The syllable *ḷ* is on the right cheek, and the syllable *ḹ* is on the left cheek;
*e* and *ai* are in the cavities of the palate, and *o* and *au* are likewise on both rows of teeth.
Having placed *aṃ* and *aḥ* on the two ears, as well as the sixteen digits (*kalā*s),
one should place the *ka*-group on the right hand and the *ca*-group on the left hand.
The *ṭa*-group [of consonants] is on the right foot, and the *ta*-group is on the left foot;
*pa* and *pha* are on the right side, and *ba* is indeed on the left side of the arm. (95)
Having placed the syllable *ma* in the heart, one should place the syllable *ya* on the skin;
likewise, the syllable *ra* on the jewel and the syllable *la* on the flesh. (96)
One should place the letter *ca* in the region of the marrow, the letter *ña* in the region of the bones,
the letter *ṣa* in the region of the marrow, and the letter *śa*, which is indeed white, in the region of the semen.
The letter *ha* is said to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the letter *i* is the penis;
the letter *kṣa* is declared to be the testicles—one should place these syllables in their respective order.
There, one should place the thirty-nine digits (kalās) beginning with *ka* and ending with *pa*. [The mantra] is *tārāsṛtā rāmaṇināthāya* and *tisṛtāraṇiḥ*. || 99 ||
The knower of reality, having sequentially deposited [the kalās]— nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti, and likewise śāntyātīta, which is the supreme ether (paraṃ vyoma)— [proceeds]. 100.
Tamas, delusion, hunger, sleep, concealment, illusion, fear, and old age; passion, protection, attachment, nourishment, the dark woman, and the performance of black rites. 101.
Dhṛti, Kāryāparātrī, Bhrāmaṇī, and likewise Rohiṇī;
Siddhibhūti, Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthiti. || 102 ||
One should indeed place these thirty-nine digits (kalās) upon the body of the disciple;
having placed Śānti in the heart, one should place Vāyu in the mouth.
In the region above the sky, at the place of ten million *apsus*,
having placed the earth upon the feet, one should deposit the portions (*kalā*) of the five elements.

Thus, the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*) is [consecrated] by the *samyamantra*; the path of the plane of *vāmadeva* (*vāmadevapadādhvaka*) by [the same]; the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) by the *aghora* mantra; and the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) by the *puruṣa* mantra. (105)
Then, with the Īśāna mantra, one should perform the fire-oblation for the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan);
in this very same sequence, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body of the disciple.
Having placed Īśāna upon the head, Viṣṇu is the deity in the mouth;
perform the temple for the Vāstu deities and the village for the Paiśācas.
One should worship Vighneśa, Kṣetrapāla, and Durgā on all sides;
establish the site for the Vāstu ritual, and the temple is said to be of two kinds. (108)
What is the yoga for the site (vāstuka) at the location already mentioned?
The abode of Śaṅkara is in the portion of Īśa, or in the portion of Parjanya, namely Jayanta. || 109 ||
Some [practitioners] have their station at the feet of Aditi;
the yoga-station for others is facing west, while for yet others it is facing east. (110)
Viṣṇumukha is situated in the middle of all the houses and the eight directions; this is called the measurement of the ground at the conclusion of the ritual for examining the site. (111)
In the odd and even feet, within each varga, there shall be either a difference or a sum; the product of doubling the subsequent [terms] occurs according to the desired measure.
The square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the two ears (sides);
the square of the neck (the base) is the sum of the squares of the two arms (sides). || 113 ||
The square root of one hundred would be ten; likewise, the square root of four would be two.
The square root of all other classes [of numbers] would be the hypotenuse, while half of that would be the side.

The solid [volume] of the three-fold [figure] is declared to be twelve-sided and six-sided; the volume of a circle with a circumference is the product of the diameter-quarter multiplied by the square root of the sum of the squares of the sides. (115)
From the junction of the bow and the arrow up to the tip of the arrow, it is declared;
its similarity to a pavilion (maṇṭapa) consists of six parts, each having six sides. || 116 ||
Having placed the cube of the side (bhujāpiṇḍa) there, flattened into a square and divided into four parts,
one should then place the arm (bāhu) therein, produced from the square of the square of the fruit (phala) by means of the excellent square (suvarga).
One should bring [the thread] together by this very sequence at the dawn-line;
having relied upon the result of the desire, one should lead it to the result as stated in the authoritative texts. || 118 ||
Having brought all that under his control, whether by means of the present [time] or otherwise, he should perform the Śreṣisaṅkavalas and other rites pertaining to Agni. || 119 ||
Thus, it has been briefly explained; this is what is called "the self.
Having realized the self, one should then observe Māyā and the other principles in their proper sequence. (120)

Having subtracted the asterism of the householder’s birth, his own [natal] asterism, his [natal] lunar day, and his [natal] division (aṃśaka), as well as the eighth and the fourteenth, from the [current] asterism, one should commence the construction of the dwelling on an auspicious day.
One should examine that heap of grain, which is [measured] by its width and its layers, as well as its height; or else, one should observe the heap as it is endowed with both width and length.

The sun [bhānu] multiplied by the objects [vastu] and divided by the fires with qualities [saguṇavahni] using the threads [sūtra] is known as the "wealth" (dhana); this is determined by the arrangement of the remainder of the division. || 123 ||
In the case of Rāmaghna, the heart has eight yonis, and it increases again by eight;
or, when divided by twenty-seven, that result is remembered as Vasvayu. 124.
The remaining asterism is declared to be *dvayata*, and it is called *prasāda*.
Furthermore, the temple shall be described as being of three types according to the measurement of the *liṅga*. (125)
The Nāgara style is for the Nāgara [region], the Vesara for the Vesara, and the Drāvida for the Drāvida; thus the temple (prāsāda) is said to be of three kinds. 126.
It is of three kinds: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
The sāttvika is declared to be Nāgara, while the rājasa is Drāviḍa. || 127 ||
The *vesara* style is said to be *tāmasa*, and likewise [it is divided into] male, female, and neuter; construct the temple of the *liṅga* according to the measurement of the *nāgara* style.
Construct a temple and a pedestal for the lingas dedicated to Śiva;
by means of the threefold calculation (trairāśika), the bed of the linga is said to be the temple.
The sitting posture is said to be *pādabandha*, and the binding posture (*pratibandha*) shall be the seat (*āsana*).
From the lotus-binding (*padmabandha*), however, the reclining posture (*śayana*) is to be known; it too possesses various distinctions. (130)
The Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra are said to be the Prāsāda;
the Nāgara is declared for the twice-born (Brāhmaṇa), while the Drāvila is for the Kṣatriya. || 131 ||

The Vesara style is said to be for the Vaiśyas and Śūdras according to their distinct castes; furthermore, the Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara styles are each presided over by their respective deities. (132)
Īśa, Pitāmaha, and Viṣṇu are the presiding deities (adhidaivata) therein;
thus has the temple (prāsāda) been described, along with its various divisions such as the Sañcinda and others.

The accumulation, the non-accumulation, and the mantra that is the intermediate accumulation—this is declared to be the establishment of the accumulation, which is the accumulation consisting of the repetition of the accumulated. || 134 ||
The "accumulated" (*upasañcita*) is known as *krīḍābhra* and the "foot-binding" (*pādabandha*).
These three obstructions (*pratibandha*) are proclaimed; however, the practitioner of yoga [transcends] waking and dreaming. (135)

The lotus-band (padmabandha) is of three types; one should contemplate it on the side during sleep. The state of dreaming is a straight shadow; thus the characteristic of the temple is threefold. (136)
The empowerment of the ground is threefold, each distinguished individually; it is traditionally known as *pādabandha*, *prabandha*, and *kaṃprabandha*. (137)
The *pratibandha*, *nāgabandha*, and *siṃhabandha*—these are the three types;
as well as *padmabandha*, *puṣpabandha*, *puṣkala*, and *padmakesara*. (138)
The lotus-binding (padmabandha) shall be of three kinds, arising according to their respective functions;
the fourteen bases will now be described in their proper order. (139)
Masculine, feminine, and neuter— each possessing threefold divisions according to its name—
the house itself has thus attained [these states] through the sequence of the genders as previously described. (140)
It should be constructed according to the measurement of the *mānāṅgula*; this is said to be the external measurement.
It may be three cubits, five cubits, or nine cubits.
It is prescribed as being equal to one *bhūmi* and so forth, up to three *bhūmis*;
it is recorded in tradition as measuring from eleven to fifty cubits.
The measurement is thus prescribed for those ranging from twelve cubits up to a vimāna;
however, for smaller structures, the width is prescribed to be twice the height.
One and a quarter [hastas] less than one and a half is called the great [measurement];
for all small [objects], however, the hand-measure is double that [of the large ones]. 144.
Up to the height of the palace, one-eighth part is prescribed;
one part is the base (adhiṣṭhāna), and two parts are called the pillar (pāda). (145)
The base (prastāra) should consist of one part; the wall (dala) is said to be one [part];
the spire (śikhara) should consist of two parts, and one should fashion the pinnacle (stūpikā) with one [part]. || 146 ||
Now hear about the portion known as the "single level" (ekabhūmi); the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) and the arrangement of the plinth (jagatī) and so forth are prescribed therein. 147.
The height of the jagatī should be twenty-four parts;
the kumuda should consist of eight parts, and one should fashion the kampam with one part.
The *karṇa* (corner) should thus consist of three parts; the *kaṃpaka* (pendant) one part;
the *paṭṭikā* (fillet) is said to be three parts; and the *kuṃbhaka* (pitcher) one part. 149.
The binding of the feet, the pedestal, and the cutting should be done as appropriate;
the obstruction is the eighteenth, and the previous [measurement] is one-seventh. (150)
The *kumuda* is said to be six parts, while the *yuk* is joined as one part;
the triangular [portion] should be one part, and the *pratimukha* two parts.
That which constitutes one part of the *vāja* is called the *pratibandha*;
one should especially construct the door above the *pratistaṃbha* and the *pratirūrdhva*. || 152 ||
The lotus consists of nineteen parts and has six limbs;
the tremor is said to be one part, and the upper lotus likewise has six limbs. (153)
Above that, there is a circular [member] (*vṛtta*) consisting of three parts and a single *kaṃpa*;
it is said that the *paṭṭa* consists of two parts, and the *kaṃpa* is said to consist of one part. (154)
This is declared to be the *padmabandha* (lotus-binding), honored in all undertakings;
it should extend as far as the width of the temple, or exactly twenty-five [units]. (155)
Whether it be twenty-four or twenty-six [units], this extent of the root-base (mūlapāda) is declared to be a single part according to the sequence. 156.
Having divided the width into eight parts, the front part consists of seven shares;
this is declared to be the two front portions, and the height of the base (upāna) is now described.
It is said that half of that [measurement] is subtracted; this is celebrated as the *upāna*.
That which is the base of the *upāna* is the *nirgama*, consisting of two parts (*vyaṃśa*) in the world.
First, the *kumuda* (fillet) should emerge [from the base] to a height equal to the neck-base (*kaṇṭhapāda*).
The *kaṃpa* (molding) should be equal to the height [of the *kumuda*], and the great fillet (*mahāpaṭṭi*) should be two-thirds of that. || 159 ||
The width of the front foot is called its *daṇḍa*.
397) The altar (*vedī*) should be made with two *daṇḍas*, and the height of the altar is determined by nine parts. || 160 ||
It is said that the *bhāgāṅgula* consists of two parts; the band (*paṭṭikā*) should be two parts.
Or else, the foot-pot (*pādakuṃbha*) is here described as being circular;
its height should be made in six parts, and one part should be the support (*dhṛk*). || 162 ||

One should fashion a water-pot (*kumbha*) with four [parts]; one is said to be the neck (*kaṇṭha*). One should make the mouth (*āsya*) with one [part], and one should have a lotus (*padma*) made with one [part]. (163)
The *nīvrā* (roof-ridge) should be one half-part; the two *hīnaka*s should each be half of that half.
The width of the mouth (*āsya*) is said to be made with exactly one half-part.
The width of the two parts [of the base] should be equal to the height; the neck and the two bases are omitted.
In the middle, there should be a swelling (*vṛddhipāda*), and the two bases should be four times [the width]. (165)

The increase at the foot should be by the middle [measure], while the forgotten part is fourfold; the height of the staff is one-third [of the total], and its elevation is said to be one part. || 166 ||
One should have the *maṇḍikā* made as one part, and the *phalaka* according to its own proportion;
the width of the *vīrakāṇḍa* should be either [the same as] that or one-quarter of the width. 167.
Alternatively, the height of the pedestal (vedikā) may be one-fourth less than its width;
with five parts, it is the best, and with four parts, it is the middling. || 168 ||
The third is said to be equal; it is called the measurement of the *potikā*.
The height of the *potikā* is remembered as being one part, while the *uttarā* is [the same].
One-third of the Mahānāsa should be the height [of the pinnacle], which is half the height of the *śikhara*.
Having divided the total height into three parts, one part is for the [*kumbha*]. (170)
In the fifth part of the *pālika*, however, the width of the lotus is equal to the length of the yoke. || 171 ||
One-third of the height of the lotus is said to be the width of the pitcher (kumbha);
one-third of the height of the pitcher is the base (valagnaka) below the pitcher.
Above the pitcher, which constitutes one-third of the *valagna*, is the neck (*kandhara*).
The rim (*pāli*) is three times the size of the neck, and the *kuśmala* is one-third of that.
The height of the *sthūpikā* (finial) is said to be one-twenty-second part [of the total height];
the height of the lotus is one-sixteenth part, and its glossy portion is half of that part. (174)
Half of half a *padma* should be the height of the lower lip, and a portion of seven *ṛṣis* (twenty-one units) the accumulation of wealth (*dhanoccaya*).
One and a half *padmas* should be the upper lip, and a portion of six (*rasa*) the height of the neck. (175)
The *kaṃpantī* measures one and a half parts, the neck of the *lagna* is equal to Śiva (one part), and the height of the *kumu* is five and a half parts; thus is the *sthūpi* described.
In this very manner, one should then have the temple constructed;
a half-maṇḍapa is prescribed with a measurement equal to half that of the temple.
